stem: A 35-year-old man has developed an itchy rash over the last 4 weeks. Examination shows discrete excoriated papules over the elbows, buttocks and back. Apart from well-controlled asthma, he has no other medical history but has felt lethargic over the last few months. Which one of the following would be most likely to lead to the diagnosis?
explanation:
Tissue transglutaminase antibody
The clinical features are typical of dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) DH most commonly begins in early adulthood; vesicles are the primary lesions, although these are usually quickly excoriated, so may not be seen HLA associations (B8, DR3, DQ2 in 80–90% of cases) are similar to those for coeliac disease, which virtually always co-exists Skin biopsy reveals subepidermal blisters with neutrophil microabscesses in the dermal papillae On immunofluorescence, there is positive granular staining for IgA in the dermal papillae Coeliac disease is often asymptomatic, so the patient should be investigated for this, making tissue transglutaminase antibody (tTG) the best of the above options; jejunal biopsy should also be considered Treatment is with a gluten-free diet; control of the skin disease may also require dapsone or other sulfur drugs Dapsone may cause haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia, as well as liver pathology and polyneuropathy, so regular monitoring of liver enzymes, blood count and reticulocytes is necessary; it is also associated with drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS)

A detailed drug history
A detailed drug history is incorrect. The clinical features are not suggestive of a drug eruption so a medication history is unlikely to be helpful.

Autoimmune screen
Autoimmune screen is incorrect. An autoimmune screen (which may include antinuclear antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, extractable nuclear antigens and other tests) is useful in the context of vasculitis or suspected connective tissue disease, but this presentation does not suggest such diagnoses.

Skin scrapings
Skin scrapings is incorrect. Skin scrapings are performed for the diagnosis of fungal infections such as tinea corporis. These do not present with excoriated papules.

Trial of prednisolone
Trial of prednisolone is incorrect. A trial of oral prednisolone is sometimes used in dermatology when investigations have been non-diagnostic. DH does not usually respond at all, although this is not sufficiently specific to confirm the diagnosis. In the absence of an option to biopsy the skin, investigating for underlying coeliac disease is much more likely to be fruitful.

stem: A 64-year-old woman presents with lip and tongue swelling that began 6 h before and has steadily progressed. She reports one previous episode 3 weeks earlier, which was milder and resolved without treatment. She gives a history of angina and hypertension, both diagnosed 6 months ago. Her regular medication comprises aspirin, bendroflumethiazide, bisoprolol, perindopril and simvastatin. She took ibuprofen the day before for a headache. She was adopted and is unaware of her family history. Examination shows only marked swelling of the lips and tongue. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Reaction to perindopril
Angio-oedema is due to swelling in the deep dermis and subcutis It is most common on the face, but other sites may be affected There may be associated discomfort and tightness, but itching does not usually occur Angio-oedema commonly occurs with urticaria: recurrent attacks without an obvious trigger are much more likely to be spontaneous than due to allergy Angio-oedema in the absence of urticaria should prompt consideration of C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency or ACE-inhibitor-induced angio-oedema Although it would be appropriate to check the blood count and C4 level (perhaps progressing to C1- esterase inhibitor testing), the onset a few months after starting perindopril is highly suggestive of ACE inhibitor-induced angio-oedema

Acquired C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency
Acquired C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency is incorrect. Acquired C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency, which is most often associated with B-cell lymphoproliferative disorders, is a possibility. However, it is rare and the ACEinhibitor is a much more likely cause in this case.

Anaphylaxis
Anaphylaxis is incorrect. Angio-oedema alone is insufficient to diagnose anaphylaxis, which presents with some or all of urticaria, bronchospasm and hypotension in addition.

Hereditary angio-oedema
Hereditary angio-oedema is incorrect. The clinical picture is compatible with hereditary angio-oedema, but this usually presents in childhood or adolescence.

Idiopathic angio-oedema
Idiopathic angio-oedema is incorrect. Idiopathic angio-oedema is not impossible, but this can only be diagnosed in this case if attacks continue after stopping the ACE-inhibitor – the likely cause – and C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency is excluded.

stem: A 45-year-old man is admitted to hospital with a diagnosis of mycoplasma pneumonia. Which one of the following rashes is most closely associated with this type of pneumonia?
explanation:
Erythema multiforme
Erythema multiforme is a reactive eruption, which is charactised by target lesions (concentric rings with a least three hues per individual lesion); these tend to predominate at acral sites and mucosal involvement is common. It is typically associated with infection, most commonly herpes simplex virus. It can also follow mycoplasma infection. It has been associated with a variety of other viral infections, including human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) and hepatitis viruses. Occasionally, erythema multiforme occurs as a drug eruption. Culprit drugs include anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and penicillins.

Epidermolysis bullosa (EB)
EB is not associated with infection; most types are congenital, although there are acquired forms (EB acquisita) which mostly resemble bullous pemphigoid.

Acanthosis nigricans
Acanthosis nigricans is associated with diabetes mellitus. Not mycoplasma pneumoniae.

Pityriasis rosea
Pityriasis rosea is thought to be due to a virus. It begins with a ‘herald patch’, which is followed after a few days by a widespread truncal eruption of plaques with fine peripheral scaling. These are classically arranged in a 'Christmas tree' configuration. The rash is typically asymptomatic and resolves after a few weeks.

Urticaria
Acute urticaria can be a manifestation of type I hypersensitivity, but can also occur through non-allergic mechanisms. It can be triggered by infection, but there is no specific link with mycoplasma. She is fit and well otherwise. Examination shows a solitary, shallow ulcer of 3 cm diameter. The edges are heaped up. There is a family history of inflammatory bowel disease, although she reports no symptoms of this. Her last holiday was 6 months ago and was spent camping in North Africa.

stem: A 35-year-old White woman presents with a painless ulcer on the back of the hand. It started as a small spot 2 months before and has gradually enlarged. She is fit and well otherwise. Examination shows a solitary, shallow ulcer of 3 cm diameter. The edges are heaped up. There is a family history of inflammatory bowel disease, although she reports no symptoms of this. Her last holiday was 6 months ago and was spent camping in North Africa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Leishmaniasis
Leishmaniasis is caused the protozoan species Leishmania and is transmitted by female sandflies Sandflies are only 1.5–3 mm in length, and tend to feed at dawn and dusk Their small size allows them to pass through standard mosquito nets: measures to prevent bites and thereby Leishmania infection include covering up with clothing, insect repellents, and spraying of sleeping areas and clothing with permethrin Manifestations of Leishmania infection depend on the species and the host response Cutaneous leishmaniasis usually appears 2 weeks to 6 months after infection, but sometimes longer Lesions are typically painless and most will resolve spontaneously to leave atrophic scarring Treatment may be instituted to minimise complications such as scarring, superadded infection, and, in American leishmaniasis, the risk of later mucocutaneous disease Antimonials are usually preferred: sodium stibogluconate may be administered intralesionally, or by intramuscular or intravenous injection

Ecthyma gangrenosum
Ecthyma gangrenosum is incorrect. Ecthyma gangrenosum is a cutaneous infection usually due to Pseudomonas. It occurs in patients who are severely ill and immunocompromised. It presents with pustules, which evolve into necrotic ulcers and eschars.

Pyoderma gangrenosum
Pyoderma gangrenosum is incorrect. Pyoderma gangrenosum typically presents with a painful, rapidly enlarging ulcer on the leg. It is associated with various underlying conditions, including inflammatory bowel disease and myeloproliferative disease. The edges of the ulcer are classically violaceous and undermined, rather than heaped up.

Squamous cell carcinoma
Squamous cell carcinoma is incorrect. Squamous cell carcinoma is very unlikely to occur in such a young patient, although it could manifest as an ulcerated nodule on a sun-exposed site such as the hand.

Tularaemia
Tularaemia is incorrect. Tularaemia can present with a cutaneous ulcer, but affected individuals are usually markedly unwell. It has been reported from most European countries, as well as the USA, but doesn’t quite fit with the clinical picture seen here. LeishmaniasisFlashcards A 17-year-old girl with learning difficulties is admitted to hospital following an epileptic fit. The patient has a history of seizures since aged 12. The admitting doctor has documented hypopigmented macules on her abdomen and an acne-like eruption on her face. Examination of her fingers shows small periungual fibrous papules.

stem: A 55-year-old man with a background of alcohol-induced liver disease gives a history of a blistering rash on his hands after a holiday in Greece. Examination shows several bullae as well as scars from previous blisters. There are a few milia. He says that he developed a similar rash last year following a holiday in Majorca. Which one of the following investigations might best establish the diagnosis?
explanation:
Urinary uroporphyrins
The information in the scenario points to a diagnosis of porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT) Clues include photosensitivity, blistering resulting in scars and milia (tiny inclusion cysts), and the history of chronic liver disease; skin fragility is usually present and other features can include hypertrichosis and sclerodermatous changes PCT is due to a deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase, which leads to the accumulation of uroporphyrinogen III Diagnosis is made by demonstrating raised levels of urinary uroporphyrins Repeated venesection leads to prolonged clinical and biochemical remission Chloroquine promotes the urinary excretion of uroporphyrin, but must be used in very low doses in the context of chronic liver disease

Anti-epidermal antibodies
Anti-epidermal antibodies is incorrect. Testing for anti-epidermal antibodies is useful when an immunobullous disease is suspected.

Antinuclear antibody
Antinuclear antibody is incorrect. Antinuclear antibody should be checked as part of a photosensitivity screen; positivity seems to be more prevalent in those with PCT than the general population.

Monochromator phototesting
Monochromator phototesting is incorrect. Monochromator phototesting aims to identify the wavelengths of light to which patients are photosensitive. This can provide useful diagnostic information in many of the photodermatoses, but in this case, checking the urinary porphyrins is a more direct and accurate way to confirm the diagnosis.

Skin biopsy
Skin biopsy is incorrect. Although skin biopsy may show corroborating signs of PCT, the findings are usually not sufficiently specific to seal the diagnosis. The endocrinologist makes a diagnosis of necrobiosis lipoidica.

stem: A 52-year-old obese man presents to the GP with a rash on his inner upper thigh. It consists of an erythematous plaque with a scaling border. The central part of the plaque appears to have partially cleared. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Tinea cruris
Tinea cruris is a dermatophyte fungal infection of the groin or thigh. It is most common during the summer months and men are affected more frequently than women. As with most other dermatophyte infections (also referred to as tinea or ringworm), an annular appearance with peripheral scaling is characteristic; occasional pustules may be seen in the active edge. Diagnosis is confirmed on a skin scraping by the demonstration of fungal hyphae on microscopy or by culture of the causative organism; usually dermatophytes of the genus Trichophyton, Epidermophyton or Microsporum are responsible. Species are variably anthropophilic, zoophilic or geophilic, acquired from contact with infected humans, animals or soil, respectively. Treatment is with topical antifungals (e.g. terbinafine, miconazole) for localised disease or with oral antifungals (e.g. terbinafine, itraconazole) for more severe cases.

Candidiasis
Candidiasis is incorrect. Candidiasis commonly affects moist, flexural areas, causing erythematous plaques sometimes with satellite lesions; annularity is absent.

Intertrigo
Intertrigo is incorrect. Intertrigo (inflammation in a skin fold) tends to occur in obese individuals: common sites include the inframammary area, groins and beneath the abdominal pannus; it can involve a variety of bacteria and yeasts, and leads to moist, inflamed plaques.

Psoriasis
Psoriasis is incorrect. Flexural psoriasis affects the actual flexures, rather than the upper thigh. The appearance can look very similar to intertrigo. There is often a fissure in the skin crease itself. It is usually symmetrical and there is no annularity.

Seborrhoeic dermatitis
Seborrhoeic dermatitis is incorrect. Seborrhoeic dermatitis does cause redness and scaling, but is usually symmetrical. Annularity is not a feature. Typical sites include the scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, central chest and back, and genitals. Fungal InfectionsA pregnant woman started to notice lumps on her skin as well as freckles in her armpit. One of her relatives had similar problems.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the dermatology clinic with two well-demarcated bald areas on the scalp. She has a past history of autoimmune hypothyroidism, but a recent TSH measurement was within the normal range on thyroxine therapy. On examination the affected areas of scalp look normal, with no signs of inflammation or scarring. Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Alopecia areata
Alopecia areata typically causes single or multiple, discrete, often round areas of complete baldness. It most commonly occurs on the scalp, but can affect the face or any hair-bearing part of the body. It is a form of non-scarring alopecia and lost hair may therefore regrow. Signs of disease Exclamation-mark hairs – short, tapered hairs of a few millimetres in diameter are characteristic but not universally seen. There may be nail pitting. Autoimmune associations Alopecia areata is considered to be an autoimmune disease and may be seen in association with other diseases such as: Vitiligo Thyroid disease Pernicious anaemia Rheumatoid arthritis Diabetes. No specific antibody has been identified. Approximately one-third of patients have a positive family history, implying that a genetic component is involved. Prognosis The condition is very unpredictable. Many patients experience hair regrowth within 6–12 months – new hair is often fine and initially white; some find that new areas of alopecia appear as older ones regrow; others have a more progressive pattern. Some cases progress to complete loss of scalp hair (alopecia totalis) and occasionally complete loss of all hair (alopecia universalis). Treatment Alopecia areata is difficult to treat. Possible options include: Topical or intralesional steroids Topical minoxidil Contact allergen therapy Janus kinase inhibitors are a possible new avenue for treatment. Some patients will benefit from a hairpiece or wig, false eyelashes or eyebrow tattooing

Discoid lupus erythematosus
Discoid lupus erythematosus is incorrect. This is a form of scarring alopecia which causes well-defined erythematous plaques with scaling, atrophy and follicular plugging; these affect light-exposed areas of the body and are exacerbated by sunlight.

Fungal scalp infection
Fungal scalp infection is incorrect. This may give rise to well-defined areas of alopecia, but the scalp skin in these areas is not normal and complete baldness not typical: scaling and broken hairs are are usually seen; scarring is unusual unless there has been very florid or long-standing inflammation.

Telogen effluvium
Telogen effluvium is incorrect. This is a cause of transitory, generalised, diffuse hair loss over the scalp, which classically occurs a few months after high fever, stress, malnutrition, surgery or childbirth.

Trichotillomania
Trichotillomania is incorrect. This is the self-inflicted pulling out of hair. Short, broken hairs are seen, differentiating it from the typical complete baldness of areas of alopecia areata.

stem: You recommend barrier sun creams. Which other step is likely to be most successful in reducing the severity of his skin condition?
explanation:
Avoidance of alcohol
The acute history of a photosensitive bullous eruption that heals with milia formation is typical of porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT), which is known to be associated with alcohol consumption and exposure to certain drugs, including the combined oral contraceptive pill. Diseases associated with PCT include hepatitis C, HIV, haemochromatosis, SLE and hepatitis. Avoidance of sunshine and alcohol is important, as is venesection if there is iron overload. Treatment with chloroquine may also be required (helps increase the excretion of porphyrins in the urine).

Avoidance of smoking
Avoidance of smoking is incorrect. Smoking is not linked to the development of PCT. However, cigarette smoking has been linked to a variety of skin disorders such as premature skin ageing, poor wound healing, psoriasis, hidradenitis suppurativa and cutaneous lupus.

PUVA
PUVA is incorrect. PUVA is a type of ultraviolet light therapy (phototherapy) that is used in the treatment of a number of cutaneous conditions such as psoriasis, eczema and cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. Given the fact that PCT is a photosensitive rash, the patient should be told to avoid sunlight and to wear sun protection creams. Treating him with PUVA would lead to a deterioration of his symptoms and should therefore be avoided.

Retinoids
Retinoids is incorrect. Retinoids come in both topical and systemic forms and are commonly used to treat acne. In addition, systemic retinoids are used in psoriasis, hidradenitis suppurativa and pityriasis rubra pilaris but not in PCT.

Topical steroids
Topical steroids is incorrect. Topical corticosteroids are used to treat a wide range of cutaneous disorders such as eczema, psoriasis, bullous pemphigoid and lichen planus, but have no role to play in the management of PCT. Porphyria Cutanea TardaA 42-year-old man with a history of diabetes mellitus presents with a large lesion on his left shin that over time has become scarred and yellowish in the middle. On examination, you can see a 6cm lesion on the left shin. The centre of the lesion is waxy, yellow and atrophic, with prominent blood vessels and evidence of ulceration. The edges are red–brown in colour. He has bilateral peripheral neuropathy and doesn’t report the area as being particularly painful.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with an intensely itchy rash, particularly affecting her scalp, buttocks, elbows and knees. The lesions formed are either papules or blisters up to 1 cm across, and intense itching can predate the appearance of new lesions by a few hours. She has also suffered from diarrhoea, which has waxed and waned over the past few months. The GP suspects the rash may be dermatitis herpetiformis and arranges a skin biopsy. Which one of the following immunoglobulins is likely to be found on immunostaining of the skin sample?
explanation:
IgA
This patient has dermatitis herpetiformis, which is characterised by subepidermal blisters, inflammatory cells grouped in the dermal papillae and IgA deposits within the dermal papillae being revealed on immunostaining. There is an association with coeliac disease, which may also explain the presence of intermittent diarrhoea in this patient, and she should be screened with antibody testing for coeliac. A gluten-free diet may skin symptoms; dapsone is the pharmacological treatment of choice for dermatitis herpetiformis.

IgD
IgD is incorrect. IgA is likely to be found on immunostaining.

IgE
IgE is incorrect. IgA is likely to be found on immunostaining.

IgG
IgG is incorrect. IgA is likely to be found on immunostaining.

IgM
IgM is incorrect. IgA is likely to be found on immunostaining.

stem: Which one of the following is the most appropriate therapy for her?
explanation:
Gluten-free diet
The skin biopsy picture seen here and her history are very suspicious of dermatitis herpetiformis, the mainstay for management of which is the adherence to a gluten-free diet. In patients whose symptoms fail to resolve, dapsone is the treatment of choice, although sulphapyridine or topical corticosteroids may be an option for patients who are dapsone-intolerant. Tissue transglutaminase and anti-endomyseal antibody testing should be undertaken, as this patient may well have undiagnosed underlying coeliac disease.

Dairy-free diet
Dairy-free diet is incorrect. The only dietary modification for dermatitis herpetiformis (and coeliac) is a glutenfree diet.

Elemental diet
Elemental diet is incorrect. The only dietary modification for dermatitis herpetiformis (and coeliac) is a glutenfree diet.

Low-fat diet
Low-fat diet is incorrect. The only dietary modification for dermatitis herpetiformis (and coeliac) is a gluten-free diet.

Low-protein diet
Low-protein diet is incorrect. The only dietary modification for dermatitis herpetiformis (and coeliac) is a glutenfree diet.

stem: A 17-year-old boy comes to the dermatology clinic for review. He has severe acne vulgaris, which has resulted in facial scarring. He is being teased by his college friends which is causing him to avoid classes. On examination he is apyrexial, his BP is 122/72 mmHg, and pulse is 65 bpm and regular; he has severe acne over his face and neck; his BMI is 23 kg/m 2. He has completed a 6-month course of oral antibiotics with no significant improvement. Which one of the following is the next most appropriate choice?
explanation:
Isotretinoin
Isotretinoin is a vitamin A analogue that is useful in patients who do not respond to other systemic therapies for acne. Significant cautions exist with respect to therapy, particularly for use in women of childbearing age, as it is highly teratogenic. An association with mood disorders was identified through post-marketing surveillance; it is therefore important to establish baseline psychiatric history before commencing treatment, and warn patients to present for review if they have a significant change in their mood. Topical potent steroids should be avoided with respect to application on the face, and topical tetracycline is unlikely to be more effective than systemic antibiotics.

Coal tar
Coal tar is incorrect. Coal tar is typically reserved for psoriasis, not acne treatment.

PUVA
PUVA is incorrect. PUVA is typically reserved for psoriasis, not the treatment of acne.

Topical beclomethasone
Topical corticosteroids are not a conventional acne treatment and have no effect on the bacteria causing the acne. While they can the inflammatory appearance this is not the next most appropriate choice.

Topical tetracycline
Topical tetracycline is incorrect. Given the disappoint lack of positive results achieved from the course of antibiotics, the symptoms are too severe for topical antibiotics.

stem: A 32-year-old woman comes to the Emergency Department complaining of skin blistering and flaccid blisters in her mouth, which have worsened over the past few days. She has also suffered from coryzal symptoms, fevers and itching. Phenytoin therapy was started for recurrent seizures some 3 weeks earlier. On examination her temperature is 38.8°C and her blood pressure is 110/60 mmHg; there are a number of ulcers within her oropharynx and extensive flaccid blistering over her skin. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN)
TEN presents with symptoms similar to an upper respiratory tract infection, fever and a blistering rash. Phenytoin is recognised as a cause of TEN; other agents recognised to lead to the condition include sulphonamides, ampicillin, carbamazepine, valproate, allopurinol, corticosteroids, piroxicam and paroxetine. The phenytoin should be immediately discontinued, and she should be admitted to a unit with experience of managing extensive burns. Therapy is supportive, with management of fluid and electrolytes, infection and nutritional requirements. Mortality is up to 70%.

Bullous lichen planus
Bullous lichen planus is incorrect. Bullous lichen planus is not usually associated with systemic upset.

Pemphigoid
Pemphigoid is incorrect. Pemphigoid occurs in older patients, and rarely affects the mouth.

Pemphigus
Pemphigus is incorrect. As a result of the temporal relationship with drug commencement TEN is far more likely.

Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome
Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome is incorrect. Unlike toxic epidermal necrolysis, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome spares the mucous membranes. The disease presents with the widespread formation of fluidfilled blisters that are thin-walled and easily ruptured, and the patient can be positive for Nikolsky sign. Stevens-Johnson Syndrome and Toxic Epidermal NecrolysisA 17-year-old with a history of atopic eczema, managed with corticosteroid cream, presents to the Emergency Department with an extensive eruption of small pustules and vesicles; some of them are crusted over with yellow exudate. Apparently, they have increased significantly over the past 7–10 days, he feels systemically unwell with a fever and there is widespread lymphadenopathy. The pustules and vesicles have erupted in areas where he has previously suffered from eczema.

stem: A 62-year-old woman presented with a two week history of mouth and skin changes. On examination she had a small, thickened, velvety patch on the lower lip, and some similar hyperpigmented patches around the skin fold at the back of her neck. She was otherwise well. Which of the following can be associated with this condition?
explanation:
Endometrial carcinoma
This patient has acanthosis nigricans; dry, dark patches of skin that normally appear in body folds such as the armpits or groin. They are associated with many conditions including insulin resistance, acromegaly, Cushing’s syndrome and malignancy (typically gastric adenocarcinoma, but also endometrial carcinoma and many others). Classically acanthosis nigricans associated with malignancy appears abruptly, as in this case, and it can precede the diagnosis of malignancy.

Addison’s disease
Addison’s disease is incorrect. This patient’s skin changes are consistent with acanthosis nigricans; although hyperpigmentation is seen in Addison’s disease, it is not velvety or thickened. Acanthosis nigricans is not specifically associated with Addison’s disease.

HIV infection
HIV infection is incorrect. This patient has acanthosis nigricans, which is not particularly associated with HIV. It is associated with insulin resistance and, therefore, may be seen after treatment with some anti-retrovirals.

Hypertension
Hypertension is incorrect. This patient has acanthosis nigricans, which is associated with insulin resistance. Therefore, a patient with acanthosis nigricans may have hypertension as part of the metabolic syndrome, but there is no specific association between the two.

Polymyositis
Polymyositis is incorrect. This patient has acanthosis nigricans; uncommonly this can be associated with dermatomyositis, but not polymyositis. Other associations of acanthosis nigricans include insulin resistance and malignancy such as endometrial carcinoma.

stem: A 62-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department with a severe erythematous rash on sun-exposed areas. He tells you that because it was the first sunny day of the year he had decided to work out in the garden. He takes a number of medications for diabetes and ischaemic heart disease, including ramipril, amlodipine, indapamide, amiodarone, aspirin and atorvastatin. Which of the following medications is the most likely cause of his rash?
explanation:
Amiodarone
It is very important to warn patients who are taking amiodarone about the risks of sun exposure. According to the prescribing information: 'Patients should be instructed to avoid exposure to sun and to use protective measures during therapy as patients taking amiodarone tablets can become unduly sensitive to sunlight, which may persist after several months of discontinuation of amiodarone tablets. In most cases symptoms are limited to tingling, burning and erythema of sun-exposed skin but severe phototoxic reactions with blistering may be seen.' Other significant risks of amiodarone therapy include hepatic and pulmonary fibrosis, and the development of thyroid disorders.

Amlodipine
Amlodipine is only very rarely associated with hypersensitivity to sunlight. A number of skin reactions are uncommonly seen. These include alopecia, purpura, skin discoloration, hyperhidrosis, pruritus, rash, exanthema and urticaria.

Aspirin
Photosensitivity is not usually seen in patients taking aspirin. Urticaria is uncommonly seen. Other adverse effects of therapy are thankfully rare; they include Stevens–Johnson syndrome, Lyell syndrome, purpura, erythema nodosum and erythema multiforme.

Atorvastatin
Atorvastatin is not associated with photosensitivity. Adverse effects on the skin are similar to those of amlodipine, with urticaria, skin rash, pruritus, alopecia uncommonly seen. More significant adverse effects of atorvastatin therapy are thankfully rare; these include angioneurotic oedema, dermatitis bullous including erythema multiforme, Stevens–Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis.

Ramipril
Maculopapular rashes are commonly seen in patients who take ramipril. In contrast, photsensitivity is very rarely seen and is reported in less than 1 in 10 000 patients. Of particular concern with angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors is angioedema which, although uncommonly seen, carries potentially life-threatening consequences.

stem: A 19-year-old woman who has not previously engaged with medical services is reviewed on the Medical Ward following admission with an upper gastrointestinal (GI) haemorrhage. It appears following endoscopy that she had a bleed from a small vessel within the stomach. General examination reveals ‘plucked chicken skin’ around her neck, and loose folds of skin under both axillae. You note angioid streaks on retinal examination. Which of the following is the best way to confirm the underlying diagnosis here?
explanation:
Skin biopsy
Skin biopsy is the optimal way to confirm the diagnosis of pseudoxanthoma. In pseudoxanthoma, elastic fibres of the dermis are short and fragmented. The abnormal fibres are basophilic and can be seen on haemotoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained histology sections. Rarely, the abnormal fibres can elicit granuloma formation. A special stain for pseudoxanthoma, Van Kossa stain, also exists, which can show calcium deposits.

Alkaline phosphatase
Although angioid streaks are seen in patients with Paget’s disease, the clinical scenario here does not fit with Paget’s, hence alkaline phosphatase is not of value. The skin appearances seen here and the GI haemorrhage fit with a diagnosis of pseudoxanthoma elasticum. Calcium and phosphate are occasionally elevated in patients with pseudoxanthoma, but are usually normal, especially early in the disease.

Ankle brachial pressure index
Ankle brachial pressure index is useful to confirm clinically significant peripheral vascular disease; it does not reveal the underlying cause. Intermittent claudication is often the first sign of cardiovascular disease in patients with pseudoxanthoma and is seen in 30% of patients with the disease. Coronary artery disease and mitral valve prolapse are also seen.

Coronary angiography
Accelerated coronary artery disease is seen in patients with pseudoxanthoma elasticum. The process of arterial calcification is further accelerated by concomitant tobacco use. Although coronary angiography may confirm the presence of disease, it will not confirm the underlying cause.

Fibrillin 1 (FBN1) gene testing
FBN1 gene testing is used to diagnose patients with Marfan syndrome. It does not have a role in the diagnosis of pseudoxanthoma, the problem here. Pseudoxanthoma elasticum is caused by mutations in the ABCC6 gene on chromosome 16, which leads to fragmentation and mineralisation of elastic fibres in the skin.

stem: A 48-year-old man comes to the clinic for review. He complains of gradually worsening skin changes affecting his cheeks, forehead and nose. On examination, there is erythema and there are telangiectasias over the forehead and cheeks. The nose appears enlarged and reddened, and you note particularly prominent sebaceous glands. Which of the following may this patient’s condition?
explanation:
Avoidance of alcohol
This patient has rosacea, with the typical erythematous changes affecting both cheeks and the forehead with telangiectasia. Rosacea often goes hand in hand with rhinophyma, with enlarged sebaceous glands around the nose. In patients with rosacea, avoidance of activities which can increase facial flushing and blood supply to the skin, including reducing alcohol consumption, is important in managing the condition. A Cochrane meta-analysis has reviewed available treatments for rosacea and has concluded that high-quality evidence exists to support the effectiveness of topical azelaic acid, topical ivermectin, brimonidine, doxycycline and isotretinoin for rosacea. Moderate-quality evidence is available for topical metronidazole and oral tetracycline. There is low-quality evidence to support the use of low-dose minocycline, laser and intense pulsed light therapy and ciclosporin ophthalmic emulsion for ocular rosacea.

Benzoyl peroxide
Benzoyl peroxide is not effective in treating rosacea. It is effective in treating mild-to-moderate acne, where it has been shown to skin appearance.

Caffeine consumption
Caffeine consumption can increase facial flushing and is therefore an activity that is not recommended in patients with rosacea. Even spicy food consumption may exacerbate erythema and lead to increased prominence of telangiectasias. Drugs which lead to vasodilatation and consequently drive increased blood supply to the skin should also be avoided if possible.

Sun exposure
Sun exposure can worsen rosacea and should be avoided if possible. Use of a potent sun block of at least factor 50 is recommended for patients with the disease.

Topical steroids
Topical steroids can worsen the skin appearance of rosacea, and there is no evidence that they have any positive effect on managing the condition. Topical azelaic acid, topical ivermectin and topical metronidazole have all shown positive impact on the symptoms of rosacea.

stem: A 25-year-old man presents with a papular rash over his lower abdomen. He says he noticed the smooth flesh coloured rash appearing a few weeks earlier. On examination, there are crops of firm, smooth umbilicated papules around 2–5 mm in diameter over the lower abdomen. Which of the following is the most effective intervention for his rash?
explanation:
Cryotherapy
Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen was found to be the most effective intervention in a Cochrane meta-analysis for patients with molluscum contagiosum, the underlying cause of this patient’s rash. Podophyllotoxin has also demonstrated efficacy in some studies, although it does result in a local inflammatory reaction which limits its use in some patients. Many patients elect not to have intervention for molluscum, with the rash resolving spontaneously over the course of up to 18 months.

Benzoyl peroxide
Although benzoyl peroxide is effective in treatment of mild acne, a Cochrane review suggests it is ineffective in treating molluscum contagiosum, the most likely diagnosis here. Many patients do not require treatment for molluscum, and the rash resolves spontaneously over the course of 18 months. Patients should be advised to avoid scratching because it increases the risk of spread and secondary infection.

Imiquimod
Imiquimod cream has not shown any convincing benefit in patients with normal immune function who have molluscum contagiosum. In patients who are immunocompromised, such as those with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), it may enhance the resolution of lesions.

Potassium hydroxide
Like a number of other therapies, topical potassium hydroxide is not effective in the treatment of molluscum contagiosum, either at the 5 or 10% concentration. It is available for sale over the counter, but most prescribing groups direct against its use because of the negative Cochrane meta-analysis.

Topical corticosteroids
Topical corticosteroids are only an option to treat local inflammation surrounding the papules. They do not enhance or speed up resolution of the rash. A low dose of topical hydrocortisone is usually prescribed.

stem: A 54-year-old man presents to his GP with a scaly rash on his scalp and the extensor aspects of his knees and elbows. Psoriasis is diagnosed. Which HLA subtype is most closely associated with chronic plaque psoriasis?
explanation:
HLA-CW6
In line with its familial tendency, psoriasis has now been linked with a variety of heritable factors, but most notably HLA-CW6. Many such factors appear to confer susceptibility to the disease, and it is thought that particular combinations as well as a trigger are important in precipitating it.

HLA-B27
HLA-B27, is incorrect, although this is associated with psoriatic arthritis and pustular psoriasis.

HLA-DR2
HLA-DR2, is incorrect as this is associated with multiple sclerosis, narcolepsy, systemic lupus erythematosus and other conditions, but not psoriasis.

HLA-DR3
HLA-DR3, is incorrect as this is particularly associated with Type I diabetes mellitus.

HLA-DR4
HLA-DR4, is incorrect as this is associated with Type I diabetes mellitus, as well as rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, autoimmune hepatitis and others.

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with a 6-week history of an itchy rash, which appeared on the medial and anterior aspects of the thigh and trunk. It consisted of numerous small fluid-filled vesicles, and a number of larger lesions measuring 2-3 cm filled with serous fluid. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Bullous pemphigoid
This is an older patient with intact blisters on the limbs, suggestive of bullous pemphigoid. This is an autoimmune blistering disorder characterised by the presence of autoantibodies to hemidesmosome proteins, which attach the basal keratinocytes to the basement membrane and dermis. A split occurs between the epidermis and dermis so that blisters are tense and do not spontaneously rupture; blisters are usually symmetrical and involve trunk and limbs, but the mouth is involved in 10% of cases.

Bullous impetigo
Bullous impetigo is incorrect. Impetigo is a very superficial infection of the stratum corneum caused by Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus spp. It is most common in children and is characterised by a golden crusted eruption on a background of erythema. Occasionally the organism produces a toxin, which binds to superficial keratinocyte adhesion molecules, causing an intraepidermal superficial blister. Bullous impetigo occurs most often in children as a result of rapidly spreading infection

Dermatitis herpetiformis
Dermatitis herpetiformis is incorrect. Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is intensely pruritic and typically causes tiny vesicles on the extensor aspects of the elbows, knees and buttocks. All patients have some degree of gluten intolerance, and coeliac disease is common. Gluten exclusion leads to remission of DH and dapsone may be used to control active disease.

Scabies
Scabies is incorrect. Scabies occurs as itchy excoriated papules on the finger webs, elbows, ankles, axillae and genitalia, and only rarely causes blistering. Burrows of the scabies mite are seen, and patchy excoriated fissured eczema occurs. Adult men may develop itchy penile nodules, and infants may develop nodules on the palms or soles. Norwegian (crusted) scabies causes a hyperkeratotic reaction of the hands and occurs in debilitated, immunosuppressed or institutionalised individuals.

Vesicular insect-bite eruption
Vesicular insect-bite eruption is incorrect. Insect bites are often linear or grouped in distribution, and are usually short-lived. Tense blisters may occasionally occur on a background of an urticarial-like wheal at the site of the bites.

stem: A 45-year-old man known to be alcoholic presents to the clinic with severe dermatitis affecting his face and legs predominantly. He also admits to chronic diarrhoea, and increasing lethargy over the past few weeks. On examination he has extensive dermatitis with some evidence of ulceration and crusting, particularly where he has scratched himself. His nails show evidence of nail bed infections and he has hair loss. Which deficiency is the most likely cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Zinc
Zinc deficiency is common in association with alcoholism, and it is associated with a number of features including: Anorexia, lethargy, diarrhoea Growth retardation, delayed sexual maturation, hypogonadism and hypospermia Alopecia, dermatitis, paronychia Intellectual disability, impaired nerve conduction and nerve damage Hepatomegaly Immune disorders and susceptibility to infections Magnesium deficiency is associated with muscle weakness and fatigue, ascorbic acid deficiency is associated with scurvy, and hypophosphataemia occurs in response to re-feeding in patients with a history of alcoholism. Niacin deficiency is also associated with dermatitis, although psychosensory, psychomotor, and emotional disorders are also seen.

Ascorbic acid
Ascorbic acid is incorrect. This presents with symptoms of scurvy rather than the dermatitis picture seen here.

Magnesium
Magnesium is incorrect. Magnesium deficiency is primarily associated with muscle weakness and fatigue, and is associated with PTH resistance leading to concomitant hypocalcaemia.

Niacin
Niacin is incorrect. Although niacin deficiency is also associated with dermatitis, at least some degree of emotional disorder, (depression), and / or dementia would be expected.

Phosphate
Phosphate is incorrect. Hypophosphataemia occurs as a response to re-feeding in patients with alcoholism or chronic malnutrition and is associated with muscle weakness.

stem: A 62-year-old man who has recently been diagnosed with bronchial carcinoma comes to the Dermatology Clinic for review. Over the past few weeks he has begun to suffer from a number of painful mouth ulcers and a generalised blistering, itchy skin rash. On examination, his BP is 132/82 mmHg, pulse is 82/min and regular and there are decreased breath sounds on the left hand side consistent with the known carcinoma. In addition, examination reveals widespread tense blisters in various skin and mucosal sites. Which of the following antibodies is most likely to be found?
explanation:
Anti-envoplakin
A number of antibodies are demonstrated in paraneoplastic pemphigus; these include envoplakin, periplakin, bullous pemphigoid antigen I, desmoplakin, desmoplakin II, plectin and alpha2-macroglobulin-like-1. They can also exhibit antibodies to antigens associated with pemphigus vulgaris (desmoglein 3) and pemphigus foliaceus (desmoglein 1).

cANCA
cANCA is incorrect. This man has cancer-associated pemphigus, a recognised paraneoplastic syndrome. cANCA is associated with the development of granulomatosis with polyangiitis but is not associated with the development of bullous diseases.

Anti-Hu
Anti-Hu is incorrect. Anti-Hu antibodies are associated with the development pf paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, but not paraneoplastic pemphigus.

Anti-Ro
Anti-Ro is incorrect. Anti-Ro antibodies are associated with the development of SLE. They are also associated with the development of neonatal heart block when present during pregnancy.

Anti-tissue transglutamase
Anti-tissue transglutamase is incorrect. Anti-tissue transglutamase antibodies are associated with coeliac disease but not with paraneoplastic pemphigus.

stem: A 22-year-old woman with a history of three previous paracetamol overdoses over the past 2 years comes to the Emergency Department. She is suffering from a rash which apparently appeared overnight. On examination, there is linear scarring with surrounding erythema on the flexural surfaces of both arms and behind both knees. Routine bloods including inflammatory markers are all unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Dermatitis artefacta
A history of deliberate self-harm and a linear rash which has appeared ‘overnight’ are highly suggestive of dermatitis artefacta. Management is usually shared between dermatology and psychiatry services. Management is difficult, as many patients react poorly when challenged about how their rash /skin changes occurred.

Flexural eczema
Flexural eczema is incorrect. This is a chronic condition that does not typically appear overnight. Even though flexural involvement is typical for this condition, the distribution does not follow a linear pattern.

Morphea
Morphea is incorrect. This is thought to be limited form of scleroderma that consists of localised areas of thickened skin. The distribution is not linear and the course of the condition is chronic.

Psoriasis
Psoriasis is incorrect. This is another chronic condition that typically affects extensor surfaces, causing a scaly and thickened rash. The clinical picture does not fit with the acute, flexural and linear pattern described above.

Pityriasis rosea
Pityriasis rosea is incorrect. This is a rash that occurs following a viral infection. It is characterised by the presence of a large, scaly, oval patch, known as the herald patch, followed by similar, smaller oval red patches that are located mainly on the chest and back. Pityriasis rosea plaques usually follow the relaxed skin tension lines on both sides of the upper trunk, and have been described as looking like a fir tree.

stem: A 55-year-old woman known to suffer from primary biliary cirrhosis complains of a rash over her wrists and ankles. She has recently seen her gastroenterologist who has told her to continue cholestyramine, which she has been taking for 3 years. Examination shows purplish, polygonal, flat-topped papules on her wrists and ankles. She also has a fine, white, lacy network in her mouth. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Lichen planus
Classical lichen planus is characterised by an itchy, violaceous, polygonal, flat-topped rash most commonly developing over the wrists and ankles. A pale, lacy network develops and is often found in the mouth, although this may be asymptomatic. The presence of Wickham’s striae – a fine, white lacy pattern over the papules – is characteristic. The Koebner phenomenon is typically seen in lichen planus (whereby the rash ‘colonises’ sites of trauma a few days later). It has been associated with liver disease including hepatitis C, primary biliary cirrhosis and chronic active hepatitis. It usually resolves in 6–18 months. Lichen planus often responds to potent or very potent topical steroid, but some patients will require oral prednisolone.

Candidiasis
Candidiasis is incorrect. Candidiasis is common in the mouth, but gives rise to white plaques (or a glazed erythematous appearance), rather than a lacy network. Although it may affect other sites, such as the genitals and skin flexures, it does not lead to a violaceous, papular eruption.

Drug reaction
Drug reaction is incorrect. Most types of drug reaction are more widespread than in this case. They typically occur relatively soon (1–8 weeks) after initiation of a drug. Lichenoid drug eruptions can begin later than this, but tend to be widespread. They often lack some of the characteristic features of lichen planus described in this case.

Pityriasis rosea
Pityriasis rosea is incorrect. Pityriasis rosea typically begins with a herald patch (a solitary red plaque), which is followed a few days later by a widespread truncal rash comprising superficial plaques with peripheral scaling, in a ‘Christmas tree’ configuration. It is self-limiting, usually resolving after approximately 6 weeks and no treatment is required.

Scabies
Scabies is incorrect. Scabies presents with intense pruritus and excoriation. Burrows should be sought. Typically affected sites include the hands and wrists, around the nipples and the genital area. Penile papules are a characteristic finding. Treatment is usually with topical permethrin (two applications a week apart), and is required for the patient and their close contacts. Pruritus may continue for weeks after successful eradication. Lichen Planus A 25-year-old pregnant woman complains of painful lumps on her shins for the last 2 weeks. She is 32 weeks’ pregnant and suffers from asthma, which is well controlled with inhalers. Examination shows tender red nodules over her shins.

stem: A 25-year-old pregnant woman complains of painful lumps on her shins for the last 2 weeks. She is 32 weeks’ pregnant and suffers from asthma, which is well controlled with inhalers. Examination shows tender red nodules over her shins. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Erythema nodosum
Erythema nodosum is an acute panniculitis (inflammation in the fat) that produces tender nodules or plaques on the shins and occasionally elsewhere. Lesions are usually well circumscribed. The overlying skin is erythematous but otherwise normal, with no scaling. Firm induration is typical and the lesions may be exquisitely tender. It may be idiopathic, but is associated with: Sarcoidosis Inflammatory bowel disease Streptococcal infections Tuberculosis Treatment with sulfonamides or the oral contraceptive pill Pregnancy Treatment is usually with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs

Cellulitis
Cellulitis is incorrect. Cellulitis presents with confluent erythema and swelling. Although it is most common on the leg, it is almost always unilateral, does not lead to discrete nodules and pain or tenderness are not typically severe.

Drug eruption
Drug eruption is incorrect. Drug eruptions can present in many different ways, most commonly with a widespread exanthem (a morbilliform or maculopapular eruption). Inhaled drugs for asthma are exceptionally unlikely to lead to drug eruptions. Although erythema nodosum can be precipitated by certain drugs, this rather than drug eruption is clearly the best answer.

Erythema multiforme
Erythema multiforme is incorrect. Erythema multiforme presents with target lesions mostly at acral sites. It commonly affects the oral mucosa. It is a reactive condition and is most closely associated with herpes simplex virus infection.

Granuloma annulare
Granuloma annulare is incorrect. Granuloma annulare gives rise to annular plaques (annular means ring-like, such that the centre of the lesion is relatively clear and the border relatively pronounced). Scaling is not seen. It is usually asymptomatic. It is more commonly seen in patients with diabetes.

stem: A 55-year-old man complains of nausea, loss of appetite and dyspepsia after meals for the last 2 weeks. He is a smoker and has a past history of pernicious anaemia. He is pale, cachexic and tender at the epigastrium. His skin is velvety and hyperpigmented at the neck and axillary folds. What is the correct diagnosis for his skin condition?
explanation:
Acanthosis nigricans
Acanthosis nigricans is characterised by velvety thickening and pigmentation of the flexures, notably on the neck and axillae, but sometimes elsewhere. It is divided into benign and malignant forms depending on the underlying cause; benign is sometimes referred to as pseudoacanthosis nigricans and malignant as true acanthosis nigricans. Benign acanthosis nigricans is usually associated with insulin resistance and the metabolic syndrome, such as with type II diabetes, obesity or polycystic ovarian syndrome. Malignant acanthosis nigricans is particularly associated with gastric cancer, as is suggested in this scenario.

Lentigines
Lentigines is incorrect. Lentigines are types of freckles which are usually sun-induced.

Melasma
Melasma is incorrect. Melasma (also known as chloasma) gives rise to facial hyperpigmentation. It is exacerbated by sunlight and oestrogens.

Pyoderma gangrenosum
Pyoderma gangrenosum is incorrect. Pyoderma gangrenosum gives rise to ulcers; it can occur in association with a variety of conditions including inflammatory bowel disease, myeloproliferative disease and rheumatoid disease.

Tylosis
Tylosis is incorrect. Tylosis is a type of palmoplantar keratoderma, which can be associated with oesophageal carcinoma.

stem: A 23-year-old woman has acne vulgaris with scarring. She has only used over-the-counter wash products to date. She is 20 weeks’ pregnant. Which of the following treatment plans is most appropriate?
options: Benzoyl peroxide and clindamycin gel for 3–6 months
Moderate potency topical steroid in 1-week bursts
Retinoid cream until the end of the pregnancy
explanation:
Benzoyl peroxide and clindamycin gel for 3–6 months
The combination of benzoyl peroxide and topical clindamycin is commonly used to treat acne; there is no evidence that either constituent leads to adverse effects in pregnancy. Acne vulgaris is a chronic disorder of the pilosebaceous unit. It most commonly affects teenagers, but not infrequently occurs in older adults. Key pathophysiological mechanisms include an increase in sebum production, proliferation of Propionibacterium acnes, a commensal bacterium that resides in the hair follicle, and comedone formation (blockage of the pilosebaceous duct); these all contribute to inflammation. Clinical features of acne include papules, pustules, nodules, and open and closed comedones. Treatments target different aspects of the pathogenesis, but treating acne in pregnancy is difficult as most options are teratogenic.

Moderate potency topical steroid in 1-week bursts
Moderate potency topical steroid in 1-week bursts is incorrect. Topical steroids are not an appropriate treatment for acne, whether or not the patient is pregnant. Indeed, more potent steroids can precipitate acne.

Oral doxycycline for 3–6 months
Oral doxycycline for 3–6 months is incorrect. Oral doxycycline for 3–6 months would be reasonable if the patient was not pregnant; however, tetracycline drugs are associated with foetal bone and tooth abnormalities so are contra-indicated in pregnancy.

Oral isotretinoin for 3 months
Oral isotretinoin for 3 months is incorrect. Oral isotretinoin is the most effective treatment for acne, but is highly teratogenic. Women of child-bearing potential who are to receive the drug are usually enrolled in a pregnancy prevention programme.

Retinoid cream until the end of the pregnancy
Retinoid cream until the end of the pregnancy is incorrect. As oral retinoids are such potent teratogens and systemic absorption of topical retinoids is potentially possible, the latter are also contra-indicated in pregnancy.

stem: A 59-year-old man develops a rash, comprising large erythematous, scaly plaques at multiple sites. He has a history of hypertension, angina, rectal cancer and knee pain diagnosed as osteoarthritis. Which one of the following is true regarding psoriasis?
options: It affects 4–8% of the world population
It is an independent risk factor for cardiovascular disease
It usually improves after infection with HIV
Psoriatic arthropathy occurs in over 70% of people with psoriasis
explanation:
It is an independent risk factor for cardiovascular disease
Psoriasis is a very common dermatosis, which presents with well-defined erythematous, scaly plaques of varying sizes. It has a predilection for extensor surfaces and also commonly affects the scalp. It has been shown in various studies to be associated with obesity, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia, type II diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and specifically cardiovascular disease including myocardial infarction.

It affects 4–8% of the world population
It affects 4–8% of the world population is incorrect. Psoriasis affects 2–3% of the population.

It suggests underlying abdominal malignancy
It suggests underlying abdominal malignancy is incorrect. Psoriasis has been variably associated with an increased risk of certain malignancies, but it appears that the consequences of its immunosuppressive treatment are more relevant than the disease itself.

It usually improves after infection with HIV
It usually improves after infection with HIV is incorrect. Psoriasis tends to deteriorate in association with HIV infection.

Psoriatic arthropathy occurs in over 70% of people with psoriasis
Psoriatic arthropathy occurs in over 70% of people with psoriasis is incorrect. Estimates of the prevalence of psoriatic arthritis in patients with psoriasis vary widely from around 6 to 42%.

stem: A 32-year-old man presents with painful mouth sores, a painful red eye and polyarthralgia. Ulcers on a yellow base with erythematous edges are seen in the buccal mucosa. He gives a history of recurrent painful genital ulcers in the past few months which have now healed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Behçet syndrome
Behçet syndrome is a multisystem disorder characterised by recurrent orogenital ulceration, uveitis and arthritis, and is more common in Turkish and Chinese populations. It is an autoimmune disease associated with HLA-B12, -B51 and -B5. Features may include: Cutaneous: erythema nodosum, acneiform lesions, pathergy (abnormal response to tissue injury, eg skin ulceration following trauma or venepuncture) Gastrointestinal: abdominal pain and diarrhoea Neurological: headache, confusion, aseptic meningitis, coma, cranial nerve palsies, seizures, papilloedema Vascular: large vessel disease can lead to venous thrombosis, and arterial vasculitis and aneurysms. Diagnosis and treatment There is no specific diagnostic test; blood tests tend to be unhelpful as there is no acute-phase response; negative autoantibodies may help to exclude other diagnoses such as SLE. Treatment options include oral steroids and azathioprine.

Crohn’s disease
Crohn’s disease is incorrect. Crohn’s disease may present with similar oral aphthous ulceration, but the other features in combination are much more suggestive of Behçet syndrome.

Reactive arthritis
Reactive arthritis is incorrect. Reactive arthritis usually follows a sexually transmitted infection (especially chlamydia) or gastroenteritis; as well as arthritis, there may be urethritis and conjunctivitis. The recurrent nature of the ulceration and the relative chronicity of symptoms over several months fit better with Behçet syndrome.

Syphilis
Syphilis is incorrect. Primary syphilis may present with orogenital ulceration, although classically such lesions are painless. Although there may be associated symptoms in syphilis, the recurrent nature of the ulcers makes this diagnosis less likely.

Systemic lupus erythematosus
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is incorrect. Oral ulcers and arthralgia are often seen in SLE, and a variety of ocular complications can occur, including anterior uveitis. However, genital ulceration is very unusual. Although the symptoms described in the scenario demand that SLE be excluded, the features are most in keeping with Behçet syndrome. Behçet.

stem: A 55-year-old woman had been gardening on a warm spring day. In the evening she noticed erythema and blistering over the dorsum of her hands, face and neck. She has a background of Type II diabetes, angina and rosacea. Which of the following drugs is most likely to have induced photosensitivity?
explanation:
Doxycycline
A wide variety of drugs can cause photosensitivity (i.e. burning after an unusually short exposure to ultraviolet (UV) light). Doxycycline is a well-recognised culprit and other tetracyclines can also be involved. Other photosensitising agents include: NSAIDs Retinoids Diuretics (thiazide and loop) Other cardiovascular drugs (eg amiodarone, diltiazem, enalapril, quinidine) Sulfonylurea drugs Phenothiazines. Treatment includes ideally stopping the causative agent and good sun protection measures.

Aspirin
Aspirin is incorrect. Aspirin has no association with photosensitivity.

Bisoprolol
Bisoprolol is incorrect. Bisoprolol has no association with photosensitivity.

Isosorbide mononitrate
Isosorbide mononitrate is incorrect. Isosorbide mononitrate has no association with photosensitivity.

Metformin
Metformin is incorrect. There is one report of three cases of photosensitivity induced by metformin, but there is certainly no strong link.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with mouth ulceration, and target lesions on the palms and soles. Which one of the following disorders is most commonly associated with erythema multiforme?
explanation:
Herpes simplex infection
Erythema multiforme is a reactive eruption, which is charactised by target lesions (concentric rings with a least three hues per individual lesion); these tend to predominate at acral sites and mucosal involvement is common. It is typically associated with infection, most commonly herpes simplex virus; it can also follow mycoplasma infection; it has been associated with a variety of other viral infections including HIV and hepatitis viruses. Occasionally, erythema multiforme occurs as a drug eruption: culprit drugs include anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and penicillins.

Coeliac disease
Coeliac disease is incorrect. Coeliac disease is closely associated with dermatitis herpetiformis, but not EM.

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis is incorrect. Rheumatoid disease is not associated with EM.

Sarcoidosis
Sarcoidosis is incorrect. EM can occur in sarcoidosis, but the association is rare. A diverse spectrum of skin changes can arise in sarcoidosis.

Tuberculosis infection
Tuberculosis infection is incorrect. EM has been reported occasionally in the context of tuberculosis, but generally linked to its drug treatment rather than the infection itself.

stem: A 44-year-old man presents complaining of vague joint pains for over 2 months. He mentions that he had a circular red rash on his leg a few weeks before, which settled without treatment. According to his partner, he has suffered two episodes of unresponsiveness within the last 3 weeks, from which he recovered spontaneously. He is a salesman in a sports shop and had been to the USA 12 months ago with friends on a 3month long camping holiday. He is a non-smoker and does not drink alcohol. Which one of the following tests is most likely to establish the diagnosis?
explanation:
Serology for infection
This patient has Lyme disease, which is caused by a spirochaete, Borrelia burgdorferi This is transmitted by the bite of an ixodid tick Its early cutaneous manifestation is called ‘erythema chronicum migrans’, a slowly spreading annular, erythematous macule or plaque around the site of the bite Neurological or cardiac problems such as arrhythmias, heart block, etc may develop Diagnosis is made by detecting the antibody to B. burgdorferi in serum and cerebrospinal fluid Lyme disease is usually successfully treated by a 2-4 week course of doxycycline or amoxicillin.

Autoimmune screen
Autoimmune screen is incorrect. Checking autoantibodies including antinuclear antibody would be reasonable in a patient with multisystem symptoms including rash and arthralgia, but is not likely to be diagnostic in this case.

Cardiac enzymes
Cardiac enzymes is incorrect. Cardiac enzymes may be raised in myocarditis, a possible complication of Lyme disease, but checking the Borrelia serology will give a much more specific diagnosis.

Echocardiogram
Echocardiogram is incorrect. An echocardiogram may be appropriate as part of the cardiac work-up, but will not confirm the underlying diagnosis.

Holter ECG
Holter ECG is incorrect. A Holter ECG will not reveal the underlying diagnosis.

stem: A 75-year-old man has a squamous-cell carcinoma of his lower lip. Which one of the following most applies to this type of carcinoma?
options: It is capable of metastasising via the lymphatics
It is commonly seen in patients under 45 years of age
It is unrelated to sun exposure
explanation:
It is capable of metastasising via the lymphatics
Squamous-cell carcinoma (SCC) is the second most common type of non-melanoma skin cancer; incidence increases with age. It usually occurs in chronically sun-exposed areas such as the face and scalp. It may arise from areas of actinic keratosis or Bowen’s disease and occasionally chronic wounds or areas of inflammation (when it is known as Marjolin’s ulcer). Excision is usually curative, although radiotherapy is an effective alternative; overall about 10% of cutaneous SCCs metastasise via lymphatics. Features denoting a higher risk of metastasis in SCC include large tumour size and depth, poor differentiation and site (including nose, lip, ear and mucosal).

It is commonly seen in patients under 45 years of age
It is commonly seen in patients under 45 years of age is incorrect. SCC is very unusual in younger patients.

It is unrelated to sun exposure
It is unrelated to sun exposure is incorrect. Most SCCs are associated with chronic sun exposure.

Overall 5-year survival is approximately 50%
Overall 5-year survival is approximately 50% is incorrect. Overall prognosis for cutaneous SCC is in excess of 95% 5-year survival, not 50%.

Radiotherapy is an inappropriate treatment
Radiotherapy is an inappropriate treatment is incorrect. Radiotherapy is an effective treatment and gives particularly good results on the lip. Squamous Cell Carcinoma An 81-year-old former farmer presents with a pigmented lesion on the cheek. It began as a light brown mark 10 years previously, but has gradually enlarged and developed some darker areas. It is asymptomatic. Examination shows a 2 cm diameter pigmented macule. It is mostly light brown in colour, but there are a few much darker areas. The borders are irregular and poorly defined.

stem: A 65-year-old man complains of muscle weakness and finds it difficult to get up from a chair. His wife mentions that over the last few months he has developed dyspnoea on exertion. He has lost some weight over the previous 3 months and also complains of a scaling rash over his hands and a purplish rash of the eyelids. He is an ex-smoker and used to work as a car salesman. He drinks 40 units of alcohol a week. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Dermatomyositis
Dermatomyositis is a rare disease in which a characteristic rash is associated with myositis. When it develops over the age of 40 years, about one third of patients prove to have an underlying carcinoma. It is more common in females. Typical features include: a red or violaceous peri-orbital eruption known as the ‘heliotrope rash’; there may be associated oedema violaceous ‘Gottron’s’ papules over the knuckles linear violaceous changes over the dorsal surfaces of the fingers nail fold inflammation with dilated capillaries the ‘shawl sign’ describes erythema over the upper back and posterior neck weakness of the major proximal muscle groups, although some patients will have skin involvement alone (‘amyopathic dermatomyositis’). Rarely, involuntary muscles may be involved, leading to potentially dangerous or even fatal difficulties in swallowing or breathing. Calcification can occur in juvenile dermatomyositis, but is uncommon in adults. Diagnostic investigations include creatine kinase, antinuclear antibody and skin biopsy; electromyography and/or muscle biopsy can confirm myositis. Screening for underlying neoplasia (such as CT chest, abdomen and pelvis) is generally advised in adult cases.

Alcohol-induced myopathy
Alcohol-induced myopathy is incorrect. Alcohol is another cause of proximal myopathy, but would not explain the skin features.

Osteomalacia
Osteomalacia does present with proximal myopathy, although the other features consistent with dermatomyositis are inconsistent with this as the underlying diagnosis. Osteomalacia is seen more commonly in women of South Asian descent who may well follow a vegetarian diet, high in phytates and have limited sun exposure.

Cushing syndrome
Cushing syndrome is incorrect. Cushing syndrome is another cause of proximal myopathy but would not explain the skin features.

Motor neurone disease
Motor neurone disease is incorrect. Motor neurone disease might explain the muscle weakness, but not the skin features. Corroborative neurological signs are not mentioned in the scenario.

stem: A 67-year-old man has been diagnosed with Kaposi’s sarcoma of the legs and feet. Which one of the following best applies to the classical form of this disease?
options: It can be cured by surgical excision
It does not spread to the lymph glands
It is associated with human herpes virus 6
Patients usually complain of severe nocturnal itching
explanation:
It affects elderly, non-immunosupressed men
In its classical form, Kaposi’s sarcoma (KS) is a rare tumour of elderly men; other types comprise HIV-associated KS, immunosuppression-related KS and endemic KS, which affects younger individuals in parts of Africa It is a tumour of multicentric origin with vascular endothelial and fibroblastic elements It is associated with human herpes virus 8 (HHV-8), which is also known as Kaposi sarcoma herpes virus It tends to present with red, purple or brown cutaneous nodules or plaques; lesions may occur in the mouth and in the internal organs It typically affects the legs, head and neck Lesions are usually asymptomatic The classical form is generally indolent and death usually occurs due to other causes; the HIVassociated form tends to be more aggressive Where possible, management involves optimising immune function (eg treating HIV with antiretrovirals, reducing immunosuppressive drugs); other treatments include cryotherapy, excision, chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

It can be cured by surgical excision
It can be cured by surgical excision is incorrect. Individual lesions of KS can be excised if symptomatic, but local recurrence is common and new lesions will be liable to appear over time.

It does not spread to the lymph glands
It does not spread to the lymph glands is incorrect. KS can affect lymph nodes and internal organs.

It is associated with human herpes virus 6
It is associated with human herpes virus 6 is incorrect. KS is associated with HHV-8, not HHV-6.

Patients usually complain of severe nocturnal itching
Patients usually complain of severe nocturnal itching is incorrect. The skin lesions are usually asymptomatic. stem: A 55-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis has developed painful ulcers on both legs. These have rapidly enlarged over the last week. Examination confirms multiple ulcers with a sloughy base and a raised purplish prominent rim. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
explanation:
Prednisolone
The description is suggestive of pyoderma gangrenosum (PG). Many associations have been described, the strongest of which seem to be: 1. inflammatory bowel disease, either ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s disease 2. haematological disorders including myeloid leukaemias, myelofibrosis, myeloma and monoclonal gammopathies 3. arthritides, especially rheumatoid disease 4. diabetes. Each lesion typically begins with a papule or pustule most commonly on the leg; it is commonly multifocal. Lesions rapidly enlarge and break down to form painful, necrotic ulcers; these may be deep and purulent, and the border is undermined and violaceous. Patients with inflammatory bowel disease may develop PG adjacent to a stoma. Treatment options include 1. very potent topical steroids 2. prednisolone 3. ciclosporin or other immunosuppressive agents 4. dapsone 5. tetracycline antibiotics (for their anti-inflammatory effects). Prednisolone is generally the mainstay of treatment, often alongside steroid-sparing agents.

Compression bandaging
Compression bandaging is the treatment of choice for venous ulceration. It is usually not tolerated in the context of PG due to the associated pain and tenderness.

Intravenous antibiotics
Intravenous antibiotics are only indicated in the context of infection. Despite its name, PG is an inflammatory condition.

Intravenous immunoglobulins
Intravenous immunoglobulins are used in the treatment of PG, but are very expensive and not regarded as a first-line option.

Local application of silver nitrate
Topical silver nitrate is used to treat overgranulation. It is not a treatment for PG.

stem: An elderly woman complains of long-standing vulval itching. Examination shows pale, atrophic plaques affecting the labia majora and extending around the anus. There is a similar plaque on her abdomen. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lichen sclerosus
The pathophysiology of lichen sclerosus is not fully understood, but the condition is associated with autoimmune diseases such as pernicious anaemia and alopecia areata. It is most common in post-menopausal women. Urologists often refer to the disease in men as balanitis xerotica obliterans. Clinical features include hypopigmented plaques which are usually atrophic but may be thickened; purpura and erosion can occur; most cases are confined to the genital area, with extension around the anus seen in women. In men, lichen sclerosus mostly affects the glans penis and foreskin, leading to painful fissures and phimosis. Extra-genital lichen sclerosus is seen occasionally. The cardinal symptom is pruritus, although fissures or erosions can lead to pain. The diagnosis may be clinical, but is often confirmed histologically. In women, lichen sclerosus usually responds well to treatment with a very potent topical corticosteroid; in men, circumcision may be required. Genital lichen sclerosus carries a small increased risk of squamous-cell carcinoma developing in the affected area.

Lichen planus
Lichen planus is incorrect. Erosive lichen planus often affects the vulva. It tends to be painful rather than itchy and is not usually pale or atrophic.

Lichen simplex
Lichen simplex is incorrect. Lichen simplex is thickening of the skin, secondary to chronic rubbing or scratching. It is often seen in association with underlying eczema.

Morphoea
Morphoea is incorrect. Morphoea gives rise to atrophic plaques, but does not tend to affect the genital area. It is not usually pruritic and can lead to Hypopigmentation, hyperpigmentation, alopecia secondary to loss of hair follicles, and a shiny cutaneous surface are common additional features of sclerotic lesions.

Vitiligo
Vitiligo is incorrect. Vitiligo manifests as depigmented macules. It is not uncommon on the genitals, but is asymptomatic with no atrophy.

stem: A 19-year-old woman presented with erythematous macules on the back, chest and forearm. She reported that the eruption had started with one red patch, and then had developed into multiple patches over the following 2 weeks. Routine bloods including FBC, U&E, LFT and ESR are normal. Which of the following would help most with making the diagnosis?
explanation:
None of the above
This patient has pityriasis rosea, which is a clinical diagnosis and usually requires no further investigations. It typically presents with a ‘herald patch’ followed by widespread similar red patches with a fine collaret of scale. Although it can affect any age group, it most commonly affects young adults and is usually asymptomatic, although in some cases it can be slightly itchy. It can sometimes follow an upper respiratory tract viral infection, but often the patient denies any preceding infection at all. Treatment is conservative, and it usually resolves up to 12 weeks later. The lack of any past medical history and the normal routine blood tests make SLE, porphyria and primary biliary cholangitis highly unlikely, and therefore other blood tests are not indicated.

Anti-nuclear antibody
Anti-nuclear antibody is incorrect. This is most useful in screening for SLE, where a photosensitive rash and joint pain would be expected.

Anti-smooth muscle antibodies
Anti-smooth muscle antibodies is incorrect. Anti-smooth muscle antibodies are associated with autoimmune hepatitis.

Anti-phospholipid antibodies
Anti-phospholipid antibodies is incorrect. Anti-phospholipid antibody syndrome is associated with increased risk of venous thrombosis.

Porphyria screen
Porphyria screen is incorrect. Acute porphyria is associated with a photosensitive rash, hypertension and hyponatraemia. Pityriasis roseaA 68–year-old gentleman presents with a lesion on his temple that looks shiny, has a rolled edge and is gradually increasing in size. Routine blood tests are unremarkable.

stem: A 23-year-old man with type 1 diabetes has noticed an unusual lesion on the dorsum of his left hand. On examination, he has a circle of small erythematous papules that are beginning to coalesce into a contiguous area of erythema. HbA1c is well controlled at 52 mmol/mol, and other bloods are unremarkable. Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Granuloma annulare
Granuloma annulare or necrobiotic papulosis, is a relatively common skin condition often associated with diabetes mellitus, but also with autoimmune thyroiditis and hyperlipidaemia. It most commonly presents as an annular, skin-coloured or pinkish plaque, although it can take several forms, including a disseminated type. They often resolve without intervention; however they can sometimes persist for several years. Treatment might include topical/intralesional corticosteroid systemic therapy (eg methotrexate or biological therapy).

Necrobiosis lipoidica
Although necrobiosis lipoidica is also commonly associated with diabetes, it is far less common and presents as tender yellow–brown patches on the shins, which are prone to ulceration.

Psoriasis
Localised psoriasis tends to present as a scaly eruption on a salmon-pink background, and therefore this option is incorrect.

Pyoderma gangrenosum
Pyoderma gangrenosum is an autoinflammatory disease that presents as a painful, rapidly enlarging ulcer. It can be associated with inflammatory bowel disease and rheumatoid arthritis, but an association with internal disease is not always found and can simply occur at the site of injury. Treatment includes removal of the necrotic tissue, potent topical steroids and oral/intravenous antibiotics if systemically unwell.

Scabies infection
One would expect scabies to be extremely itchy, and rather than presenting as a single lesion on the hand, there may be clues between the webspaces of the fingers/toes of burrows where the mites have entered under the skin. Diabetes - Type I.
