stem: A 21-year-old man presents with hyperkeratotic scaly plaques on the elbows, knees and at the scalp margin. Mycology of hair pullings showed no growth, and routine bloods showed a mildly raised ESR of 33 mm/hr, but were otherwise normal. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Psoriasis
This patient is presenting with chronic plaque psoriasis. It typically looks like plaques of silver scale on a salmon-pink background, particularly affecting the extensor surfaces such as the knees and elbows, but also the scalp, hairline and behind the ears. Other types of psoriasis include guttate psoriasis (typically poststreptococcal infection), palmar–plantar psoriasis (typically associated with smoking), pustular psoriasis (indicating instability in disease and possibly warranting hospital admission) and psoriasis associated with sites of trauma – the Koebner’s phenomenon. Treatment modalities include topical therapies: for example, vitamin D analogues or coal tar preparations, systemic therapies (eg cyclosporine or methotrexate), phototherapy or biologic agents.

Discoid eczema
Discoid eczema is incorrect. Discoid eczema appears as coin-shaped, scaly, red lesions that are typically intensely itchy. Although it can appear anywhere (dissimilar to atopic eczema, which is most common in the flexures), it is unusual for it to be at the scalp margin.

Lichen simplex
Lichen simplex is incorrect. Lichen simplex often occurs after excessive rubbing and scratching of an area and is most commonly found on the lower legs, genitals and the back of the neck. The skin typically looks ‘lichenified’ (thickened with exaggerated skin markings). Treatment includes moisturisers and topical or intralesional steroids.

Seborrhoeic dermatitis
Seborrhoeic dermatitis is incorrect. Seborrhoeic dermatitis is a sensible differential for psoriasis. It is caused by the yeast Malassezia and most commonly appears in the greasy skin zones, for example the creases of the nose, forehead, scalp and chest. It typically arises in the very young (where it forms cradle cap) or the elderly. Treatment includes antifungals like ketoconazole.

Tinea capitis
Tinea capitis is incorrect. Although tinea capitis is another good differential, the negative mycology is reassuring, and although scaly, tinea does not typically look ‘hyperkeratotic’ (thickening of the stratum corneum). Psoriasis A 19-year-old woman presented with erythematous macules on the back, chest and forearm. She reported that the eruption had started with one red patch, and then had developed into multiple patches over the following 2 weeks. Routine bloods including FBC, U&E, LFT and ESR are normal.

stem: Which one of the following organisms is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Group A Streptococcus
This lady has erysipelas, a superficial form of cellulitis affecting the upper dermis. Although it can potentially affect any age group, it is most common in the very young and elderly populations. It is caused by group A βhaemolytic streptococci (streptococcus pyogenes) and is associated with systemic upset including fever and chills. The area affected has a sharp, raised border and may blister. Treatment involves intravenous penicillin or in penicillin allergy, erythromycin. Complications include abscesses and infections distant to the site of infection, such as infective endocarditis, although this is a rare complication.

Group G Streptococcus
Group G Streptococcus is incorrect. Although Group G streptococcus can also cause erysipelas, it is a far less frequent causative organism and more commonly implicated in deep infections, such as bone and joint infections and other bacteraemias.

Herpes zoster infection
Herpes zoster infection is incorrect. Herpes zoster or shingles, is a localised blistering, painful rash following the path of the nerve distribution and is caused by reactivation of varicella zoster virus. It is most common in the elderly or those who are immunocompromised. It is usually treated conservatively with rest and pain relief; however, antivirals can be given if extensive.

Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus is incorrect. Staphylococcus aureus most commonly infects broken or injured skin, for example in eczema where the skin is dry and cracked. It is also the most implicated organism in impetigo and follicular infections such as folliculitis, carbuncles and furuncles. It manifests far less commonly as the causative organism in erysipelas.

Staphylococcus epidermidis
Staphylococcus epidermidis is incorrect. Staphylococcus epidermidis is a normal skin commensalism and rarely causes serious skin disease. It s more commonly implicated as an opportunistic organism causing nosocomial infections and infecting indwelling medical devices. Cellulitis A 26-year-old man returns from a holiday in Spain. He is concerned that he has multiple patches of depigmentation on his upper chest where he has failed to gain an adequate suntan. On examination these patches consist of well-demarcated, scaly white skin, with a marked absence of pigmentation compared with the tanned areas.

stem: A 17- year-old gentleman presents with a single scaly, annular patch on the dorsum of his right hand. Recently he has been doing work experience at a petting farm. He reports that his GP had given him a cream for the rash, which he has been using for 2 weeks, but feels that the lesion has got larger and scalier since using it. It is minimally itchy. The rest of his skin examination is unremarkable. What is the reason for the worsening appearance of the rash?
explanation:
Inappropriate treatment with steroid cream
This gentleman has a fungal infection that has been inappropriately treated with steroids. Although initial improvement may be seen, continued use of a steroid on an area of fungal infection can cause it to get worse. This is termed tinea incognito, when the clinical appearance of tinea has been altered by the use of inappropriate steroid treatment. Often this happens when the fungal infection is mistaken for an inflammatory dermatosis such as eczema.

Bacterial superinfection
Bacterial superinfection is incorrect. In a bacterial superinfection we would expect the lesion to become weepy or develop yellow crusting; therefore, this is not the answer here.

Excessive scratching
Excessive scratching is incorrect. Excessive scratching can indeed make a rash appear worse than it started, but the appearance would be different. Generally, clues for scratching would be lichenification of the skin (thickening of the skin with increased creases), as is seen in eczema. Additionally, we are told that the itch is minimal, so this seems unlikely.

Fungal superinfection
Fungal superinfection is incorrect. Fungal infection is the underlying basis of the presentation anyway.

Inappropriate treatment with antifungal cream
Inappropriate treatment with antifungal cream is incorrect. As this question is depicting a fungal infection, inappropriate treatment with antifungal cream does not make sense. The latter would of course have improved the rash.

stem: A 26-year-old man returns from a holiday in Spain. He is concerned that he has multiple patches of depigmentation on his upper chest where he has failed to gain an adequate suntan. On examination these patches consist of well-demarcated, scaly white skin, with a marked absence of pigmentation compared with the tanned areas. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment in this case?
explanation:
Clotrimazole ointment
This is a typical story of pityriasis versicolor, which is caused by the yeast infection Malassezia furfur and appears as hypopigmented, well-demarcated macules covered in a very fine scale. They most often occur on the chest, back and abdomen. The macules often go unnoticed until the patient tans the surrounding skin – this is when they become more obvious. Treatment is usually with a topical antifungal such as clotrimazole.

1% hydrocortisone cream
1% hydrocortisone cream is incorrect. Fungal infections should never be treated with a steroid alone as this can cause them to flare and change in appearance (tinea incognito).

Fluconazole tablets
Fluconazole tablets is incorrect. The outcome is usually good with topical antifungals alone; however, in recurrent episodes of pityriasis versicolor, an oral antifungal agent may be used. Usually, fluconazole is chosen for this purpose and is given for up to 3 days each month.

Fusidic acid ointment
Fusidic acid ointment is incorrect. Fusidic acid ointment is effective at treating staphylococcal skin infections and therefore is not the correct treatment here.

Ketoconazole tablets
Ketoconazole tablets is incorrect. Ketoconazole tablets are another oral antifungal agent, but tend to be used in difficult-to-treat candidiasis, such as thrush, that is frequently recurring or not resolving with pessaries or topical treatments.

stem: A middle-aged man is referred with mildly itchy, warty papules on his back and chest, along with nail dystrophy. His father had a similar eruption. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Darier's disease
The features described are typical of this condition. Darier’s disease is an autosomal dominant condition with characteristic cutaneous features It typically becomes apparent in early adulthood Features include warty papules and plaques in seborrhoeic areas (eg central chest and back, scalp, flexures), palmar pits and nail dystrophy Secondary infection of the lesions can lead to crusting and malodour The retinoid acitretin can be used to treat symptomatic cases

Lichen planus
Lichen planus is incorrect as the constellation of features described is specific for Darier’s disease. Lichen planus is typically intensely pruritic, does not especially affect the torso and its papules are usually described as violaceous and flat-topped rather than warty. It can, however, lead to nail dystrophy.

Pemphigus foliaceus
Pemphigus foliaceus is incorrect. This is a rare form of the blistering condition, pemphigus, which presents with widespread crusted erosions. Unlike pemphigus vulgaris, mucosae are usually unaffected.

Psoriasis
Psoriasis is incorrect. Although this can cause a rash with nail dystrophy and there may be a family history, it gives rise to well-defined, scaly plaques rather than warty papules.

Seborrhoeic dermatitis
Seborrhoeic dermatitis is incorrect. Seborrhoeic dermatitis leads to scaly plaques rather than warty papules. The distribution may be the same as Darier’s disease, but the positive family history supports the diagnosis of the latter.

stem: A 67-year-old heavy smoker presents to his GP for review. He has developed a violaceous rash on his face, particularly around the eyes. Past history of note includes hypertension, hypothyroidism, for which he is taking thyroxine, and hypercholesterolaemia, for which he takes simvastatin. There is also erythema on the back of his hands, and nail-fold haemorrhages are present. On examination there is mild proximal muscle weakness. Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Dermatomyositis
The answer is dermatomyositis. Dermatomyositis is a rare disease in which a characteristic rash is associated with myositis. When it develops over the age of 40 years, about one-third of patients prove to have an underlying carcinoma. It is more common in women. Typical features include: A red or violaceous periorbital eruption known as the ‘heliotrope rash’; there may be associated oedema Violaceous ‘Gottron’s’ papules over the knuckles Linear violaceous changes over the dorsal surfaces of the fingers Nail-fold inflammation with dilated capillaries The ‘shawl sign’ describes erythema over the upper back and posterior neck Weakness of the major proximal muscle groups is typical, although some patients will have skin involvement alone (‘amyopathic dermatomyositis’) Rarely, involuntary muscles may be involved, leading to potentially dangerous or even fatal difficulties in swallowing or breathing Calcification can occur in juvenile dermatomyositis, but is uncommon in adults Diagnostic investigations include creatine kinase, anti-nuclear antibody and skin biopsy; electromyography and/or muscle biopsy can confirm myositis Screening for underlying neoplasia (such as CT chest, abdomen and pelvis) is generally advised in adult cases

Cushing’s disease
Cushing’s disease, is incorrect. Although this can lead to proximal myopathy, cutaneous features include facial plethora (erythematous, rather than violaceous), atrophy, purpura, striae, acne, hirsutism and male-pattern hair loss.

Discoid lupus erythematosus
Discoid lupus erythematosus, is incorrect. This is also known as chronic cutaneous lupus and is not associated with extracutaneous features (except in patients with concurrent systemic lupus erythematosus). It typically presents with scaly, erythematous plaques on sun-exposed sites; scarring and alopecia can result.

Hypothyroid proximal myopathy
Hypothyroid proximal myopathy, is incorrect as it would not explain the acral skin changes.

Statin-related rhabdomyolysis
Statin-related rhabdomyolysis, is incorrect as it would also not explain the acral skin changes.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with darkening of the skin on her face; it worsens with sun exposure. Apart from the appearance, it is asymptomatic, and she is otherwise fit and well. Examination shows well-defined but irregular macular hyperpigmentation over the malar area and upper lip. Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Melasma
Melasma (also known as chloasma) is a hormonally stimulated increase in melanogenesis that mainly appears on the face. It is more common in those with darker skin types. Oestrogens, either endogenous or exogenous, play an important role: the condition is much more common in women and can be precipitated or exacerbated by pregnancy or oestrogen-containing contraceptives. It is worsened by sun exposure. It is usually symmetrical, most commonly affecting the malar areas and upper lip; it can also occur on the forehead and more widely over the cheeks. The pigmentation may take many months to resolve after parturition or contraceptive discontinuation. Rigorous sun protection is an important part of management. The condition is difficult to treat otherwise, though some patients with bleaching creams or laser treatment. Skin camouflage can be used to disguise the colour change very effectively.

Addison's disease
Addison's disease is incorrect. This is a good differential diagnosis, but patients are usually unwell. Pigmentation in Addison’s is often generalised and preferentially affects skin creases, nipples, genitals and oral mucosa, which are not mentioned in the scenario.

Eczema
Eczema is incorrect as this would be expected to cause dryness, scaling and itching. It can, however, result in postinflammatory hyperpigmentation, which can look similar to melasma.

Lupus
Lupus is incorrect. Although systemic lupus erythematosus is photoaggravated, its classic malar rash is red rather than hyperpigmented (brown).

Vitiligo
Vitiligo is incorrect, as this causes depigmentation (white lesions), not hyperpigmentation (brown lesions).

stem: A 31-year-old man presents with a number of small blisters, predominantly affecting his scalp, scapular area and buttocks. The blisters are intensely itchy. Skin biopsy is positive for IgA immunofluorescence. Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Dermatitis herpetiformis
The clinical description fits best with dermatitis herpetiformis, which most commonly begins in early adulthood; vesicles are usually quickly excoriated, so may not be seen. HLA associations (B8, DR3, DQ2 in 80–90% of cases) are similar to those for coeliac disease, which virtually always coexists. Skin biopsy reveals subepidermal blisters with neutrophil microabscesses in the dermal papillae. On immunofluorescence, there is positive granular staining for IgA in the dermal papillae. The patient should have appropriate investigations for coeliac disease. Treatment is with a gluten-free diet; control of the skin disease may also require dapsone or other sulpha drugs. Dapsone may cause haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia, as well as liver pathology and polyneuropathy, so regular monitoring of both liver enzymes and blood count is necessary; it is also associated with drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS).

Erythema multiforme
Erythema multiforme is incorrect. This typically presents with target lesions, which sometimes blister centrally. It tends to be tender rather than itchy, and immunofluorescence is negative.

Pemphigoid
Pemphigoid is incorrect. Bullous pemphigoid usually presents with larger blisters; there may be significant pruritus. Immunofluorescence demonstrates C3 and linear IgG deposition.

Pemphigus
Pemphigus is incorrect. Pemphigus vulgaris usually presents with erosions and marked mucosal involvement. Immunofluorescence demonstrates intercellular IgG deposition.

Porphyria cutanea tarda.

stem: Which of the following represent the most appropriate first-line treatment for this man?
explanation:
Gluten-free diet and dapsone
This man has symptoms and a skin biopsy result consistent with dermatitis herpetiformis. It is not surprising that no gastrointestinal symptoms are identified as these are only found in around 10% of patients, although abnormalities on endoscopy are found in 90%. Management of choice is a gluten-free diet, although patients can find this very difficult to achieve. Other autoimmune diseases occur more commonly in patients with dermatitis herpetiformis, including Type 1 diabetes, autoimmune thyroid disease (as in this case) and myasthenia gravis.

Atkin's diet
Atkin's diet is incorrect. The Atkins (low-carb) diet is not a treatment for dermatitis herpetiformis.

Colchicine
Colchicine is incorrect. Colchicine is a second-line alternative to dapsone in dermatitis herpetiformis.

Dapsone
Dapsone is incorrect. Dapsone is often needed to resolve symptoms, as a gluten-free diet is difficult to adhere to.

Prednisolone
Prednisolone is incorrect. Prednisolone is not often used for this purpose.

stem: Which one of the following would be the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
options: Biopsy from the ulcer margin, with microscopy and culture from the ulcerated tissue
explanation:
Biopsy from the ulcer margin, with microscopy and culture from the ulcerated tissue
The answer is a biopsy from the ulcer margin, with microscopy and culture from the ulcerated tissue. Biopsy of the ulcerated tissue reveals intense neutrophilic infiltration, haemorrhage and necrosis of the overlying epidermis; culture is important to rule out infection as a cause of the presentation. Treatment includes topical corticosteroids, with oral corticosteroids and cyclosporine being alternative additional agents. This patient has a clinical history which is suggestive of pyoderma gangrenosum, a condition that may be associated with: Vasculitis Haematological malignancy Inflammatory bowel disease

Angiography and venous Doppler studies
Contact dermatitis

Autoimmune profile
Dermatitis artefacta

Chest X-ray (CXR)
Pityriasis versicolor

Fasting plasma glucose
Psoriasis Submit.

stem: A patient presents with multiple cutaneous nodules, predominantly on his trunk, but also on his hands and face. He also has a number of café au lait spots, and the GP reports axillary freckling. The GP is concerned that he may have neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). Which one of the following is usually associated with neurofibromatosis type 1?
explanation:
A gene defect on chromosome 17
Chromosome 17 is affected in NF1 and chromosome 22 in NF2. Café au lait spots, axillary/inguinal freckles, neurofibromas, optic nerve gliomas, Lisch nodules and sphenoid dysplasia are all seen with neurofibromatosis type 1. Hypertension is also strongly associated with NF1; while the usual cause is essential hypertension, phaeochromocytomas also occur more commonly in association with the condition, and should be excluded if hypertension is present.

Hyperparathyroidism
Hyperparathyroidism is incorrect. NF can be associated with phaeochromocytomas, but the full spectrum of MEN2A is rarely reported. N.B. neurofibromas can occur in MEN2B.

Juvenile cataracts
Juvenile cataracts is incorrect. Juvenile cataracts are usually associated with neurofibromatosis type 2.

Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid
Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid is incorrect. NF can be associated with phaeochromocytomas, but the full spectrum of MEN2A is rarely reported. N.B. neurofibromas can occur in MEN2B.

Schwannomas
Schwannomas is incorrect. Schwannomas are usually associated with neurofibromatosis type 2.

stem: A 24-year-old woman presents with a rapidly changing mole on her right forearm and is concerned it may be a malignant melanoma. On examination she has a lesion on the right forearm that is blue–black in colour with evidence of ulceration; it is 6 mm across. You arrange an excision biopsy, which confirms melanoma with a thickness of 5 mm. Which one of the following is the worst prognostic sign with respect to this lesion?
explanation:
5 mm depth
Both Breslow thickness and the presence of ulceration have an impact on prognosis for malignant melanoma. The third aspect of staging according the American Joint Committee is the presence of lymph node micrometastases. Overall 5-year survival rates for melanoma are around 75% in men and 83% in women. The primary treatment for malignant melanoma is wide local excision.

6 mm width
6 mm width is incorrect. The width is not greatly significant with respect to prognosis.

Blue-black discolouration
Blue-black discolouration is incorrect. The colour of the lesion does not impact significantly on prognosis.

Position on the forearm
Position on the forearm is incorrect. The position of the lesion does not impact significantly on prognosis.

Female sex
Being female and younger age at diagnosis are both positive prognostic factors in this case.

stem: A 22-year-old woman presents with an asymptomatic eruption over her chest and interscapular area, which she noticed recently. Examination shows scattered warty brown papules. Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Darier’s disease
The features are compatible and none of the other options give rise to asymptomatic papules. Darier’s disease is an autosomal dominant condition with characteristic cutaneous signs. It typically becomes apparent in early adulthood. Features include warty papules and plaques in seborrhoeic areas (e.g. central chest and back, scalp, flexures), palmar pits and nail dystrophy. Secondary infection of the lesions can lead to crusting and malodour. The retinoid acitretin can be used to treat symptomatic cases.

Lichen planus
Lichen planus is incorrect. This is typically intensely pruritic, does not especially affect the torso and its papules are usually described as violaceous and flat-topped rather than warty.

Lichen simplex
Lichen simplex is incorrect. This is essentially an eczematous process, with thickened plaques due to repetitive rubbing or scratching.

Pityriasis rosea
Pityriasis rosea is incorrect. This typically begins with a herald patch (a solitary red plaque), which is followed a few days later by a widespread truncal rash comprising superficial plaques with peripheral scaling, in a ‘Christmas tree’ configuration.

Pityriasis rubra pilaris
Pityriasis rubra pilaris is incorrect. This is a rare skin condition of unknown aetiology. Features include extensive psoriasiform plaques with a rather orangey colour, palmoplantar hyperkeratosis and follicular plugging.

stem: A 32-year-old army corporal has returned to the UK after 4 months in Central America. He complains of intense itching affecting the finger webs, chest and the flexural aspect of the wrists. On examination there appears to be excoriation in the finger webs and a couple of linear scabs on the wrists measuring a few millimetres in length; he also has eczematous changes around the nipples. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Sarcoptes scabiei infestation
This man has been in close contact with his comrades during a foreign tour of duty, a situation which can lead to transmission of S. scabiei, the cause of scabies. Scabies presents with severe pruritus and usually prominent excoriation. Burrows (linear crusted lesions of a few millimetres in length) are pathognomonic; penile papules are also highly suggestive, but these are not always evident. It also has a predilection for the webspaces and around the nipples. Secondary eczematisation is not unusual, as in this case. Scalp involvement only occurs in young babies and very debilitated adults. Treatment is usually with permethrin; close contacts should be treated concurrently.

Cutaneous larva migrans
Cutaneous larva migrans is incorrect. This is caused by hookworm larvae. It can be acquired in Central America and many other regions, but affects a single area, most commonly a foot. Like scabies, it is intensely pruritic, but gives rise to serpiginous tracks.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis
Cutaneous leishmaniasis is incorrect. Although this is endemic in parts of Central America, this typically presents with a solitary ulcer.

Dermatitis herpetiformis
Dermatitis herpetiformis is incorrect. This condition can present at any age and is compatible with intense pruritus; however, it gives rise to vesicles which quickly become excoriated. Classically, these favour extensor surfaces and not the sites described in the scenario.

Eczema
Eczema is incorrect. While some of the features described in the scenario are compatible with eczema, the involved sites and description of burrows are highly suggestive of scabies.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with a rash on her trunk and limbs, which she describes as burning rather than itchy; she is otherwise well. Examination reveals scattered papules and small nodules, some with fine peripheral scale; several have a pronounced haemorrhagic crust on the surface. Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Pityriasis lichenoides et varioliformis acuta
The scenario is typical for PLEVA, a rare skin condition of uncertain aetiology. PLEVA lies at one end of a spectrum with pityriasis lichenoides chronica at the other. There may be mild systemic symptoms, and spontaneous remission occurs after a period of months or years. Lesions may be itchy or burning. The diagnosis should be confirmed by skin biopsy. Treatment options include topical corticosteroids, anti-inflammatory antibiotics, phototherapy and systemic immunosuppressants.

Dermatitis herpetiformis
Dermatitis herpetiformis is incorrect. This tends to manifest as excoriated papules with intense itching, though the primary lesions are vesicular.

Erythema nodosum
Erythema nodosum is incorrect. This causes tender lumps, usually confined to the legs.

Insect bites
Insect bites is incorrect. Some insect bites do become necrotic, which could lead to surface crusting and pain more than itching. However, the scenario is characteristic for PLEVA, making this the better option.

Secondary syphilis
Secondary syphilis is incorrect. This is typically associated with systemic symptoms and lymphadenopathy, and classically also affects the palms and soles; surface crust would not be typical.

stem: A 22-year-old White woman with a history of Type 1 diabetes presents for review. She has just returned from a summer holiday in Spain and has noticed some patches on her body that do not appear to have tanned. Examination shows depigmented macules symmetrically on the hands, feet and chest. Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Vitiligo
Vitiligo is characterised by acquired areas of clearly defined depigmentation owing to loss of melanocytes. It is characteristically symmetrical. There is an association with other autoimmune disease such as Type 1 diabetes, coeliac disease, autoimmune thyroid disease and Addison’s disease. It is said to affect around 0.4% of the White population. The condition often becomes obvious to Whites during the summer months, as affected areas fail to tan and are highly susceptible to sunburn. The condition is much more noticeable in darker-skinned races, and may be stigmatised in some communities. Treatment of vitiligo is generally unsatisfactory; potent topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors sometimes help, and phototherapy can be used for widespread disease.

Leprosy
Leprosy is incorrect. Tuberculoid leprosy gives rise to areas of hypopigmentation (partial loss of pigment) rather than depigmentation (complete loss of pigment); there may also be palpable thickened peripheral nerves.

Melasma
Melasma is incorrect. This causes hyperpigmentation rather than depigmentation and is almost always confined to the face.

Morphoea
Morphoea is incorrect. This can lead to hypo- or hyperpigmentation, but causes associated textural change; it is not usually symmetrical.

Pityriasis versicolor
Pityriasis versicolor is incorrect. This is caused by overgrowth of the (usually) commensal yeast, Malassezia furfur. While it typically presents in young adults in warm weather or after a sunny holiday, it leads to discrete hypo- or sometimes hyperpigmented macules with very fine peripheral scaling; it is usually confined to the trunk.

stem: A 19-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department complaining of an intensely itchy rash, predominantly affecting the webspaces on his hands and feet, groin, upper thighs and buttocks. He has recently returned from a lads’ holiday to Spain, during which he had unprotected sexual intercourse with a number of women. On examination these areas are covered with a maculopapular rash, with evidence of excoriation. Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following treatments is most likely to be effective?
explanation:
Permethrin
The clinical picture here is consistent with a diagnosis of scabies, and topical permethrin is the first-line treatment of choice. Screening of partners and for other sexually transmitted infections are, of course, advised.

Dapsone
Dapsone is incorrect. Dapsone is the treatment for dermatitis herpetiformis.

Hydrocortisone cream
Hydrocortisone cream is incorrect. While this would be a potential option for inflammatory skin rashes, the rash’s distribution and the Spanish holiday’s timing make scabies a far more plausible diagnosis.

Ivermectin
Ivermectin is incorrect. Oral ivermectin has been shown in clinical trials of scabies to be less effective than permethrin.

Oral prednisolone
Oral prednisolone is incorrect. While this would be a potential option for inflammatory skin rashes, the rash’s distribution and the Spanish holiday’s timing make scabies a far more plausible diagnosis. ScabiesAn 18-year-old man who has used topical corticosteroids for many years for eczema comes to the clinic with a new rash. He has an extensive rash consisting of 2–5mm violet/red papules affecting his wrists, forearms, legs and genitals. He tells you that he finds the rash itchy, particularly at night. There is no other past medical history of note, although he has recently completed a course of amoxicillin for a respiratory tract infection.

stem: In the pathogenesis of psoriasis, which cell type is most implicated in the epidermal inflammatory response?
explanation:
T-lymphocytes
In psoriasis the epidermis is invaded by large numbers of activated T-lymphocytes, which appear to be able to induce keratinocyte proliferation. This then drives local inflammation, with upregulated production of TNFalpha, interferon gamma and IL-12; and in particular, elevated TNF-alpha levels correlate well with flares of psoriasis. An alteration in the epidermal cell cycle then occurs in response to inflammation and vascular engorgement, leading to an accelerated cell turnover rate, which is reduced from 23 days to 3–5 days.

B-lymphocytes
B-lymphocytes is incorrect. The T-cell is the dominant type.

Fibroblasts
Fibroblasts is incorrect. The T-cell is the dominant type.

Macrophages
Macrophages is incorrect. The T-cell is the dominant type. Psoriasis A 52-year-old man who has recently emigrated from Uganda presents to the clinic with a number of hypopigmented areas over his arms and legs, which are accompanied by reduced sensation. He also complains of weakness of his left ankle. He has a history of hypertension and treated hypothyroidism. On examination you confirm the hypopigmented lesions, which are associated with fibrosis and decreased sensation. He has leftsided foot-drop.

Mast cells
Mast cells is incorrect. The T-cell is the dominant type.

stem: A 17-year-old with a history of atopic eczema, managed with corticosteroid cream, presents to the Emergency Department with an extensive eruption of small pustules and vesicles; some of them are crusted over with yellow exudate. Apparently, they have increased significantly over the past 7–10 days, he feels systemically unwell with a fever and there is widespread lymphadenopathy. The pustules and vesicles have erupted in areas where he has previously suffered from eczema. Which of the following is the mainstay of therapy?
explanation:
IV aciclovir
The extensive rash is most consistent with eczema herpeticum, which is known to occur when existing areas of eczema are superinfected with herpes simplex or herpes zoster virus. IV aciclovir is the mainstay of therapy. Additional antibiotics are required only if there are signs of a superimposed bacterial cellulitis, such as localised erythema, warmth, tenderness and pus formation. Systemic viraemia and/or extensive bacterial infection of lesions are the most common sequelae of concern.

IV benzylpenicillin
IV benzylpenicillin is incorrect. IV benzylpenicillin would be required in the event that the rash was thought to be streptococcal in origin. The nature of the rash, with small vesicles, is more consistent with herpetic infection.

IV corticosteroids
IV corticosteroids is incorrect. This young man has herpetic superinfection of his eczema, and therefore requires acyclovir. Only in the event that an eczema flare alone were suspected would steroids be the appropriate option. The eruption of pustules and vesicles is more typical of herpes infection.

IV flucloxacillin
IV flucloxacillin is incorrect. More localised erythema with pus formation in association with the eczema would signify staphylococcal superinfection and hence drive use of flucloxacillin.

Oral corticosteroids
Oral corticosteroids is incorrect. Much like iv corticosteroids, oral corticosteroids could potentially drive increased spread of the herpetic superinfection seen here.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents to the Dermatology Clinic for review. He has noted a blistering skin rash, which affects his face and arms, and is particularly bad when he goes out in the sun and wears a teeshirt. He owns a pub, is obese, and admits to drinking 8–10 units of alcohol per day. On examination his BP is 155/85 mmHg, pulse is 70/min and regular. Heart sounds are normal, chest is clear. Abdomen is soft and non-tender, and he is obese with a BMI of 36. You note erythema and bullae affecting sun-exposed areas of his face and upper limbs. Which one of the following porphyrias is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Porphyria cutanea tarda (cutaneous hepatic porphyria)
Although in some instances porphyria cutanea tarda is inherited (autosomal dominant), most cases are sporadic, and are seen in patients who use significant amounts of alcohol and in patients treated with long-term oestrogen-based therapies, those with haemochromatosis, and patients who are hepatitis C positive. It occurs due to a defect in uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase.

Acute intermittent porphyria
Acute intermittent porphyria is incorrect. Acute intermittent porphyria is associated with acute presentation with symptoms of hypertension, abdominal pain and psychiatric disturbance, but not with skin rashes.

Congenital erythropoietic porphyria
Congenital erythropoietic porphyria is incorrect. Congenital erythropoietic porphyria carries autosomal recessive inheritance, is caused by a defect in uroporphyrinogen III synthase, and its presentation is not strongly associated with alcohol consumption.

Erythropoietic protoporphyria
Erythropoietic protoporphyria is incorrect. Erythropoietic protoporphyria is associated with deficiency of ferrocheletase; it does cause cutaneous symptoms, but is not associated with alcohol consumption.

Variegate porphyria
Variegate porphyria is incorrect. Variegate porphyria presents with a mixed picture of acute features including abdominal pain and hypertension, and skin rashes. It is due to a defect in the gene for protoporphyrinogen oxidase. Porphyria Cutanea TardaA 27-year-old patient with ileocaecal Crohn’s disease presents to his GP with a non-pruritic rash on his right leg which has been progressing in the last 2 weeks. The rash looks like a collection of discrete pustules, some of which had coalesced to form what looks like an ulcer. There are no other rashes and his nails look normal. He has no other past medical history and is on azathioprine and infliximab for the Crohn’s disease.

stem: A 26-year-old woman presented with a six month history of skin lesions. She also complains of patchy hair loss of a year’s duration. On examination, she has multiple asymmetrical depigmented patches over the face and extremities. She has small patches of hair loss throughout the scalp, leaving smooth skin with scattered exclamation mark hairs. Which of the following conditions are typically associated with this patient’s skin lesions?
explanation:
Diabetes mellitus
The examination findings in this patient are consistent with vitiligo. Vitiligo tends to be associated with other autoimmune diseases (such as in this case where there is associated alopecia areata), although it can occur in the absence of other autoimmune conditions. Insulin-dependent diabetes is associated with vitiligo; therefore both type 1 and type 2 can be associated with it.

Cushing’s syndrome
Cushing’s syndrome is incorrect. The examination findings in this patient are consistent with vitiligo. There is no particular association between Cushing’s syndrome and vitiligo. Vitiligo tends to be associated with autoimmune diseases (such as in this case where there is associated alopecia areata), and Cushing’s syndrome is not an autoimmune condition; the most common cause is administration of exogenous steroids. Other causes include adrenal hyperplasia or adenomas, or a pituitary adenoma (Cushing’s disease). Cushing’s syndrome is associated with acanthosis nigricans, a velvety-like skin lesion found in the axilla.

Nelson’s syndrome
Nelson’s syndrome is incorrect. Nelson’s syndrome is an extremely rare condition where a patient develops a pituitary adenoma secreting adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH) following bilateral adrenal resection for Cushing’s disease. It can be life-threatening. The examination findings in this patient are consistent with vitiligo, which is typically associated with other autoimmune diseases (such as in this case where there is associated alopecia areata). Nelson’s syndrome is not an autoimmune disease and is not known to be associated with vitiligo.

Polymyositis
Polymyositis is incorrect. The examination findings in this patient are consistent with vitiligo, which is typically associated with other autoimmune diseases (such as in this case where there is associated alopecia areata). Polymyositis is a connective tissue disease, and although autoantibodies may be positive (anti-Jo1) it is not typically associated with vitiligo.

Toxic multinodular goitre
Toxic multinodular goitre is incorrect. The examination findings in this patient are consistent with vitiligo, which is typically associated with autoimmune conditions (such as in this case where there is associated alopecia areata). A toxic multinodular goitre is not autoimmune; instead it is caused by germline mutations leading to overproduction of thyroid hormones from autonomous nodules. VitiligoA 64-year-old man presented with a 2 month history of a progressive rash. He also complained of 4 months of loose stools, persistent headache and mild confusion. Three months previously he had been admitted to hospital with pneumonia but otherwise he had no past medical history. There was no family history of similar conditions. On examination he had an erythematous rash with some scaling over his face (with sparing of the upper lip), and neck. The same rash was present on the dorsum of the hands with a clearly demarcated edge at the wrist. Investigations.

stem: What is the likely cause of his rash?
explanation:
Pellagra
Pellagra is caused by chronic niacin (vitamin B 3) deficiency, and is characterised by the three Ds: photosensitive dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia. Pellagra can also be seen in conditions affecting protein metabolism such as carcinoid syndrome. The abnormal LFTs here do raise the possibility of pellagra due to underlying carcinoid with hepatic metastases.

Cefuroxime therapy
Cefuroxime therapy is incorrect. The distribution and nature of this patient’s rash suggests photosensitivity. Combined with the diarrhoea and confusion, pellagra is the most likely diagnosis. There are many antibiotics that do cause photosensitive rashes, particularly tetracyclines (e.g. doxycycline), quinolones (e.g. ciprofloxacin), or sulfonamides. However, cefuroxime is a second generation cephalosporin that is not known to cause a photosensitive rash.

Hereditary haemochromatosis
Hereditary haemochromatosis is incorrect. Haemochromatosis causes a slate grey discolouration in the skin due to the deposition of iron, but does not cause any photosensitive rashes. This patient’s symptoms and signs are better explained by pellagra (vitamin B3 deficiency) leading to the three Ds of diarrhoea, dementia and a photosensitive dermatitis.

Porphyria cutanea tarda
Porphyria cutanea tarda is incorrect. Although cutaneous porphyria does cause a photosensitive rash (due to oxidative damage from photo-excited porphyrins in the skin), it could not explain the symptoms of confusion and diarrhoea. These are much better explained by a diagnosis of pellagra leading to the three Ds of diarrhoea, dementia and photosensitive dermatitis. Furthermore, porphyria cutanea tarda is typically hereditary (this patient has no family history).

Systemic sclerosis
Systemic sclerosis is incorrect. Systemic sclerosis causes various skin changes including taut, shiny skin, telangiectasis, salt and pepper discolouration, ulceration and sclerodactyly. However, it does not cause erythematous and scaly rashes. Furthermore, this patient’s rash is consistent with photosensitivity, which is not a feature of systemic sclerosis. Although diarrhoea is a common symptom in systemic sclerosis due to small bowel bacterial overgrowth, this patient’s constellation of symptoms would be better explained by pellagra (vitamin B3 deficiency) leading to the three Ds of dementia, diarrhoea and photosensitive dermatitis.

stem: A 23-year-old man presented with a six month history of an itchy rash. On examination, he had purple, scaly plaques underneath the waistband of his jeans where his skin had been rubbed by the fabric. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lichen planus
This patient’s rash demonstrates the Koebner phenomenon, where new disease lesions develop at the site of skin injury. Lichen planus, psoriasis and vitiligo are the only conditions that demonstrate a true Koebner phenomenon, where new lesions form at sites of skin injury. Typically, these lesions are linear as they follow the pattern of the skin injury. As this patient has an itchy, pigmented rash, lichen planus is the most likely diagnosis.

Atopic eczema
Atopic eczema is incorrect. This patient’s rash demonstrates the Koebner phenomenon, where new disease lesions develop at the site of skin injury; this is not observed in eczema. The only skin conditions that demonstrate a true Koebner phenomenon are lichen planus (the most likely diagnosis here as the rash is pigmented and itchy), psoriasis and vitiligo.

Herpes simplex
Herpes simplex is incorrect. This patient’s rash demonstrates the Koebner phenomenon, where new disease lesions develop at the site of skin injury; this is not seen in herpes simplex. Herpes simplex causes cold sores (predominantly type 1) or anogenital herpes (predominantly type 2). Only lichen planus (the most likely diagnosis here as the rash is pigmented and itchy), psoriasis and vitiligo demonstrate a true Koebner response.

Kaposi sarcoma
Kaposi sarcoma is incorrect. Kaposi sarcoma is an AIDs-defining illness in HIV, with dark red or purple patches appearing throughout the skin or in the oral mucosa. It can also arise idiopathically in a classical form, or in any patient with severe immunosuppression. This patient’s rash demonstrates the Koebner phenomenon, where new disease lesions develop at the site of skin injury; Kaposi sarcoma does not demonstrate this. The Koebner phenomenon is only seen in lichen planus (the most likely diagnosis here as the rash is pigmented and itchy), psoriasis and vitiligo.

Lichen sclerosus
Lichen sclerosus is incorrect. Lichen sclerosus is predominantly a genital and perianal skin condition whose cause is not understood, though it may be autoimmune-mediated. It results in thickened, scarred patches of skin or genital mucosa. This patient’s rash demonstrates the Koebner phenomenon, where new disease lesions develop at the site of skin injury. Lichen sclerosus does not demonstrate the Koebner phenomenon, where new disease lesions develop at the site of skin injury; only lichen planus, psoriasis and vitiligo demonstrate a true Koebner phenomenon. Lichen planus is the most likely diagnosis in this patient.

stem: Which of the following is the most useful next test?
explanation:
Anti-mitochondrial antibody
Pyoderma gangrenosum, the likely cause of this patient’s shin lesion, is associated with both autoimmune hepatitis and primary biliary cholangitis (PBC). The predominant elevation in ALP here coupled with a prolonged period of tiredness and itching fits best with a diagnosis of PBC, where anti-mitochondrial antibodies are present in over 90% of patients with the disease.

Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) testing
The skin rash seen here is consistent with pyoderma gangrenosum, with an initial nodular rash which progressed to form an ulcer with a boggy base and raised inflammatory border. Although pyoderma is seen in ANCA-positive vasculitis, the abnormal liver function tests (LFTs) here with a predominant rise in ALP are more suggestive of PBC, where anti-mitochondrial antibodies are likely to be positive.

Human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-B27
Pyoderma gangrenosum is seen with increasing frequency in patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), where HLA-B27 is likely to be positive; the absence of bowel symptoms here counts against a diagnosis of IBD. The isolated liver symptoms coupled with a raised ALP are much more consistent with a diagnosis of PBC.

Liver biopsy
If the ALP is elevated but the AMA is negative, alternative diagnoses should be considered. A liver biopsy should only be obtained if additional noninvasive testing does not yield an alternative diagnosis.

Rheumatoid factor (RF)
Positive RF is found in both patients with cryoglobulinaemia and those with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), both of which are causes of pyoderma gangrenosum. There is no evidence to suggest either RA or cryoglobulinaemia as drivers for this patient’s symptoms, while the liver symptoms and signs are a pointer towards PBC as the underlying diagnosis.

stem: Which of the following antibodies is most likely to be positive?
explanation:
Anti-nuclear antibodies
This patient is most likely to have systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), as evidenced by a classical photosensitive rash and small joint polyarthritis in the presence of a negative rheumatoid factor (RF) test. 95% or more of patients with symptoms of active SLE have anti-nuclear antibodies, although they are not specific for the diagnosis. Anti-ds DNA is more specific but only positive in around 70%; anti-Sm (Smith) antibodies are most specific, but only positive in 30–40% of patients.

Anti-ribosomal P antibodies
Anti-ribosomal P antibodies are found in patients with SLE, but they are thought to be most specific to lupus cerebritis, and we have no evidence of cerebral symptoms here, making this less likely to be a feature of her disease.

Anti-smooth muscle antibodies
Anti-smooth muscle antibodies are most commonly associated with autoimmune hepatitis. Patients may complain of lethargy and itching with autoimmune hepatitis for some weeks/months before they present to medical services, where the predominant picture on liver function testing is elevated transaminases.

Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (cANCA)
Anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (cANCA) cANCA is most strongly associated with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA). Patients with GPA often have symptoms of sinusitis before they present with more severe symptoms such as pulmonary haemorrhage. They also have evidence of renal vasculitis and may have episodes of mononeuritis.

Perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (pANCA)
Perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (pANCA) pANCA is seen in patients with ulcerative colitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, and in some patients with rheumatoid arthritis. It is not associated with SLE. Systemic Lupus Erythematosus A 45-year-old man of Chinese ethnic origin comes to the Emergency Department with a generalised erythematous rash, and extensive sloughing of skin, including from mucus membranes. He has a fever which has worsened significantly over the past 24 hours. A few days earlier, he started treatment with carbamazepine for partial epilepsy. Examination reveals extensive erythema with bullae and skin sloughing. He is pyrexial with a temperature of 38.8 °C.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?
explanation:
Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma
Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (NHL) makes up the majority of cases of paraneoplastic pemphigus at around 39%, and this fits with the patient’s age and prodromal symptoms of weight loss and night sweats. Unfortunately, paraneoplastic pemphigus appears to worsen even when underlying NHL is adequately treated. High-dose corticosteroids are the intervention of choice. Previously, prognosis was extremely poor, with mortality > 70% at one year. Now, up to 60% of patients can be managed for a number of years with combination systemic immunosuppressive agents.

Gastric cancer
This patient’s skin rash is suspicious of pemphigus. He has also lost weight and suffered from night sweats; both are suspicious of an underlying lymphoma. The anaemia with a reduced platelet count and elevated ESR are also supportive of a lymphoma diagnosis. Gastric cancer is only rarely associated with paraneoplastic pemphigus and around 9% of cases are down to an underlying carcinoma. Gastric cancer is sometimes associated with acanthosis nigricans, with hyperpigmentation and thickening of the skin under the axillae and the back of the neck in particular.

Malignant melanoma
The scenario described here is not suggestive of malignant melanoma. Hodgkin’s lymphoma, monoclonal gammopathy and melanoma make up only less than 1% each of cases of paraneoplastic pemphigus. Autoimmune bullous skin disorders can be seen in melanoma when patients are prescribed immune checkpoint inhibitors.

Sarcoma
The absence of signs of local malignancy count against a sarcoma as the underlying cause of this patient’s pemphigus. Types of sarcoma seen in pemphigus include liposarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, reticulum cell sarcoma and malignant nerve sheath tumours. Some rare retroperitoneal sarcomas are also identified as causes of pemphigus. In total, they make up only around 6% of cases of paraneoplastic pemphigus, however.

Thymoma
Thymomas make up around 6% of cases of paraneoplastic pemphigus. Thymoma is associated with both symptoms of local compression, including shortness of breath and localised chest pain, and with systemic autoimmune pathologies including myasthenia gravis. We are given no hints of these symptoms here, and the blood picture with other symptoms is more consistent with an underlying lymphoma.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Hepatitis B and C antibody screening
explanation:
No further investigation is needed
This patient has lichen planus as exemplified by the intensely itchy papular rash on the flexural surface of the wrists. The violet top and white streaks over the surface of the papules, known as Wickham's striae, fit with the diagnosis. Usually, the diagnosis is a clinical one, with the rash resolving slowly over a period of weeks to months.

Anti-mitochondrial antibodies
Although the diagnosis here of lichen planus is associated with primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), we are given no indication that this patient has symptoms of PBC. Lichen planus is a clinical diagnosis and usually no further investigations are needed unless there are atypical features of the rash.

Anti-tissue transglutiminase (tTG) antibodies
The rash of dermatitis herpetiformis is intensely itchy, but the distribution seen here is wrong. Dermatitis herpetiformis begins usually over the buttocks and the upper posterior thighs. There may well also be symptoms of coeliac disease. Strict avoidance of gluten is the most important intervention.

Hepatitis B and C antibody screening
Patients with hepatitis B or hepatitis C are twice as likely to have lichen planus as the general population, although, in this case, there is no reason to suspect exposure to viral hepatitis and carry out screening.

Skin biopsy
Skin biopsy is only required in the event that there are unusual features of the rash or it fails to resolve. Biopsy usually shows a 'saw-tooth' pattern of epidermal hyperplasia and vacuolar changes in the basal layer of the epidermis along with an intense upper dermal lymphohistiocytic infiltrate (mainly T cells). The changes initially develop around blood vessels at the dermal–epidermal junction.

stem: Which vitamin deficiency is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?
explanation:
Vitamin B 3
This patient has the triad of dementia, diarrhoea and dermatitis which is particularly prominent on the hands and around the neck. This is typical of a patient with vitamin B 3 (niacin) deficiency. In this age group, with a raised ALT on blood testing, there is a suspicion of underlying carcinoid syndrome, where tryptophan is consumed to serotonin and is therefore no longer available for conversion to niacin. This leads to an overall niacin-deficient state which improves with treatment of the underlying carcinoid tumours, usually with a somatostatin analogue.

Vitamin A
Vitamin A deficiency is rare in the United Kingdom, but is common in developing countries, particularly subSaharan Africa. In contrast to the dermatitis seen here, it presents with dry skin, dry hair and itching. Finger nails break easily and there is hyperkeratosis of the skin. Particularly important in vitamin A deficiency is eye disease, where there is night blindess, keratomalacia with thinning and ulceration of the cornea, and conjunctival dryness.

Vitamin B 6
Vitamin B 6, or pyridoxine, deficiency is rare, and occurs in association with pyridoxine-depleting drugs such as isoniazid, a very low consumption of protein, malabsorption and alcoholism. The skin rash seen is very similar to pellagra which is caused by vitamin B 3 deficiency. In this age group, without other pointers towards B 6 deficiency, carcinoid syndrome leading to a reduction in tryptophan available for conversion to niacin is more likely to be the diagnosis.

Vitamin B 12
B 12 deficiency does not present with the dermatitis described here. Peripheral neuropathy with loss of vibration and position sense are usual early presenting features. Glossitis, oral ulceration and pale skin with a yellow tinge are findings in B 12 deficiency. In this age group, pernicious anaemia would be considered a potential cause of the deficiency.

Vitamin D
Vitamin D deficiency in adults presents with proximal myopathy and bone pain. Skin erythema and itching is seen in patients with vitamin D deficiency, but the changes do not follow the pattern seen here. In vitamin D deficiency, low normal calcium and elevated alkaline phosphatase are usual laboratory findings.

stem: Which of the following is the most useful next investigation for this patient?
explanation:
Abdominal ultrasound scan
This patient has symptoms of niacin (vitamin B 3) deficiency, with pellagra and the triad of diarrhoea, dermatitis and dementia. Given an enlarged liver and abnormal liver function, the possibility of underlying carcinoid syndrome is raised with hepatic metastases. For this reason, an ultrasound is advised, which is likely to demonstrate the liver lesions. 24-hour 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), a metabolite of serotonin, is likely to be elevated. Tryptophan is an amino acid which is a precursor to niacin and serotonin; in carcinoid syndrome there is excess serotonin production, leading to a deficiency of niacin production. Treatment of this patient will involve niacin supplementation and an agent to reduce tumour activity such as a somatostatin analogue.

Anti-tissue transglutaminase (TTG) antibodies
Although there is a second peak of coeliac disease in the seventh and eighth decades of life, and it is associated with diarrhoea, the rash here does not fit with a diagnosis of coeliac, nor does the enlarged liver with raised ALT. Coeliac disease may be associated with dermatitis herpetiformis, where there is a vesicular, highly itchy rash, particularly over the bottom and the upper posterior thighs.

Autoimmune profile
An autoimmune profile is unlikely to reveal the cause of this patient’s skin lesions. There is a risk that it may indeed reveal a weakly positive autoantibody that has no link to this patient’s underlying disease. Given the features of pellagra and liver dysfunction, ruling out carcinoid syndrome with liver metastases is much more important.

Small bowel biopsy
Small bowel biopsy is usually performed in patients with diarrhoea and symptoms of malabsorption to confirm a diagnosis of coeliac disease or to rule out alternatives. Here, although the patient has diarrhoea, abnormal liver function tests and findings on examination fit much more with underlying carcinoid syndrome. Where small bowel biopsy is indicated and confirms coeliac disease, avoidance of gluten is the most important step in therapy.

Vitamin D levels
Although the ALP is elevated here, the elevation in ALT fits more with this being due to a primary hepatic cause, rather than being bony in origin. Features of vitamin D deficiency in adults (osteomalacia) include proximal bone pain and muscle weakness.

stem: A 22-year-old man has returned from a summer season working in Ibiza. He is concerned as he has noticed a patch of skin on his abdomen that has become depigmented in comparison to the tan on the rest of his upper body. There is fine scaling over the area of depigmentation. He is otherwise well. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his depigmentation?
explanation:
Malassezia globosa infection
This patient has pityriasis versicolor, characterised by an area of depigmentation, which usually occurs over an area of skin which is covered by occlusive clothing or is more subject to sweating. It is more likely to occur in hotter periods of weather, or where individuals have been spending time in a hotter country. Malassezia globosa is the fungus responsible for pityriasis versicolor, and infection is thought to lead to apoptosis of melanocytes, which account for the depigmentation seen. Topical antifungal agents are the intervention of choice.

Autoimmune melanocyte destruction
Vitiligo leads to the autoimmune destruction of melanocytes. It causes patchy depigmentation across a much wider area of skin than is apparent here and occurs more commonly in patients with other autoimmune diseases such as coeliac disease, type I diabetes and autoimmune thyroid disease.

Human herpes virus 6 infection
Human herpes virus 6 infection has been implicated as a potential cause of pityriasis rosea, as has herpes virus 7. Rosea-like rashes are also seen in some patients who take ACE inhibitors, metronidazole and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). A primary plaque erythematous plaque, known as a 'herald patch', is found on the abdomen or chest, and is followed by a distinctive, generalised itchy rash 1–2 weeks later.

Streptococcus pyogenes infection
Streptococcus pyogenes leads to superficial skin infection with erythema and crusting yellow exudate. For limited bacterial skin infection, topical antibiotics such as fucidin ointment are an appropriate intervention.

Trichophyton rubrum infection
Trichophyton rubrum is the cause of tinea. Infections lead to a rash which grows outwards, creating a ring-like pattern of skin changes with an active edge where the fungus is growing. This is where the term ‘ringworm’ has been coined from. For most skin infections, it is sufficient to apply a topical antifungal twice a day to achieve clearance.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely cause of his skin rash?
explanation:
Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) infection
This patient has pityriasis lichenoides et varioliformis acuta (PLEVA), characterised by an initial area of erythema which develops rapidly into multiple pus-filled papules. The aetiology of PLEVA is unknown, but a number of diseases are associated with the development of PLEVA. These include: toxoplasmosis EBV human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) cytomegalovirus parvovirus (fifth disease) Staphylococcus aureus septicaemia group A beta-haemolytic streptococcal infection. In this case, the recent pharyngitis and atypical lymphocytes on blood film are strong pointers towards EBV as the underlying diagnosis. PLEVA often resolves on its own with resolution of the precipitating infection; in the event that it persists, then topical corticosteroids and systemic immunomodulators are potential treatment options.

Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma
Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma is a disease most often found in the elderly, and symptoms are usually widespread. They can include: erythematous itchy rash covering large portions of the body enlarged lymph nodes alopecia thickened skin on the palms of the hands and soles of the feet ectropion.

Influenza
The rash is consistent with PLEVA, which is not associated with influenza infection. Skin rashes per se are not commonly associated with influenza infection, and the clinical scenario is more consistent with EBV.

Parvovirus infection
Parvovirus is a common childhood infection and it can precipitate an episode of PLEVA, the skin rash described here, although it does not fit with the clinical scenario as described. Parvovirus is also known as ‘slapped cheek’ disease, because patients often present with bright red, erythematous cheeks.

Toxoplasmosis
Toxoplasmosis is a known precipitant of PLEVA, but generalised toxoplasma infection with symptoms does not occur in immunocompetent patients. The sore throat and atypical lymphocytes seen on the blood film are also not in keeping with toxoplasmosis.

stem: A 19-year-old woman comes to the Dermatology Clinic for review. She had an episode of Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) infection, the symptoms of which have now resolved. However, she is now left with a papular rash affecting her abdomen and chest that she finds very distressing. Each of the papules is 0.5–1.5 cm across, and they are filled with pus. She asks about treatment for the rash. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Topical tacrolimus
This patient has pityriasis lichenoides. Topical tacrolimus is the intervention of choice because it avoids exposure to corticosteroids in a young patient and has been used successfully to treat patients with the condition, which was potentially triggered by EBV infection. It is potentially effective because it modulates Tcell function, and T cells are thought to be closely involved in the pathogenesis of pityriasis lichenoides. The tacrolimus is applied twice a day.

Oral co-amoxiclav
This patient’s rash is consistent with pityriasis lichenoides that has now become chronic. Although the EBV infection has now resolved, the rash has continued, and the patient is distressed by it. The rash does not respond to antibiotic therapy because it is thought to be due to a chronic inflammatory process which may be Tcell mediated.

Oral prednisolone
Although this patient has chronic pityriasis lichenoides, which is thought to be due to a chronic inflammatory process, alternatives exist to systemic corticosteroids for treatment of the condition. In this case, the fact that she is only 19 prompts us to avoid higher doses of systemic corticosteroids.

Topical 0.05% clobetasol
Topical clobetasol should be avoided if possible. Concerns in recent years about systemic side-effects of topical steroids delivered over a potentially large skin area have promoted a move towards non-steroidal topical therapies.

Topical fucidin
Topical fucidin is not of value because the skin rash is not bacterial in origin. The most likely diagnosis is chronic pityriasis lichenoides, related to previous EBV, and driven by a chronic inflammatory process, likely to be in part mediated by T-cell overactivity.

stem: An 18-year-old man presents to the clinic for review. He has developed an erythematous macular rash, with a number of small lesions radiating out from a central larger patch in a Christmas tree pattern. He tells you that the larger patch, which measures around 5–6 cm across, appeared a few days before the smaller lesions. The rash is mildly itchy and is otherwise well. The rash is salmon pink in colour. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
Reassurance
Reassurance is the most appropriate step here. This patient has pityriasis rosea which may be related to herpes virus infection, although the exact aetiology is currently unknown. A herald patch of erythema is seen first, followed by a number of smaller erythematous lesions which develop in a Christmas tree pattern. No treatment is warranted and the rash resolves spontaneously over a number of days/weeks. No interventions are proven to be of benefit, although topical corticosteroids or oral antihistamines may be of value in treating itch for some patients.

Oral prednisolone
This patient’s rash is consistent with pityriasis rosea, the aetiology of which is unknown, but it may be related to viral infection with human herpes virus 6 or human herpes virus 7. There is no value in oral prednisolone in this situation because the rash resolves spontaneously over a number of days. Oral sedative antihistamines are occasionally prescribed to control itching in the condition.

Topical calcipotriol
Topical vitamin D 3 (calcipotriol) is used in the treatment of guttate psoriasis. Guttate psoriasis is an alternative diagnosis, although much greater inflammation, with skin scaling over plaques, would be expected. It has no value in the treatment of pityriasis rosea.

Topical corticosteroids
This patient has pityriasis rosea, and although topical corticosteroids are a possible intervention to treat itching in the condition, there is no randomised controlled clinical trial evidence to support their use. Topical corticosteroids are indicated for the treatment of psoriasis, but the absence of marked inflammation or skin scaling/hyperkeratosis counts against psoriasis as the diagnosis here.

Ultraviolet (UV) light therapy
UV light therapy is not proven in the treatment of pityriasis rosea. It is used in the treatment of guttate psoriasis, where a greater level of skin inflammation and skin scaling would be expected than that seen here. Pityriasis roseaA 25-year-old healthcare assistant comes to the Dermatology Clinic for review. She has developed an extensive erythematous papular rash which she describes as intensely itchy. The itching is apparently worse at night, particularly in the web spaces between the fingers of both hands. Examination confirms the presence of scratch marks over the arms and upper body; the palms of the hands and soles of the feet appear to have been spared from the rash.

stem: An 18-year-old man comes to the Dermatology Clinic for review. He is concerned by some skin changes he has noticed. He has pseudoxanthoma elasticum with ‘plucked chicken’ skin around his neck, and lax, saggy folds of skin affecting both axillae. Which of the following complications is he most likely to suffer from?
explanation:
Upper GI haemorrhage
Upper GI haemorrhage is a significant problem in patients with pseudoxanthoma elasticum. It can be seen early in the disease and happen without warning, because calcified submucosal vessels in the stomach are thought to be very fragile. Bleeding is also seen from the urinary tract, and pseudoxanthoma may be a cause of cerebral haemorrhage in some patients.

Aortic stenosis
Accelerated atherosclerosis is seen in pseudoxanthoma elasticum because of calcification of the elastic media and intima of blood vessels. This is the most common cardiovascular symptom of pseudoxanthoma, seen in 30% of patients. Aortic stenosis is not the most common valvular disorder – mitral valve prolapse is the most common feature.

Lens dislocation
Lens dislocation is not usually seen in pseudoxanthoma. The disease is characterised by angioid streaks, which are also seen in patients with Paget’s disease. Fibrovascular ingrowth affecting the retina can lead to retinal haemorrhages, a serious and significant complication of pseudoxanthoma.

Lower gastrointestinal (GI) haemorrhage
Lower GI haemorrhage is seen less commonly versus upper GI haemorrhage in patients with pseudoxanthoma. This is more likely to occur from the stomach. Bleeding may also be seen from the urinary tract.

Thoracic aorta dissection
Aortic dissection is seen in Marfan syndrome, not normally in pseudoxanthoma elasticum. Intermittent claudication is the most common presenting feature of cardiovascular disease in people with pseudoxanthoma. Calcification of renal artery vessels can drive renovascular disease, hypertension and accelerated coronary artery disease. Mitral valve prolapse is the most common valvular disorder seen.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely cause of her skin changes?
explanation:
Melasma
Melasma is characterised by increased skin pigmentation over sun-exposed areas, predominantly the cheeks, and the pattern is usually symmetrical. Although pregnancy and the use of the combined oral contraceptive pill is recognised to worsen melasma, it can also be seen without an obvious precipitant, particularly in patients with naturally increased skin pigmentation. Year-round sun protection/use of sun block is recommended for patients with melasma, in conjunction with camouflage cream where patients want to use it. Skin lightening creams are not routinely recommended as there is a question around them being carcinogenic in animal studies.

Lentigo maligna
Lentigo maligna is an early form of melanoma in which the malignant cells are confined to the epidermis. It is often reported as ‘in situ’ melanoma. It is most likely to occur on sun-damaged skin areas, so the face is a very common site in which to find these lesions. The extensive nature of these lesions, affecting both cheeks, counts against them being due to an underlying malignancy.

Makeup allergy
Makeup allergy may affect the cheeks, but an erythematous rash akin to dermatitis would be expected, rather than the increased melanosis described here. It would also be unusual for the rash to be confined only to the cheeks.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
SLE is associated with an erythematous rash on sun-exposed skin areas. It is also associated with other features such as small joint polyarthritis and evidence of renal vasculitis which are not seen here in a patient with no other medical history and normal blood tests.

Vitiligo
Vitiligo is associated with skin depigmentation because of autoimmune destruction of melanocytes rather than increased skin pigmentation. It does not therefore fit with the clinical scenario here. Vitiligo is seen more commonly in patients with other autoimmune conditions, such as coeliac disease and type I diabetes.

stem: A 27-year-old woman of Middle Eastern origin comes to the clinic for review. She has noted increased skin pigmentation over both cheeks during the past few months. Of note is that her weight has increased by 4 kg, she feels tired and lethargic and she has not had a menstrual period for four months. You confirm symmetrical increased skin pigmentation over both cheeks 5–6 cm in diameter. Which of the following is the most useful next investigation?
explanation:
Urine pregnancy test
This patient has melasma with typical symmetrical areas of increased skin pigmentation affecting both cheeks. Patients with darker skin types, including those from the Mediterranean and Middle East, are at increased risk of developing melasma. Increased sun exposure and exposure to oestrogens, either from pregnancy or from the oral contraceptive pill, are risk factors for worsening of symptoms. Given the weight gain and absence of menses, pregnancy is the most likely cause of the rash seen here. Use of sun block is key to reducing progression of skin pigmentation once other causes have been ruled out.

Fasting glucose
Although this patient has increased in weight and she is from a population at increased risk of developing type II diabetes, we are given no indication that this may be the problem. She is very young at only 27, and the cessation of menses, coupled with likely melasma, is much more consistent with pregnancy as the underlying cause of her presentation.

Morning cortisol
Autoimmune adrenal insufficiency is associated with increased skin pigmentation, but this is not confined to the face only. Adrenal insufficiency is also associated with weight loss, anorexia and persistent nausea, often in addition there are symptoms of postural hypotension. A morning cortisol is therefore not useful here.

Prolactin
Hyperprolactinaemia is not a cause of melasma, the underlying skin condition here. Hyperprolactinaemia is a cause of amenorrhoea, but the other symptoms including weight gain are a better pointer towards pregnancy. Other symptoms of hyperprolactinaemia include loss of libido and galactorrhoea.

Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)
Hypothyroidism leads to weight gain and menorrhagia, rather than the absence of menses reported here. It is also classically described as leading to a peaches and cream complexion rather than the increased skin pigmentation seen here, and hair often becomes brittle.

stem: A 59-year-old woman presents to the Dermatology Clinic with vulval itching and pain on sexual intercourse which has increased significantly over the past 3–4 months. She has examined herself and notes some areas of white, thickened skin around the vulva. You note the thickened skin and evidence of vulval scarring. Routine bloods are unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lichen sclerosus
Lichen sclerosus is characterised by white, atrophic skin patches and scarring, over the ano-genital region in both men and women. It accounts here for the patches seen on examination, and the chronic itching and pain on intercourse over the past few months. A reducing dose of topical clobetasol 0.05% is usually prescribed, where the corticosteroid is applied nightly for the first month, then alternate nights for the second month, then for the third month it is used twice per week. At the end of this time, the response to therapy is assessed.

Chronic candida infection
Chronic candida is more likely to lead to areas of erythema with scarring, and white adherent discharge, rather than the presentation described here with atrophied, pale areas of skin. In the event that chronic candida fails to respond to local therapy with a clotrimazole pessary, or to a single high dose of fluconazole, then a week’s course of 50 mg fluconazole is a logical next step.

Lichen planus
Lichen planus is a pruritic, papular eruption. The papules are violet and topped with fine white streaks. They are seen most commonly on the flexural surface of both wrists. Mucous membranes are also commonly involved where white lace like lesions are seen on the inside of the mouth. Lichen planus may resolve spontaneously within a the course of a year. Topical steroids may be used when lesions are particularly itchy.

Pityriasis rosea
Pityriasis rosea is an itchy erythematous skin rash with scaling, that usually begins as a herald patch, around 10 cm across, on the torso. Over a few days, it progresses to a generalised rash over the upper body with smaller areas of erythema. The cause is unclear, although it may be triggered by a viral illness. Symptoms may take up to ten weeks to completely resolve and no treatment is needed.

Vitiligo
Vitiligo is an autoimmune disorder which results in T-cell mediated destruction of melanocytes. This leads to patchy areas of skin depigmentation, which are usually not confined to one area, and are seen most often on the face, neck, forearms, feet and the dorsum of the hands. Vitiligo is seen more commonly in patients with other autoimmune diseases such as coeliac disease, type I diabetes and autoimmune thyroid disease.

stem: A 65-year-old woman presents to the Dermatology Clinic with chronic itching affecting her vulval region. She has hypertension and type II diabetes and takes a range of medications for cardiovascular disease and glucose control. Examination in the clinic reveals multiple areas of white, scarred skin over the vulva. You suspect a diagnosis of lichen sclerosus. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
Topical clobetasol therapy
Topical clobetasol 0.05% is the initial intervention of choice for lichen sclerosus, the diagnosis here. Biopsy is not required because there are no unusual features of this patient’s disease. The cream is applied daily for the first month, every other day in the second month, then twice a week for the third month. Response is reassessed and biopsy instituted in the event that there is an inadequate response to treatment.

Autoimmune profile
Although lichen sclerosus may be autoimmune in origin, an autoimmune profile is only indicated if there are signs of a systemic autoimmune disease, such as symptoms of hypo- or hyperthyroidism. In this case, there are no symptoms of systemic disease, so blood testing is not of value and may only increase patient anxiety with little gain.

Herpes simplex testing
Herpes simplex testing is only of value in patients with erosive disease. Given there is no sign of erosions here, herpes simplex screening is not required. Where there is erythema and erosive disease in addition to the white sclerotic lesions, candida screening should also be considered.

Lesion biopsy
Lesion biopsy is not normally required in lichen sclerosus where there are no abnormal features, as here. It is usually considered at diagnosis when young adult women present with the lesions, there are extragenital lesions or pigmented lesions.
