Biopsy is also essential where lesions do not respond to treatment.

Oral ciclosporin
Ciclosporin is only instituted for patients with refractory lichen sclerosus. The impact of systemic immunomodulators is, however, debated for lichen sclerosus, with small open label studies suggesting a much greater impact in comparison to subsequent double blind studies or clobetasol.

stem: A 33-year-old woman reports that some of her nails have changed. Which one of the following is most associated with onycholysis?
explanation:
Doxycycline
Onycholysis is separation of the nail plate from the nail bed, generally extending from the free edge of the nail. It is relatively commonly seen in psoriatic nail disease. Many other causes have been described, including trauma, infection and drugs such as tetracyclines and psoralens.

Arsenic poisoning
Arsenic poisoning is incorrect. Arsenic poisoning has been associated with Mees’ lines (transverse lines across the nail plate) but not onycholysis.

Bullous pemphigoid
Bullous pemphigoid is incorrect. Onycholysis is recognised in pemphigus rather than pemphigoid.

Mycoplasma pneumonia
Mycoplasma pneumonia is incorrect. There are no reports of onycholysis occurring in association with mycoplasma infection.

Pityriasis rosea.

stem: A 20-year-old woman with acne has been started on isotretinoin. Which one of the following statements best applies to treatment with isotretinoin?
options: It can cause hyperkalaemia and hence electrolytes should be checked every month
It is contraindicated in patients with renal artery stenosis
Pregnancy should be avoided during and for 1 month after treatment
explanation:
Pregnancy should be avoided during and for 1 month after treatment
Isotretinoin is indicated for the treatment of acne in the following contexts: Severe or scarring disease Disease unresponsive to other treatments Recurrent relapse on stopping other treatments Significant associated psychosocial impact However, it causes marked dryness of the skin and mucous membranes, especially leading to cheilitis and sometimes epistaxis Dryness of the lips or the nasal mucosa can be managed with petroleum jelly Simple emollients may be required elsewhere It is a potent teratogen: the pregnancy prevention programme dictates that pregnancy must be excluded prior to its initiation; a barrier method of contraception is required in addition to a hormonal method or intrauterine device; a pregnancy test must be checked monthly; precautions should be maintained until a month after cessation Chateyes, with Other relatively common side-effects include difficulty wearing contact lenses due to dry myalgia after exercise and photosensitivity Increases in liver enzymes and triglycerides can occur, so monitoring is required Isotretinoin has anecdotally been associated with mood changes, including depression and even suicide attempts; studies have failed to show a link, although acne itself is well-recognised to have a major effect on psychological well-being; however, the possibility of a rare, idiosyncratic effect on mood from the drug cannot be excluded, so patients are warned of this possibility

It can cause hirsutism
It can cause hirsutism is incorrect. Isotretinoin does not cause hirsutism. Occasionally diffuse hair loss occurs.

It can cause hyperkalaemia and hence electrolytes should be checked every month
It can cause hyperkalaemia and hence electrolytes should be checked every month is incorrect. Isotretinoin does not cause hyperkalaemia; urea and electrolytes are usually monitored alongside the liver tests and lipids, as renal function is rarely affected.

It is associated with haemoptysis
It is associated with haemoptysis is incorrect. Isotretinoin is associated with epistaxis but not haemoptysis.

It is contraindicated in patients with renal artery stenosis
It is contraindicated in patients with renal artery stenosis is incorrect. Isotretinoin is not contra-indicated in renal artery stenosis: the drug has no effect on this or on blood pressure generally.

stem: A 25-year-old man presents with recurrent nocturnal convulsions. He has seven café au lait spots on the buttocks. Clinical examination of the nervous system was normal. Complete blood counts were normal with normal electrolytes and renal functions. Liver profile was normal. An ECG showed sinus rhythm. Which of the following would provide a diagnosis?
options: Slit lamp examination of the eye
explanation:
Slit lamp examination of the eye
The presence of at least two Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas) is one diagnostic criterion for neurofibromatosis type 1. Thus, a slit lamp examination will reveal the presence of Lish nodules. The diagnostic criteria for NF1 (two or more of seven) are: at least six café au lait spots (5 mm diameter in prepubertal patients and 1.5 cm in postpubertal patients) typically on the trunk axillary freckling and/or inguinal freckling at least two Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas) neurofibromas (more than one cutaneous neurofibroma or one plexiform neurofibroma) characteristic bone abnormalities optic nerve glioma diagnosis of NF1 in first-degree relative.

Computed tomography (CT) brain
Computed tomography (CT) brain is incorrect. Based on the available clinical history the most likely diagnosis is NF1. None of the diagnostic criteria for NF1 can be diagnosed with a CT brain.

Cutaneous biopsy of buttock lesion
Cutaneous biopsy of buttock lesion is incorrect. A biopsy is not needed for the confirmation or diagnosis of the dermatological manifestations.

EEG
EEG is incorrect. Interictal EEGs are negative more than 50% of the time. Even if the EEG is positive it will suggest a seizure activity but not a diagnosis of NF1. Seizure is not a diagnostic criterion for neurofibromatosis.

Echocardiogram
Cardiac involvement in neurofibromatosis is rare. Neurofibromas are occasionally identified near to or within the heart, including occasionally within atrial tissue. Notes Neurofibromatosis presents with cognitive deficits, learning disabilities, optic gliomas, seizures, headaches and progressive neurological deficits. Early cutaneous signs of neurofibromatosis include café au lait spots and axillary freckling. Diagnostic criteria for neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2) (one of the following): bilateral vestibular schwannoma a first-degree relative with NF2 and unilateral vestibular schwannoma or any two meningioma, schwannoma, glioma, neurofibroma, posterior subscapular lenticular opacities unilateral vestibular schwannoma and any two of meningioma, schwannoma, glioma, neurofibroma, posterior subcapsular lenticular opacities multiple meningiomas and unilateral vestibular schwannoma or any two of schwannoma, glioma, neurofibroma, cataract.

stem: A 25-year-old man presents with a well-defined patch of hair loss on the scalp surrounded by ‘exclamation mark’ hairs. The scalp skin appears normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Alopecia areata
Alopecia areata typically causes single or multiple, discrete, often round areas of complete baldness. It most commonly occurs on the scalp, but can affect the face or any hair-bearing part of the body. It is a form of non-scarring alopecia and lost hair may therefore regrow. Signs of disease Exclamation mark hairs – short, tapered hairs of a few millimetres in diameter are characteristic. There may be nail pitting. Autoimmune associations Alopecia areata is considered to be an autoimmune disease and may be seen in association with other diseases such as: Vitiligo Thyroid disease Pernicious anaemia Rheumatoid arthritis Diabetes. No specific antibody has been identified. Approximately one-third of patients have a positive family history, implying that a genetic component is involved. Prognosis The condition is very unpredictable. Many patients experience hair regrowth within 6–12 months – new hair is often fine and initially white; some find that new areas of alopecia appear as older ones regrow; others have a more progressive pattern. Some cases progress to complete loss of scalp hair (alopecia totalis) and occasionally complete loss of all hair (alopecia universalis). Treatment Alopecia areata is difficult to treat. Possible options include: Topical or intra-lesional steroids Topical minoxidil Contact allergen therapy Janus kinase inhibitors are a possible new avenue for treatment Some patients will benefit from a hairpiece or wig, false eyelashes or eyebrow tattooing.

Discoid lupus erythematosus
Discoid lupus erythematosus is incorrect. Discoid lupus erythematosus (DLE – also known as chronic cutaneous LE) is a form of scarring alopecia which causes well-defined erythematous plaques with scaling, atrophy and follicular plugging; these affect light-exposed areas of the body and are exacerbated by sunlight.

Telogen effluvium
Telogen effluvium is incorrect. Telogen effluvium is a cause of transitory, generalised, diffuse hair loss over the scalp; it is a disorder of the hair cycle and can lead to dramatic shedding over a short space of time; there is no scarring and regrowth usually occurs after a few weeks or months. It classically occurs a few months after high fever, stress, malnutrition, surgery or childbirth.

Tinea capitis
Tinea capitis is incorrect. Tinea capitis may give rise to well-defined areas of alopecia, but the scalp skin in the areas is not normal and complete baldness is not typical: scaling and broken hairs are usually seen; scarring is unusual unless there has been very florid or longstanding inflammation.

Trichotillomania
Trichotillomania is incorrect. Trichotillomania is the self-inflicted pulling out of one’s hair; there may be associated underlying psychological morbidity particularly in adult cases. Short, broken hairs are seen, differentiating it from the complete baldness of alopecia areata. Patches of hair loss tend to be unilateral and on the same side as the dominant hand.

stem: A 46-year-old man complains of facial redness. Examination shows macular erythema with prominent telangiectasia over the cheeks and nose. He also has papules and pustules, on the nose and chin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Rosacea
Rosacea gives rise to an acneiform, papulopustular eruption mainly on the central face (medial cheeks, nose, chin, glabellum); there is also often facial erythema because of increased lability and reactivity of the facial vasculature, the cause of which is unknown; patients often complain of flushing. There may be rhinophyma, characterised by hypertrophy of the nasal skin leading to a bulbous appearance. Ocular rosacea often co-exists, which includes conjunctivitis, blepharitis and keratitis. Women are more commonly affected, although it is men who tend to develop rhinophyma. Rosacea is not a sign of alcohol excess. Exacerbation The erythema may be exacerbated by: Sunlight Heat Alcohol Consumption of spicy foods. Distinguishing features Rosacea can be distinguished from acne by: The absence of comedones The distribution of the rash (rosacea is almost always confined to the face) Lack of scarring, which is very unusual in rosacea The effect of sunlight (which often brings about an improvement in acne) Age (acne is relatively rare in patients over the age of 30 and rosacea becomes more common around the age of 40). Treatment Patients with rosacea should be advised to avoid factors that provoke facial flushing; treatment is with topical metronidazole or azelaic acid; oral tetracycline antibiotics are usually effective, although resistant cases are sometimes treated with low-dose oral isotretinoin. Topical steroids should be avoided as their withdrawal leads to rebound exacerbation.

Acne vulgaris
Acne vulgaris is incorrect. Rosacea can be distinguished from acne by: The absence of comedones The distribution of the rash (rosacea is almost always confined to the face) Lack of scarring, which is very unusual in rosacea The effect of sunlight (which often brings about an improvement in acne) Age (acne is relatively rare in patients over the age of 30 and rosacea becomes more common around the age of 40).

Allergic contact dermatitis
Allergic contact dermatitis is incorrect. Allergic contact dermatitis may present with facial redness, but itching, dryness and scaling are prominent; papules and pustules are not seen.

Seborrhoeic dermatitis
Seborrhoeic dermatitis is incorrect. Seborrhoeic dermatitis (eczema) leads to mild erythema with rather greasy scaling; it commonly affects the scalp, eyebrows and nasolabial folds. Pustules are not a feature. It may co-exist with rosacea, complicating the diagnosis and treatment.

Systemic lupus erythematosus
Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is incorrect. The butterfly rash of SLE tends to be infiltrated and thus not macular. Papules and pustules are not a feature of SLE.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with yellowish mottling and overlying ‘goose bumps’ over the skin on her neck. The skin appears puckered. She is known to have mitral valve prolapse. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pseudoxanthoma elasticum
Pseudoxanthoma elasticum is a hereditary disorder of elastic tissue with calcification involving the skin, eyes and vasculature. Skin appearance The characteristic skin appearance is of yellow papules arranged in a linear or reticular configuration, coalescing into plaques most commonly over the neck; other flexural areas may be affected. The skin resembles that of a plucked chicken. Manifestations Vascular manifestations are: Renovascular hypertension (intimal occlusion of the renal arteries) Peripheral vascular disease and claudication Premature coronary artery disease (calcification of the internal elastic laminae of arteries) Mitral valve prolapse Bleeding from the gastrointestinal tract. Angioid streaks are found in 85% of patients: linear grey or dark-red streaks with irregular edges lying beneath the retinal vessels. Visual loss may occur due to macular involvement by a streak or scarring secondary to a choroidal/retinal haemorrhage. Visual acuity may decline in young patients.

Ehlers–Danlos syndrome
Ehlers–Danlos syndrome is incorrect. This comprises a group of inherited connective tissue disorders. These variably can result in hyperelastic or fragile skin, joint hypermobility and blood vessel fragility. Mitral valve prolapse can be a feature, but the plucked chicken skin appearance is not seen.

Marfan syndrome
Marfan syndrome is incorrect. This autosomal-dominantly inherited disorder of connective tissue does lead to specific skin signs, although striae may occur. Typical features include arachnodactyly and other bony abnormalities, lens dislocation, aortic aneurysm or dissection, and mitral valve prolapse.

Necrobiosis lipoidica
Necrobiosis lipoidica is incorrect. This relatively common disorder of unknown aetiology is associated with diabetes mellitus in some cases. It presents with shiny, atrophic plaques, usually on the legs.

Xanthoma disseminatum
Xanthoma disseminatum is incorrect. This rare form of non-Langerhans cell histiocytosis presents with numerous brownish papules on the face and trunk, which may coalesce extensively. About 40% of sufferers will have diabetes insipidus. It is not associated with mitral valve disease.

stem: A 54-year-old woman visits her GP with a skin rash that has appeared a few days after commencing clarithromycin for a lower respiratory tract infection. She has multiple circular lesions, varying in size from 1 to 3 cm, with three different shades of red. Most of these are on the hands and feet. Some of the palmar lesions are blistering centrally. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Erythema multiforme
Erythema multiforme is a reactive eruption, which is charactised by target lesions (concentric rings with a least three hues per individual lesion); these tend to predominate at acral sites and mucosal involvement is common. It is typically associated with infection, most commonly herpes simplex virus; it can also follow mycoplasma infection as is likely in this scenario; it has been associated with a variety of other viral infections including HIV and hepatitis viruses. Occasionally, erythema multiforme occurs as a drug eruption: culprit drugs include anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and penicillins.

Bullous drug eruption
Bullous drug eruption is incorrect. The term ‘bullous drug eruption’ is rather non-specific, as a variety of druginduced rashes can lead to blistering. It is not particularly unusual to see central blistering in lesions of erythema multiforme, which from the description in the scenario is clearly the diagnosis. Even if the case was clearly bullous erythema multiforme secondary to a drug, bullous drug eruption would not be sufficiently accurate as a diagnosis.

Erythema nodosum
Erythema nodosum is incorrect. Erythema nodosum is a reactive panniculitis that gives rise to tender lumps usually on the shins.

Granuloma annulare
Granuloma annulare is incorrect. Granuloma annulare gives rise to annular plaques (annular means ring-like, such that the centre of the lesion is relatively clear and the border relatively pronounced). Scaling is not seen. It is usually asymptomatic. It is more commonly seen in patients with diabetes.

Pityriasis rosea
Pityriasis rosea is incorrect. Pityriasis rosea begins with a ‘herald patch’, which is followed after a few days by a widespread truncal eruption of plaques with fine peripheral scaling. These are classically arranged in a Christmas tree configuration. The rash is typically asymptomatic and resolves after a few weeks. The cause is thought to be viral.

stem: An 81-year-old former farmer presents with a pigmented lesion on the cheek. It began as a light brown mark 10 years previously, but has gradually enlarged and developed some darker areas. It is asymptomatic. Examination shows a 2 cm diameter pigmented macule. It is mostly light brown in colour, but there are a few much darker areas. The borders are irregular and poorly defined. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lentigo maligna
Lentigo maligna (LM) is a form of melanoma in situ. It occurs on chronically sun-damaged skin, mostly in the elderly. The history is typically of a slowly evolving pigmented lesion. Clinically, LM is macular, ranging in size from a few millimetres to several centimetres; some are well defined and others have imperceptible borders; there tends to be irregularity of pigmentation. Excision is curative.

Bowen's disease
Bowen’s disease is incorrect, a form of squamous-cell carcinoma in situ, presents as a red, scaly plaque.

Pigmented basal cell carcinoma
Pigmented basal cell carcinoma is incorrect. Pigmented basal cell carcinoma is not macular and usually has characteristic features such as a rolled, pearly edge and telangiectasia, in addition to focal or global pigmentation.

Seborrhoeic keratosis
Seborrhoeic keratosis is incorrect. Although seborrhoeic keratosis is classically an elevated lesion with a ‘stuck on’ appearance, some lesions are completely flat. However, irregularity of pigmentation would be atypical and they are usually sharply demarcated.

Solar lentigo
Solar lentigo is incorrect. Solar lentigo can present identically to a flat seborrhoeic keratosis; it is usually uniformly light tan in colour and well defined. Variability of colour and progressive enlargement are suggestive of progression into LM.

stem: A 23-year-old woman presents to the dermatology clinic with a severe erythematous rash on her face. She returned from a holiday in Goa some 10 days ago, and you understand that on one of the last days of her holiday she paid for a henna tattoo on her left cheek. On examination you can see the henna tattoo is surrounded by intense erythema, with papules and vesicles that the patient says are extremely itchy. Which one of the following chemicals is most likely to have been contained in the henna tattoo and caused the reaction?
explanation:
p-Phenylaminediamine
A number of hair dyes and products used for temporary henna tattooing are known to contain pPhenylaminediamine (PPD). For this reason, individuals who want to undergo this type of procedure are recommended to have a test patch dyed first, so that if allergic dermatitis occurs, it can be identified before a large area of hair or prominent area of skin is treated. Topical corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment for the condition.

Formaldehyde
Formaldehyde is incorrect. Formaldehyde is a preservative not normally found in cosmetics, as it is known to be an irritant.

Isothiazolinones
Isothiazolinones is incorrect. Isothiazolinones are present in a number of cosmetics, and are another common cause of allergic contact dermatitis.

Lanolin
Lanolin is incorrect. Lanolin is widely used in cosmetics and has low allergenic potential.

Nickel
Nickel is incorrect. Patients who are prone to allergic contact dermatitis also often suffer from nickel allergy.

stem: Which one of the following is the most appropriate investigation?
explanation:
Patch testing
The distribution of the rash in this woman suggests contact dermatitis to nickel, which is often prevalent in belt buckles and cheaper costume jewellery, such as earrings or bangles. Patch testing is the investigation of choice, where small amounts of the suspected chemical responsible for the allergy are applied to the skin and left occluded for a period of 2 days. Occupation or planned occupation will dictate testing to a number of other allergens. It is not uncommon for patients allergic to nickel to also show cross-reactivity to latex, which may be a consideration if thinking of work where gloves are required to prevent exposure to hazardous materials.

Fungal culture
Fungal culture is incorrect. Fungal infection is extremely unlikely, given that the rash is occurring in the areas where she wears jewellery, rather than in moist skin creases where fungal infections tend to occur.

Radioallergosorbent testing (RAST)
Radioallergosorbent testing (RAST) is incorrect. RAST has fallen out of favour in recent years due to the availability of more specific immune testing.

Serum immunoglobulins
Serum immunoglobulins is incorrect. Immunoglobulins will not help confirm the diagnosis.

Skin biopsy
Skin biopsy is incorrect. A skin biopsy will not be diagnostic.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with a lesion on her forehead. She tells you that it has been there for some months and has slowly got larger; it is occasionally painful. On examination it measures 9 mm in diameter, the skin over the top is smooth and intact, and it appears to be filled with fluid. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Sebaceous cyst
The site and appearance of this lesion fits best with a sebaceous cyst. The cysts are mostly painless but occasionally become painful and inflamed, and may discharge caseous material. Surgical excision is the treatment of choice as they tend to refill if aspirated or merely incised. There are no sinister features to suggest that this is a carcinoma.

Basal cell carcinoma
Basal cell carcinoma is incorrect. Basal cell carcinomas are usually ulcers with rolling edges and a pearly colour.

Benign papule
Benign papule is incorrect. A benign papule is a diagnosis of exclusion, and is usually not fluid-filled.

Macular lesion
Macular lesion is incorrect. Macules are flat.

Skin nodule
Skin nodule is incorrect. The lesion is filled with fluid.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with an area of itchy erythema on the inside of his left thigh. He has developed crops of umbilicated papules on the inside of each thigh which he relates to sharing a towel at a sports club a few weeks earlier. He has tried using salicylic acid but the lesions have not improved. Over the papules on the left-hand side, there is an area of erythema with yellow crusting pus. What is the likely reason of the erythematous lesion on his left leg?
explanation:
Secondary bacterial infection
Given the area of skin affected by molluscum, coupled with likely skin scratching due to itching, secondary bacterial infection is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms. Topical antibiotics may be an option to resolve the lesion, although more extensive lesions will require oral therapy.

Disseminated secondary eczema
This patient has molluscum contagiosum, which is caused by the molluscum contagiosum virus 1 (MCV 1) virus in non-immunocompromised patients. The rash of disseminated secondary eczema (DSE) is usually spread across the whole area of molluscum, rather than being confined just to a small area of the lesions as is seen here. DSE is caused by a T-cell driven response to the virus and often precedes resolution of the disease.

Reaction to salicylic acid
Reaction to salicylic acid may lead to erythema, but it is likely to be spread across the whole area of molluscum, rather than one specific patch. Yellow crusting pus would be unexpected and probably indicates secondary bacterial infection in this case.

Secondary fungal infection
Secondary fungal infection is likely to be associated with a wider area of erythema and skin is usually moist and inflamed, rather than crusted with areas of pus as is seen here. Topical clotrimazole is the intervention of choice for secondary fungal infection.

Secondary herpes zoster infection
Herpes zoster infection exists confined to a single dermatome. It is associated with multiple discrete shingles blisters, rather than the erythema with crusting seen here. Where herpes zoster is seen, the duration of symptoms can be shortened if aciclovir is started as soon as possible after the rash appears.

stem: A pregnant woman started to notice lumps on her skin as well as freckles in her armpit. One of her relatives had similar problems. What is the most likely cause of her problem?
explanation:
Neurofibromatosis type 1
This patient’s symptoms are most likely to be due to peripheral neurofibromatosis (neurofibromatosis type 1, NF1), which is caused by a mutation on chromosome 17. There are multiple skin neurofibromas, café-au-lait patches and axillary freckling. Neurofibromas appear to be oestrogen responsive and may increase in number and size during pregnancy; axillary freckling also becomes more noticeable. Surgical excision of larger neurofibromas may be necessary for cosmetic reasons or where there are local pressure effects on the spinal cord. Inheritance of neurofibromatosis is autosomal dominant, which accounts for the presence of another case in the family.

Multiple melanoma
Multiple melanoma is incorrect. The lesions described here are not typical of melanoma.

Neurofibromatosis type 2
Neurofibromatosis type 2 is incorrect. Neurofibromatosis 2 (NF2) manifests predominantly with central lesions (schwannomas, meningiomas and ependymomas) rather than the skin (‘peripheral’) lesions described in this case.

Tuberous sclerosis
Tuberous sclerosis is incorrect. Tuberous sclerosis is associated with a number of skin manifestations including facial angiofibromas, periungal fibromas and ‘ash leaf spots’ (seen best with Woods ultraviolet lamp).

Underlying malignancy
Underlying malignancy is incorrect. This appears to be a less likely explanation of the presentation described here, especially given the family history of similar problems.

stem: A 33-year-old woman reports changes in a mole on the left shin. Which one of the following features is most suggestive of melanoma?
explanation:
Multiple colours
Moles usually arise in childhood but can develop during puberty and sometimes later. Melanoma is a malignant tumour of melanocytes, which mostly arises de novo but may occur in a preexisting mole. Signs of melanoma include asymmetry of pigmentation, irregularity in shape and border, and multiple colours; the history may indicate enlargement, increased irregularity, or darkening; bleeding without trauma should also raise suspicion.

Bleeding
Bleeding is incorrect. As noted above, bleeding without trauma can be a sign of melanoma. However, most melanomas do not have a history of bleeding and minor trauma may go unnoticed until bleeding ensues. Multiple colours, if present, are a more reliable indicator.

Cobblestoned surface
Cobblestoned surface is incorrect. A cobblestoned surface is commonly seen in benign compound naevi.

Depigmentation around the periphery
Depigmentation around the periphery is incorrect. A mole surrounded by depigmentation is termed a halo naevus and this is almost always benign.

New central elevation
New central elevation is incorrect. Some moles go through a normal maturation process from junctional to compound to intra-dermal. The transition from junctional to compound naevus gives rise to elevation, which often begins centrally.

stem: A 35-year-old man is admitted to hospital with Mycoplasma pneumonia. As an inpatient he developed a symmetrically distributed erythematous rash, with concentric rings of varying colours on the back of his hands, palms and forearms. He has also developed lesions in his mouth. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Erythema multiforme
Erythema multiforme is a reactive eruption, which is characterised by target lesions (concentric rings with at least three hues per individual lesion); these tend to predominate at acral sites, and mucosal involvement is common. It is typically associated with infection, most commonly herpes simplex virus; it can also follow Mycoplasma infection as in this scenario; it has been associated with a variety of other viral infections including HIV and hepatitis viruses. Occasionally, erythema multiforme occurs as a drug eruption: culprit drugs include anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and penicillins.

Erythema nodosum
Erythema nodosum is incorrect. Erythema nodosum is a reactive panniculitis that gives rise to tender lumps usually on the shins.

Erythrasma
Erythrasma is incorrect. Erythrasma is a superficial infection caused by Corynebacterium. It presents with reddish-brown macular discoloration usually in the axillary or groin flexures.

Guttate psoriasis
Guttate psoriasis is incorrect. Guttate psoriasis is classically triggered by streptococcal infection. It presents with small (< 1 cm), well-defined, erythematous scaly plaques.

Lichen planus
Mucosal involvement is common in lichen planus is incorrect. Lichen planus rash is typically composed of pruritic, violaceous papules. These are frequently seen on the flexor aspect of the wrists and around the ankles.

stem: A 66-year-old woman with a recent diagnosis of lung cancer presents with a rash. Of the following paraneoplastic conditions, which is she most likely to have?
explanation:
Dermatomyositis
Dermatomyositis is a rare disease in which a characteristic rash is associated with myositis. When it develops over the age of 40 years, about one third of patients prove to have an underlying carcinoma, most commonly of the lung. It is more common in females. Typical features include: a red or violaceous peri-orbital eruption known as the ‘heliotrope rash’; there may be associated oedema violaceous ‘Gottron’s’ papules over the knuckles linear violaceous changes over the dorsal surfaces of the fingers nail fold inflammation with dilated capillaries the ‘shawl sign’ describes erythema over the upper back and posterior neck weakness of the major proximal muscle groups is typical, although some patients will have skin involvement alone (‘amyopathic dermatomyositis’) rarely, involuntary muscles may be involved, leading to potentially dangerous or even fatal difficulties in swallowing or breathing • calcification can occur in juvenile dermatomyositis, but is uncommon in adults.

Ichthyosis
Acquired ichthyosis is incorrect. Acquired ichthyosis can be a manifestation of lymphoma.

Necrolytic migratory erythema
Necrolytic migratory erythema is incorrect. Necrolytic migratory erythema occurs with a glucagonoma.

Sweet’s syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis)
Sweet’s syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis) is incorrect. Sweet’s syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis) is associated with myeloproliferative disease and solid organ malignancy (e.g. breast, bowel, genitourinary tract); it can also occur secondary to drugs.

Tylosis
Tylosis is incorrect. Tylosis (a form of palmoplantar keratoderma) is an autosomal dominantly inherited condition, associated with carcinoma of the oesophagus.

stem: A 78-year-old woman attends the dermatology clinic for review after complete excision of a 2 cm basal cell carcinoma on the left temple. What is the best estimate of her disease-specific 5-year survival rate?
explanation:
100%
The prognosis of BCC is excellent and almost never proves fatal. Metastasis is extremely rare and usually only occurs in the context of neglected lesions, after perhaps 5– 10 years or more; by this time, the primary tends to be much larger than 2 cm. BCC is, however, locally destructive. Complete excision is the treatment of choice in most cases, and is curative. BCC is radiosensitive; the superficial subtype can also be treated in a variety of other ways, including photodynamic therapy and topical imiquimod. A higher risk of local recurrence is associated with the infiltrative (morphoeic) and micronodular subtypes, and the presence of perineural invasion.

20%
20% is incorrect. While basal cell carcinoma can be locally destructive, metastasis is extremely rare.

40%
40% is incorrect. While basal cell carcinoma can be locally destructive, metastasis is extremely rare.

60%
60% is incorrect. While basal cell carcinoma can be locally destructive, metastasis is extremely rare.

80%
80% is incorrect. While basal cell carcinoma can be locally destructive, metastasis is extremely rare.

stem: A 69-year-old man with a long history of stable, chronic plaque psoriasis presents with an exacerbation. This began during a recent hospital admission for myocardial infarction complicated by lower respiratory tract infection and acute renal injury. He was discharged a fortnight earlier. He was commenced on aspirin, clopidogrel, bisoprolol and simvastatin, and finished a course of clarithromycin 10 days ago. Which one of these drugs is most likely to have contributed to his skin problem?
explanation:
Bisoprolol
Psoriasis can be exacerbated by several classes of drug, notably beta blockers, antimalarials and lithium. Withdrawal of oral corticosteroids, particularly if sudden, can also precipitate a severe exacerbation. Physical or emotional stress can worsen psoriasis: this could be relevant in the case described in the scenario. Streptococcal infection classically precipitates guttate psoriasis.

Aspirin
Aspirin is incorrect as this drug would not be expected to worsen psoriasis.

Clarithromycin
Clarithromycin is incorrect as this drug would not be expected to worsen psoriasis.

Clopidogrel
Clopidogrel is incorrect as this drug would not be expected to worsen psoriasis.

Simvastatin
Simvastatin is incorrect as this drug would not be expected to worsen psoriasis.

stem: A 60-year-old lady presents with a 4-week history of generalised rash. She complains of areas of erythema and blistering, although only excoriations are visible today. On further questioning she also admits to difficulty eating. Her past medical history includes angina and coeliac disease; her medication includes aspirin, atenolol and hydralazine. She is subsequently reviewed by the dermatologists who perform a skin biopsy; the immunofluorescence results show immunoglobulin G (IgG) staining in the intercellular substance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pemphigus
She is the right age for pemphigus (40–60 years), which is characterised by flaccid blisters that erode/rupture more easily (compared to the tense, intact blisters of pemphigoid). Pemphigus also tends to involve the mucus membranes and patients may complain of pain on eating. The diagnosis is confirmed with immunofluorescence, which shows antibodies to the cells in the epidermis. Pemphigus is common in eastern countries and also in Jewish populations. Anti-desmoglein antibodies (types 1 and 3) can actually be measured in peripheral blood of patients with pemphigus in some centres. When large areas of skin are lost in pemphigus, fluid loss can produce severe metabolic changes; treatment therefore includes accurate fluid control as well as high-dose steroids, often for prolonged periods of time.

Allergic reaction
Allergic reaction is incorrect. An allergic reaction is unlikely to be associated with blistering.

Dermatitis herpetiformis
Dermatitis herpetiformis is incorrect. Although dermatitis herpetiformis is associated with coeliac disease, which she has, this is usually an intensely itchy rash found on the extensor surfaces of the limbs and often shows IgA.

Epidermolysis bullosa
Epidermolysis bullosa is incorrect. Epidermolysis bullosa is unusual at this late age.

Pemphigoid
Pemphigoid is incorrect. Patients with pemphigoid are usually older, and the blisters are usually tense and do not rupture easily. Pemphigoid will show antibodies directed at the basement membrane and type XVII collagen, and pemphigoid is associated with C3 deposition.

stem: You are reviewing a 20-year-old woman who has presented to the acute medical admissions ward with intermittent abdominal pain, depression and anxiety for the third occasion over the past 6 months.Porphyrin screening has revealed a diagnosis of acute intermittent porphyria (AIP). Which of the following statements best fits with the diagnosis of AIP?
options: It is associated with a defect in coproporphyrinogen oxidase
It is associated with alcohol consumption
It is due to a defect in uroporphyrinogen III synthase
IV haem arginate can be used in the treatment of acute attacks
Light-sensitive porphyrins lead to formation of bullae on the skin
explanation:
IV haem arginate can be used in the treatment of acute attacks
AIP occurs because of a defect in porphobilinogen deaminase. It leads to acute presentation with episodes of abdominal pain which may mimic acute abdomen, hypertension and psychiatric disturbance. Haem arginate can lead to resolution of episodes; IV glucose is not recommended as a first-line intervention because it may exacerbate hyponatraemia.

It is associated with a defect in coproporphyrinogen oxidase
It is associated with a defect in coproporphyrinogen oxidase is incorrect. Coproporphyrinogen oxidase is the enzyme which is defective in hereditary coproporphyria. This does present with acute symptoms, but is also associated with skin rashes.

It is associated with alcohol consumption
It is associated with alcohol consumption is incorrect. It is porphyria cutanea tarda which is associated with excess alcohol consumption.

It is due to a defect in uroporphyrinogen III synthase
It is due to a defect in uroporphyrinogen III synthase is incorrect. Reduced activity of uroporphyrinogen III synthase is seen in congenital erythropoeitic porphyria, which is associated with light-sensitive skin rashes.

Light-sensitive porphyrins lead to formation of bullae on the skin
Light-sensitive porphyrins lead to formation of bullae on the skin is incorrect. AIP is not a cutaneous porphyria, and is therefore only associated with acute intermittent presentation with hypertension and abdominal pain.

stem: Which of the following is the most useful next investigation?
explanation:
Skin biopsy
This patient has symptoms characteristic of pemphigus, and the absence of other symptoms and signs of systemic disease count against triggers for pemphigus, such as underlying malignancy. The most useful investigation therefore is a biopsy from the edge of a blister to confirm the diagnosis. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) demonstrates deposits of antibodies and other immune system components, such as complement. DIF is almost always positive and usually shows immunoglobulin G (IgG) deposited on the surface of the keratinocytes in and around the lesions. Intercellular deposition of IgG throughout the epidermis consists of anti-DSG1 and anti-DSG3 antibodies.

Anti-nuclear antibodies
Although anti-nuclear antibodies are often positive in patients with pemphigus vulgaris, which is the diagnosis here, they are not specific for the condition and are positive in a number of other conditions, including systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). In this case, the skin biopsy is much more useful in confirming the diagnosis. The absence of other symptoms outside the rash points much more towards pemphigus as the underlying cause of her symptoms.

Anti-Ro antibodies
Anti-Ro antibodies are found in patients with Sjögren syndrome and in patients with SLE. They are not specific to patients with pemphigus, the underlying diagnosis here. Anti-DSG3 and anti-DSG1 antibodies are found in patients with pemphigus. They are usually demonstrated with immune staining on biopsy, but can also be measured in peripheral blood.

Anti-tissue transglutaminase (TTG) antibodies
Anti-TTG antibodies are pathognomonic of coeliac disease, which is associated with an intensely itch vesicular rash worse over the buttocks and posterior thighs. It does not fit with the rash described here, characterised by extensive blistering. Anti-TTGs are therefore not of value.

Small bowel biopsy
Small bowel biopsy is indicated to confirm a diagnosis of coeliac disease, which is associated with dermatitis herpetiformis – an itchy, vesicular rash worse on the buttocks and tops of the thighs, rather than the generalised blistering rash described here. It is usually considered for confirmation of the diagnosis of coeliac after anti-TTG results are available.

stem: A 56-year-old man with a history of psoriasis comes to the Dermatology Clinic for review. He is taking a number of medications for hypertension that his GP has endeavoured to get under control over the past 4 months, but unfortunately this has been associated with a significant worsening of his skin rash. Which of the following agents is most associated with worsening of psoriasis?
explanation:
Bisoprolol
Bisoprolol is a beta-blocker and, like other beta-blockers, it may lead to or exacerbate psoriasis. Other medications commonly known to precipitate a flare of psoriasis include lithium, antimalarials and NSAIDs.

Amlodipine
Amlodipine is incorrect. Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker used against hypertension. It is known to cause peripheral oedema and occasionally drug rashes, but is not typically associated with the development of psoriasis.

Bendroflumethiazide
Bendroflumethiazide is incorrect. Bendroflumethazine is a thiazide diuretic. Common adverse reactions include gout, hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia and potentially photosensitive eruptions.

Candesartan
Candesartan is incorrect. This is an angiotensin receptor blocker, a class of drugs that may lead to hyperkalaemia and hypotension and that are widely used as alternatives to angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors.

stem: A 30-year-old man gives a history of recurrent blistering on the hands, forearms and chest whenever he is on holiday, and mentions that lesions develop after sun exposure. He has numerous scars on his hands, forearms and upper chest. He is a fit man and works as an interior decorator. He drinks approximately 30–40 units of alcohol per week and does not smoke. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Porphyria cutanea tarda
Porphyria cutanea tarda presents with bullous eruptions after exposure to sunlight. The eruptions heal with scarring and milia (tiny inclusion cysts). Clues to the diagnosis include the photodistribution of the rash, skin fragility, blistering and the presence of scars; other features can include hypertrichosis and sclerodermatous changes. Most patients will have chronic liver disease, most commonly due to alcohol. Diagnosis depends on the presence of increased levels of urinary uroporphyrin. Remission can be induced by venesection. Chloroquine promotes the urinary excretion of uroporphyrin but must be used in very low doses in the context of chronic liver disease.

Bullous pemphigoid
Bullous pemphigoid is incorrect. Bullous pemphigoid affects a much older age group and is not related to sun exposure.

Pemphigus vulgaris
Pemphigus vulgaris is incorrect. Pemphigus vulgaris leads to superficial blistering and usually presents with erosions rather than intact blisters. It always causes mucosal involvement and is not photodistributed.

Polymorphic light eruption
Polymorphic light eruption is incorrect. Polymorphic light eruption, as the name suggests, can lead to various morphologies of rash after sun exposure. Although blistering is possible, it is not typical and does not lead to scarring. It is much more common in women than men.

stem: A 75-year-old man presents to his GP complaining of a lesion on his nose. Examination confirms a welldefined, 8 mm, shiny, pink plaque, with prominent surface telangiectasia and a small central scab. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Basal-cell carcinoma
The description is of a small BCC, probably of nodular type. Classically such lesions are described as ‘pearly’, with an impression of being shiny or translucent. There may be a rolled edge or central depression. There is often a small central scab or ulcer. Basal-cell carcinoma is the most common cancer in humans, mostly occurring on the head and neck. Subtypes include: Nodular (most common) Superficial (more common on the trunk and limbs, usually presenting as a somewhat scaly, pink plaque, often with the tell-tale rolled edge) Morphoeic (infiltrative and often poorly defined, tending to present more as a shiny, smooth, scarlike lesion with telangiectasia) Pigmented (with focal or extensive brown or grey pigmentation) Metastasis is extremely rare and usually only occurs in the context of a neglected ‘giant’ BCC. The major risk factor for BCC is chronic sun exposure. Most patients with BCC are cured by surgical excision, typically with a 4 mm clinical margin. Clinically indistinct lesions or those in sites where tissue sparing is important (e.g. lip, eyelid) are amenable to Mohs’ micrographic surgery, in which the entire cut surface of the excision specimen is checked histologically for clearance, making wide margins unnecessary. Other modalities include radiotherapy and, for superficial BCC, curettage, photodynamic therapy and imiquimod cream.

Amelanotic melanoma
Amelanotic melanoma is incorrect. Amelanotic melanoma can be difficult to diagnose clinically as the features are non-specific. The best clue to the diagnosis tends to be foci of melanoma-like pigmentation. Such lesions can mimic a variety of other benign and malignant lesions including actinic keratosis, Bowen’s disease, BCC and poorly differentiated squamous-cell carcinoma (SCC).

Dermatofibroma
Dermatofibroma is incorrect. Dermatofibroma is a common benign lesion, usually presenting as a firm pigmented papule. It most commonly occurs on the legs and is very unusual on the face.

Irritated haemangioma
Irritated haemangioma is incorrect. A traumatised or irritated haemangioma is somewhat plausible at this site and the scab would fit, but such lesions are usually red or purple rather than pink; the description in the scenario is classical for BCC.

stem: A 40-year-old man is referred with an itchy rash on the flexural aspects of the arms and some changes in the mouth including white patches on his gums inside of his cheeks. He has noticed a similar rash in a recent scar. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lichen planus
Classical lichen planus is characterised by an itchy, violaceous, polygonal, flat-topped papular rash most commonly developing over the wrists and ankles. A pale, lacy network develops, and is often found in the mouth, although this may be asymptomatic. The presence of Wickham’s striae – a fine, white lacy pattern over the papules – is characteristic. The Koebner phenomenon is typically seen in lichen planus (whereby the rash ‘colonises’ sites of trauma a few days later).

Atopic eczema
Atopic eczema is incorrect. Atopic eczema is pruritic and has a predilection for the flexures; however, it does not manifest the Koebner phenomenon or affect the mouth.

Pompholyx
Pompholyx is incorrect. Pompholyx (also known as pompholytic or dyshidrotic eczema; is a form of vesicular eczema which mostly affects the palms and fingers, and sometimes the soles.

Psoriasis
Psoriasis is incorrect. Psoriasis also demonstrates the Koebner phenomenon, but characteristically occurs on extensor rather than flexor surfaces. It rarely affects the oral mucosa.

stem: A 22-year-old primigravida in the third trimester develops pruritus. On examination, she has a few tense blisters on her abdomen, including around the umbilicus, and on the upper thighs. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Pemphigoid of pregnancy
Pemphigoid of pregnancy is correct. Pemphigoid of pregnancy (also known as pemphigoid gestationis and previously as herpes gestationis) is a rare immunobullous disease. It tends to begin in the second trimester but can do so at any point in the pregnancy; in some cases, it worsens after delivery. The presence of tense blisters makes this the most likely diagnosis; it should be confirmed via skin biopsies for histology and immunofluorescence. Treatment with oral prednisolone may be required.

Cholestasis of pregnancy
Cholestasis of pregnancy also causes itching. It is not associated with a specific rash.

Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy
Polymorphic eruption of pregnancy is also known as pruritic and urticated papules and plaques of pregnancy (PUPPP). As this name suggests, itching is prominent, but blistering is unusual. This condition classically spares the peri-umbilical area, in contrast to pemphigoid of pregnancy.

Prurigo of pregnancy
Prurigo of pregnancy is another itchy condition which presents with non-specific skin changes including prominent excoriation. Blisters do not occur. Bloods should be checked to exclude cholestasis.

stem: A 22-year-old man presents to the hospital with a pale pink, papular, non-itching symmetrical rash on his trunk, limbs, palms and soles. He also has erosions in his mouth. Examination shows generalised lymphadenopathy, and his main symptoms are lassitude, headache and joint pains. He is a plumber’s apprentice and, apart from a 2-week holiday to Thailand 4 months ago, he has never been abroad. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Secondary syphilis
Secondary syphilis develops 4–12 weeks after the primary infection. This is characterised by a macular or papular rash, which is symmetrical on the trunk and limbs, as well as characteristically affecting the palms and soles. The rash is pale pink and is non-pruritic. Confluent plaques (called ‘condylomata lata’) may form in the moist flexures. Erosions may be present on mucosal surfaces. Patients may complain of muscle and joint pains, headaches and fever. Generalised lymphadenopathy is common. There may be patchy alopecia.

Infectious mononucleosis
Infectious mononucleosis is incorrect. Infectious mononucleosis usually presents with a severe sore throat, cervical lymphadenopathy and constitutional symptoms, but not the other features described here. An exanthematous rash occurs when patients with the illness take penicillin.

Lichen planus
Lichen planus is incorrect. Lichen planus can cause a widespread papular eruption, but this is typically intensely pruritic. Erosive lichen planus causes mucosal erosions. However, the condition does not cause constitutional symptoms.

Pityriasis rosea
Pityriasis rosea is incorrect. The rash of pityriasis rosea can look identical to that of secondary syphilis on the body, but does not usually affect the limbs at all. Patients remain well.

stem: A 72-year-old man is concerned about an enlarging pigmented lesion on the sole of his foot. It is 1.5 cm in diameter with an irregular edge; it is mostly light mid-brown with an elevated dark brown area centrally. Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Acral lentiginous melanoma
Acral lentiginous melanoma is normally seen on the sole of the foot, and occasionally on the palm of the hand. It usually presents as an irregularly pigmented macule, but thicker, palpable areas may appear if it progresses; the size can range from a few millimetres to several centimetres. Due to the location, it may go unnoticed for a long period of time and eventually present late. Like other subtypes of melanoma, important prognostic factors are the Breslow thickness and the presence of ulceration; management is with wide local excision, which will typically require amputation if on a digit, or skin graft repair if on the palm or sole.

Lentigo maligna melanoma
Lentigo maligna melanoma is incorrect. This occurs on chronically sun-exposed skin, usuallyChat thewith face. Nodular melanoma
Nodular melanoma is incorrect as this aggressive type of melanoma rapidly grows deeper, so presents as a papular or nodular lesion. It is usually deeply pigmented, although it can be amelanotic.

Subungual melanoma
Subungual melanoma is incorrect. Subungual means that the melanoma is affecting the nail apparatus. This may present with a pigmented streak or more irregular lesion beneath the nail-plate; over time, nail dystrophy may occur. Associated pigmentation extending on to a nail fold (Hutchinson’s sign) is an important pointer to this diagnosis. Subungual melanoma is usually histologically of acral lentiginous type.

Superficial spreading melanoma
Superficial spreading melanoma is incorrect. This is the most common subtype of melanoma overall but not the usual type on the palms and soles.

stem: Skin biopsy – subepidermal blister, polymorphous inflammatory infiltrate with a predominance of eosinophils Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Bullous pemphigoid
The distribution of blisters (limbs and trunk) and skin biopsy fit with a diagnosis of pemphigoid. While mouth lesions are common in pemphigus, they are rarely seen in patients with pemphigoid. Various techniques exist to measure Immunoglobilin G (IgG) directed against the basement membrane, but most, such as immunoelectron microscopy and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) tests, have limited availability. Furosemide, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and penicillamine are all known to trigger the development of pemphigoid.

Dermatitis herpetiformis
Dermatitis herpetiformis is incorrect. The intensely itchy, blistering rash of dermatitis herpetiformis is usually on the extensor surfaces.

Epidermolysis bullosa
Epidermolysis bullosa is incorrect. A first presentation of epidermolysis bullosa is rare at this age.

Erythema multiforme
Erythema multiforme is incorrect. Erythema multiforme usually has target lesions – erythema with central clearing.

stem: A 44-year-old woman presented with a year’s history of progressive painful ulceration of her shins. She stated that the ulcers tended to develop where she had knocked her shins against furniture. Examination showed multiple deep, red, necrotic ulcers with undermined violaceous and oedematous borders across the lower limbs. There was also evidence of some healing, leaving a cribriform pattern of scarring. Which of the following conditions can be seen in association with this skin complaint?
explanation:
Chronic myeloid leukaemia
This patient has a history and examination consistent with pyoderma gangrenosum; the appearance of the ulcers and cribriform scarring is characteristic. Pyoderma gangrenosum is associated with myeloproliferative disorders, including chronic myeloid leukaemia. It is also associated with inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and lymphoma.

Leprosy
Leprosy is incorrect. Leprosy is caused by infection with Mycobacterium leprae and classically causes erythematous or hypopigmented skin patches with reduced sensation. This patient has a history and examination consistent with pyoderma gangrenosum; the appearance of the ulcers and cribriform scarring is characteristic. Leprosy is not known to be associated with pyoderma gangrenosum. Common associations with pyoderma gangrenosum include myeloproliferative disorders such as chronic myeloid leukaemia, inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and lymphoma.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection
Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection is incorrect. Rashes are common in Mycoplasma infection, affecting up to a third of patients. Typical rashes include a non-specific exanthem, with erythematous patches that disappear without treatment, urticarial rashes, or erythema multiforme: targetoid patches appearing on the trunk and limbs. This patient has a history and examination consistent with pyoderma gangrenosum; the appearance of the ulcers and cribriform scarring is characteristic. Mycoplasma pneumoniae is not known to be associated with pyoderma gangrenosum. Common associations with pyoderma gangrenosum include myeloproliferative disorders such as chronic myeloid leukaemia, inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and lymphoma.

Sarcoidosis
Sarcoidosis is incorrect. Sarcoidosis is associated with erythema nodosum, which are painful erythematous lumps, typically on the shins. Specific skin manifestations of sarcoidosis include lupus pernio (large dark coloured patches on the nose or extremities), skin plaques (dark red or brown patches), or subcutaneous nodules. This patient has a history and examination consistent with pyoderma gangrenosum; the appearance of the ulcers and cribriform scarring is characteristic. Sarcoidosis is very rarely associated with pyoderma gangrenosum. Common associations with pyoderma gangrenosum include myeloproliferative disorders such as chronic myeloid leukaemia, inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and lymphoma.

stem: A woman recently diagnosed with acute myeloid leukaemia presents with a rash three weeks after completing the first course of chemotherapy. She is febrile and leucopenic. A maculopapular rash is noted over much of her trunk, and several vesicles are noted. Previous serology to VZV is positive for IgG. Which of the following options is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Multi-dermatomal shingles
Immunosuppression is a common cause of atypical presentations of shingles, which may be disseminated and multi-dermatomal. Prompt treatment with IV aciclovir is essential.

Chickenpox
Chickenpox is incorrect. Chickenpox may also present as a severe infection in these patients, but serology to varicella zoster virus (VZV) IgG would be negative, as it is due to primary VZV infection.

HSV infection
HSV infection is incorrect. Significant HSV infection presents with multiple oropharyngeal or genital ulcers, rather than the typical shingles picture seen here.

Orf
Orf is incorrect. Orf is a poxvirus causing a pustular dermatitis, usually affecting the hands: it is acquired from contact with sheep.

Parvovirus infection
Parvovirus infection is incorrect. Parvoviruses can lead to chronic infection in immunosuppressed people with anaemia and possible aplastic crisis. Arthropathy is also a feature. Chronic parvovirus infection may be seen because of defective clearance.

stem: A 50-year-man presents with onycholysis. He is already being followed up for another chronic problem. Which is the most likely underlying cause for his current presentation?
explanation:
Thyrotoxicosis
Onycholysis is separation of the nail plate from the nail bed, generally extending from the free edge of the nail. It is relatively commonly seen in psoriatic nail disease. Many other causes have been described including trauma, infection, and drugs such as tetracyclines and psoralens. It is well recognised as a complication of thyrotoxicosis (which can also lead to thyroid acropachy, similar to clubbing).

Alopecia areata
Alopecia areata is incorrect. Alopecia areata is commonly associated with nail changes, especially pitting and ridging.

Cutaneous lupus erythematosus
Nail involvement in cutaneous lupus erythematosus is extremely unusual. By contrast, nail fold changes and splinter haemorrhages do occur in systemic lupus erythematosus.

Hypoproteinaemia
Hypoproteinaemia is incorrect. Hypoproteinaemia is associated with leukonychia.

Lichen planus.

stem: A 24-year-old rugby player comes to the clinic for review. He has had three episodes of facial cellulitis with boil formation around his beard line over the past few months. On the past two occasions Staphylococcus aureus has been isolated from a boil swab. Which of the following toxins is S. aureus most likely to be producing?
explanation:
Panton–Valentine Leukocidin (PVL)
PVL-producing S. aureus is responsible for recurrent skin infections. One risk factor for recurrent skin infection is thought to be close contact between others, such as might be expected during a rugby match. PVL-positive S. aureus is thought to account for less than 2% of isolates, both MRSA-positive and -negative. Mild infections may not require treatment, whereas moderate infections are usually treated with flucloxacillin, erythromycin or clindamycin monotherapy. More severe infections may require dual therapy, usually with rifampicin and doxycycline, or rifampicin and fusidic acid.

Enterotoxin
Enterotoxin is incorrect. S. aureus enterotoxin is responsible for food poisoning with a rapid onset of action (1–6 h).

Hyaluronidase
Hyaluronidase is incorrect. Hyaluronidase is thought to be utilised by a number of bacteria (such as Streptococcus and Staphylococcus) to degrade host defences and increase the pathogens’ virulence.

Serine protease ScpC
Serine protease ScpC is incorrect. The ScpC protease of Streptococcus pyogenes is responsible for immune downregulation of the host and development of soft tissue infections.

TSST-1
TSST-1 is incorrect. TSST-1 production by Staphylococcus is responsible for the development of toxic shock syndrome, which presents with a sunburn-like rash (in the early stages), malaise, high fever and hypotension. Cellulitis A 56-year-old woman with a 35-year history of type 1 diabetes comes to the clinic for review. Her main complaint is of worsening pain and stiffness of her right thumb, coupled with thickening of the skin over the palmar surface. On examination there is weakness of thumb opposition on the right-hand side. Examination of the left hand reveals normal power and there is no sensory loss. Investigations.

stem: A 25-year-old man, known to have suffered from type 1 diabetes mellitus for over 10 years, presents with a rash on his shins. The endocrinologist makes a diagnosis of necrobiosis lipoidica. Which of the following best applies to necrobiosis lipoidica?
options: It is more commonly seen in males
It is secondary to a fungal infection
It is usually poorly responsive to treatment
It most commonly occurs on the knuckles
Oral corticosteroids are usually used as first-line treatment
explanation:
It is usually poorly responsive to treatment
Necrobiosis lipoidica is an unusual complication of diabetes mellitus, but may also occur in non-diabetic patients. It is thought to be due to small-vessel damage leading to partial necrosis of dermal collagen and connective tissue, and a histiocytic cellular response. The skin over the shins is commonly affected and the disease presents as erythematous plaques that gradually develop yellowish-brown waxy discoloration with marked atrophy and prominent telangiectasia. Many treatments have been tried, including topical or intra-lesional corticosteroids, topical tacrolimus, phototherapy, oral corticosteroids and immunosuppressants, and antiplatelet agents. Evidence for any of these is sparse and many cases show little or no response.

It is more commonly seen in males
It is more commonly seen in males is incorrect. Necrobiosis lipoidica is around three times more common in females.

It is secondary to a fungal infection
It is secondary to a fungal infection is incorrect. The condition has no connection with fungal infection.

It most commonly occurs on the knuckles
It most commonly occurs on the knuckles is incorrect. Most necrobiosis lipoidica occurs on the legs.

Oral corticosteroids are usually used as first-line treatment
Oral corticosteroids are usually used as first-line treatment is incorrect. Oral corticosteroids are generally avoided, particularly in patients with diabetes. A potent topical steroid would be a reasonable first-line option. Diabetes - Type I.

stem: A 45-year-old man of Chinese ethnic origin comes to the Emergency Department with a generalised erythematous rash, and extensive sloughing of skin, including from mucus membranes. He has a fever which has worsened significantly over the past 24 hours. A few days earlier, he started treatment with carbamazepine for partial epilepsy. Examination reveals extensive erythema with bullae and skin sloughing. He is pyrexial with a temperature of 38.8 °C. Which of the following is of significant concern?
explanation:
Venous thromboembolism
Fluid loss is a significant problem in patients with toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), which is the most likely diagnosis here. The risk of TEN is significantly increased in Chinese patients treated with carbamazepine because of increased prevalence of HLA B1502 genotype. Where use of carbamazepine is planned in a patient of Chinese ethnic origin, genetic screening is recommended. Fluid loss can lead to increased viscosity. Increased viscosity, coupled with inflammation associated with SJS/TEN, drives a significant risk of venous thromboembolism, for which prophylactic anticoagulation should be considered.

High-output cardiac failure
This patient has TEN as a result of worsening Stevens–Johnson syndrome (SJS), resulting from the use of carbamazepine. Carbamazepine use is associated with significant risk of SJS in patients with the HLA B1502 genotype, which is increased significantly in patients of Chinese ethnic origin. TEN can lead to cardiac failure, but it is less likely in a patient 45 years of age with no previous cardiac history.

Hypothermia
Hyperthermia rather than hypothermia is more likely to occur in patients with TEN, as exemplified by the temperature of 38.8 °C on presentation here.

Oesophageal stricturing
Oesophageal structuring is a potential long-term complication of TEN, although prompt intervention to control the disease with discontinuation of the causative medication, coupled with supportive measures such as fluid replacement and systemic steroids where appropriate, should prevent this from happening.

Rhabdomyolysis
Rhabdomyolysis should not be seen in TEN as long as prompt treatment is instituted to control fever and maintain adequate hydration. It is usually a more significant problem in patients with neuroleptic malignant syndrome and the elderly who have spent a significant period of time immobile on the floor. Stevens-Johnson.

stem: A 62-year-old heavy smoker, with a long history of self-neglect, presents to his GP with severe leg pain. On examination there are multiple, small punched-out ulcers situated on the lower third of both legs. Both dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses appear absent. Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Multiple arterial ulcers
Painful punched-out ulcers are highly suggestive of an arterial aetiology. Associated ischaemic leg pain may be particularly intense on elevating the legs, and cause sleep interference. There may be so-called trophic changes on the legs due to peripheral vascular disease: loss of hair and a shiny, red, scaly or atrophic appearance. As well as peripheral vascular disease, as evidenced by the absent foot pulses bilaterally, there is also likely to be arterial pathology elsewhere, and it is important to assess for ischaemic heart disease and carotid disease. Angioplasty or bypass surgery may only be appropriate for improving peripheral blood supply in a limited number of cases, while peripheral vasodilating drugs are rarely effective. Sympathectomy may be of some value, and a trial nerve block to assess potential effectiveness is advised in cases of severe pain.

Flea infestation
Flea infestation is incorrect. Flea bites do tend to affect the lower legs, but are itchy rather than painful. They are usually papular, but sometimes bullous. After excoriation, it is conceivable that they might present with erosions, but not punched-out ulceration.

Multiple venous ulcers
Multiple venous ulcers is incorrect. The description is strongly suggestive of arterial leg ulceration, and this is corroborated by the absent foot pulses.

Traumatic skin damage
Traumatic skin damage is incorrect. This would not explain the severity of the pain or the absence of the foot pulses. It should be noted, however, that arterial ulceration may be precipitated by trauma.

Vasculitis
Vasculitis is incorrect. Vasculitic ulceration is most common on the legs and may be very painful. However, there is no suggestion of connective tissue disease or specific vasculitic signs, such as purpura, and vasculitis would not explain the absent foot pulses. Expanded Explanation Overview Clinical Presentation Differential Diagnosis Diagnosis /.

stem: A 54-year-old woman who has lived for many years in Kenya comes to the clinic for review. She has suffered progressive sensory loss over the last 3–4 months affecting the median nerve distribution in both arms. On examination, there is demonstrable sensory loss over the median nerve distribution, worse on the right than the left. There is peripheral hypopigmentation, and thickening along the length of the nerves bilaterally. Which of the following is the most useful diagnostic investigation?
explanation:
Skin biopsy
The best available test in confirming the diagnosis of multibacillary leprosy is finding Mycobacterium leprae in skin biopsies or slit-skin smears that show acid-fast bacilli with the Ziehl–Neelsen or Fite stains. The standard UK antimicrobial schedule for treatment of multibacillary leprosy is dapsone, rifampicin and clofazimine.

Blood cultures
Blood cultures is incorrect. This woman has lived in a high-risk area and is presenting with symptoms suggestive of leprosy. The WHO case definition of leprosy is the presence of one or more of the following: Hypopigmented or reddish skin lesions with loss of sensation Chatloss with of Involvement of the peripheral nerves as demonstrated by their thickening and associated sensation Skin smear positive for acid-fast bacilli. Blood cultures are unlikely to be positive despite ongoing infection, and are therefore not considered to be a useful diagnostic tool.

Nerve biopsy
Nerve biopsy is incorrect. A nerve biopsy may be indicated for the diagnosis of leprosy in cases without clinically visible skin lesions, or in order to evaluate the effectiveness of the treatment.

Nerve conduction studies
Nerve conduction studies is incorrect. Nerve conduction studies are not used to diagnose the condition, but may be helpful in monitoring the progress of treatment.

Serum PGL-1.

stem: You are investigating new targets in the management of psoriasis and potential monoclonal antibodies to target inflammation in the disease. Which one of the following is the most useful cytokine to target?
explanation:
IL-17
IL-17 is a pro-inflammatory cytokine which is expressed at high levels in psoriasis lesions, it drives recruitment of inflammatory cells and helps perpetuate active psoriasis. Ixekizumab is an anti-IL-17 antibody which binds to IL-17, it is effective in treating active psoriasis and in reducing the risk of recurrence.

IL-1
IL-1 is incorrect. IL-1 is a pro-inflammatory cytokine but is primarily targeted in the management of acute gout and Still’s disease.

IL-6
IL-6 is incorrect. IL-6 is targeted in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis, where it is thought to play a primary role in joint inflammation. There is a weak pathological link with psoriasis but no current drug treatments.

IL-10
IL-10 is incorrect. IL-10 is an anti-inflammatory cytokine and is therefore not targeted in the management of inflammatory disease.

IL-18.

stem: Which one of the following is the most likely clinical outcome?
options: He is likely to develop bilateral sacroiliitis
He is likely to develop enteropathy
He is likely to develop inflammatory bowel disease
He is likely to develop signs of tuberculosis
explanation:
Spontaneous resolution
This man is suffering from erythema nodosum, the most common causes of which are sarcoidosis in adults and streptococcal infection in both adults and children. With erythema nodosum and streptococcal infection (he had pharyngitis), resolution is the most likely outcome. There are no other symptoms to suggest sarcoid here. Other associations of erythema nodosum include: Tuberculosis Inflammatory bowel disease Ankylosing spondylitis Symptomatic relief of pain, using NSAIDs, is the management of choice for this condition, as the majority of patients experience spontaneous resolution.

He is likely to develop bilateral sacroiliitis
He is likely to develop bilateral sacroiliitis is incorrect. Post-streptococcal erythema nodosum is likely to resolve rather than evolve.

He is likely to develop enteropathy
He is likely to develop enteropathy is incorrect. Post-streptococcal erythema nodosum is likely to resolve rather than evolve.

He is likely to develop inflammatory bowel disease
He is likely to develop inflammatory bowel disease is incorrect. Post-streptococcal erythema nodosum is likely to resolve rather than evolve.

He is likely to develop signs of tuberculosis
He is likely to develop signs of tuberculosis is incorrect. Post-streptococcal erythema nodosum is likely to resolve rather than evolve. Erythema NodosumA 37-year-old traveller to Latin America presents with an ulcer in his nose, and says that he has suffered problems with nasal congestion for some time. He had been working for around 9 months or so on an Operation Raleigh project at a jungle school. On examination there is a firm red ulcerated papule in the left nostril that involves the nasal septum. Investigations.

stem: A 23-year-old woman who is five months' pregnant presents to the General Practitioner with concerns about changes in her skin appearance. She reports that she has always had some light-brown discolorations, a lot of freckling and lumps on her skin, but that these have worsened during the pregnancy. On examination, she has multiple light-brown pigmented areas on her skin, a number of friable cutaneous skin lesions and axillary freckling. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)
The skin manifestations of NF1 include: six or more café au lait spots (defined oval-shaped, light-brown patches greater than 0.5 cm in diameter) multiple neurofibromas (tumours on, under, or hanging off the skin) freckling (under the armpits and areas of skinfolds such as the groin) lisch nodules (tiny tumours on the iris of the eye). NF1 results from a deletion or mutation in the NF1 gene, the product of which, neurofibromin, acts as a suppressor for central nervous system (CNS) tumours. The disease is associated with less central CNS tumours than NF2, but is associated with a mixture of skin features. Skin features develop over a number of years, but the pace of development may increase during puberty and pregnancy.

Acanthosis nigricans
Acanthosis nigricans is a soft, velvety hyperpigmentation of the neck, axillae and groin. It is associated with adenocarcinoma of the gastrointestinal tract, lung cancer and lymphomas. It is also associated with diabetes, Cushing’s disease, acromegaly and oestrogens, and may be hereditary.

Multiple endocrine neoplasia 1 (MEN1)
MEN1 may be associated with café au lait spots, but there is no history of parathyroid, pancreas or pituitary tumour.

Multiple endocrine neoplasia 2 (MEN2)
MEN2B is associated with mucosal neuromas and a marfanoid habitus.

Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2)
These skin manifestations are found in NF1. NF2, also known as bilateral acoustic neurofibromatosis, is characterised by multiple tumours and lesions on the brain and spinal cord. Tumours growing on the auditory nerves, which lead to hearing loss, are usually the first symptom of the disease, but are often not apparent until the late teens or early 20s. NeurofibromatosisA 42-year-old man with a history of ulcerative colitis attends the gastroenterology clinic for review; he has noticed a deep ulcerating lesion on his leg and is concerned as to what it may be. On examination he has a deep ulcer, which has a violet border, on the left lower leg. Investigations.

stem: A 34-year-old woman who has recently undergone induction chemotherapy for leukaemia comes to the clinic for review. She has a crop of dome-shaped, flesh-coloured papules that are umbilicated across her lower abdomen; apparently one of her children has suffered from a similar looking rash over the past few weeks. Her health is otherwise fine, and she seems to be recovering after her chemotherapy. She notes that when she scratches the lesions they appear to heal/disappear more quickly. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Molluscum contagiosum
The presence of umbilicated papules and history of a similar rash in one of her children raises the possibility of molluscum. In adults it occurs in individuals with a low CD4 count, and is therefore seen in those who are immunosuppressed. The underlying cause of molluscum is a pox virus, and in immunocompetent individuals clearance occurs within 2 months. In this case, as her CD4 count recovers, she should also clear the rash.

Genital warts
Genital warts is incorrect. Genital warts are seen in the genital area and appear wart-like.

Lichen planus
Lichen planus is incorrect. Although lichen planus can take many different cutaneous forms, it is not centrally umbilicated.

Pediculosis capitis
Pediculosis capitis is incorrect. Pediculosis capitis is head lice.

Pubic lice
Pubic lice is incorrect. Pubic lice are intensely itchy and occur around the genital hair, not on the abdomen. Molluscum ContagiosumA 19-year-old woman with a history of atopic eczema affecting her face, arms and trunk comes to the Emergency Department complaining of a worsening of her rash but no further spreading. She says it has become red and inflamed over the past 24-48 hours. Normally she takes mild topical corticosteroids only. On examination she has a temperature of 36.5 °C, there is increased erythema with pustule formation (1–2 mm) and yellow crusting over the eczema on her chin, neck and upper chest. Investigations.

stem: A 52-year-old man who has recently emigrated from Uganda presents to the clinic with a number of hypopigmented areas over his arms and legs, which are accompanied by reduced sensation. He also complains of weakness of his left ankle. He has a history of hypertension and treated hypothyroidism. On examination you confirm the hypopigmented lesions, which are associated with fibrosis and decreased sensation. He has leftsided foot-drop. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Tuberculoid leprosy
The skin lesions seen here, coupled with sensory loss, are typical of those seen in patients with leprosy. The gold standard for confirming the diagnosis is finding Mycobacterium leprae on skin biopsy or slit-skin smear.
