Treatment of leprosy involves use of both effective antimycobacterial chemotherapy and agents such as corticosteroids to treat coexistent inflammation, which is thought to worsen nerve injury.

Behçet syndrome
Behçet syndrome is incorrect. Behçet syndrome is associated with orogenital ulceration, and so does not fit with the scenario here.

Cerebrovascular disease
Cerebrovascular disease is incorrect. This patient’s extra-neurological features (e.g. hypopigmented anaesthetic skin lesions and a foot-drop) make this option incorrect.

Churg-Strauss syndrome
Churg-Strauss syndrome is incorrect. Churg–Strauss syndrome would be very unlikely in the absence of symptoms of asthma.

Polyendocrine syndrome
Polyendocrine syndrome is incorrect. There is insufficient features to classify this man has having type 1 or 2 polyglandular autoimmune endocrinopathy syndromes. LeprosyA 60-year-old man who owns a bar in Tenerife returns to the UK seeking medical care. He has been suffering from a blistering rash affecting his face, arms and legs, which gets much worse when he goes out into the sun. He admits to drinking 60 units of alcohol per week. There is no past medical history of note, although he only returns to the UK once per year to visit his GP. On examination, his BP is 145/82 mmHg and pulse 80 bpm and regular. There is clear evidence of a photosensitive blistering rash on examination of his face and neck, arms and legs. Investigations.

stem: A 45-year-old woman comes to the Dermatology Clinic for review. She has been suffering from recurrent episodes of widespread hives for the past few months. There appears to be no obvious trigger for these and she is distressed by the fact that symptoms are not completely resolved despite increased doses of two combined second-generation oral antihistamines (desloratadine 10 mg OD and fexofenadine 360 mg OD). Examination and routine bloods in the clinic are unremarkable. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
Add montelukast
Montelukast (a leukotriene receptor antagonist), when added to increased doses of anti-histamines, is thought to be useful in reducing the duration and severity of episodes.

Add oral corticosteroids
Add oral corticosteroids is incorrect. This is a clear history of chronic spontaneous urticaria that typically presents with unprovoked attacks of wheals, angioedema or both. Whilst oral corticosteroids may reduce the severity of attacks, they are not preferred in the long term here because of their adverse event profile.

Add cyclosporin
Add cyclosporin is incorrect. It is added only if patient has refractory symptoms despite using other drugs like first and second generation antihistamines, montelukast etc.

Add topical corticosteroids
Add topical corticosteroids is incorrect. Evidence on the efficacy of topical corticosteroids in chronic urticaria is lacking. Therefore, these are not commonly used in everyday practice.

Add omalizumab
Add Omalizumab is incorrect. Omalizumab is a biologic drug (monoclonal antibody against IgE). It has been shown to have good effect in urticaria and can be used in patients who have failed to respond to maximum doses of antihistamines taken for a period of 4 weeks. However, given the high cost of this biologic agent, limits and restrictions apply to the eligibility for omalizumab. Currently, the use of omalizumab should be limited to the most severely affected chronic urticaria patients who remain highly symptomatic despite ongoing treatment with a combination of third-line therapies, such as immunosuppressive medications (e.g. cyclosporine). UrticariaA 52-year-old woman, who has suffered from tiredness and itching over the past few months, comes to the Dermatology Clinic with a lesion affecting her left shin. She says that she banged it in the garden, and a few days afterwards noted some nodules over the area. These then broke down to form a boggy ulcer with a raised inflammatory border. You note a number of small abscesses at the base. Her blood pressure is 132/84 mmHg; pulse is 82 bpm and regular. Her body mass index (BMI) is 29 kg/m 2. You note scratch marks over the upper body and confirm the ulcer on the shin. Investigations.

stem: A 68–year-old gentleman presents with a lesion on his temple that looks shiny, has a rolled edge and is gradually increasing in size. Routine blood tests are unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Basal cell carcinoma
This is a basal cell carcinoma, sometimes called rodent ulcers. They are the most common skin cancer and generally occur on sun-exposed areas. They are more common later on in life and tend to grow very slowly. They typically have a rolled, pearly-edged border that can give them the appearance of being shiny, and central telangiectasia is often present. Fortunately, in the majority of cases they are only locally invasive, and rarely metastasise. Treatment usually involves a surgical excision, or Mohs’ surgery for high-risk lesions.

Amelanotic melanoma
Amelanotic melanoma is incorrect. Amelanotic melanoma does not have the usual dark pigmentation, but is instead pink in colour. They are also more common in sun-exposed areas, and other risk factors would include a positive family history, skin type 1 and history of extensive sun exposure.

Lentigo maligna
Lentigo maligna is incorrect. Lentigo maligna, often referred to as melanoma in situ, is a precursor to malignant melanoma; it usually has the same alarming features as those of a malignant melanoma, such as asymmetry and variable pigmentation. Treatment involves surgical excision.

Seborrhoeic wart
Seborrhoeic wart is incorrect. A seborrheic wart is an extremely common, harmless warty lesion appearing on older people. They do not require any treatment, but can be removed with cryotherapy if unsightly or catching on clothes.

Squamous cell carcinoma
Squamous cell carcinoma is incorrect. A squamous cell carcinoma is another malignant lesion that often has an ulcerated surface. The risk factors are similar to those of malignant melanomas but can also include immunosuppression. They require surgical excision as they can metastasise if left untreated. Basal Cell Carcinoma A 17-year old girl presents with moderate acne. On examination, there are comedones and pustules affecting her face, back and chest. She has previously tried topical erythromycin offered by her GP, but found that this made no difference. Her parents report that she has been feeling low and missing school. Investigations.

stem: A 32-year-old nursing sister presents to the Dermatology Clinic with an erythematous papular skin rash, particularly marked over her hands. She says it is intensely itchy, particularly in the web spaces between her fingers, and the itching is worse at night. She takes no regular medication and is otherwise well. Examination reveals a papular rash over both hands, with evidence of scratch marks, particularly between the fingers. Which of the following is the most useful next step?
explanation:
Ink test
Clues include the position of the rash, where the itching is worst, and this patient’s occupation as a nursing sister. These are all pointers towards scabies as the cause of her symptoms. The ink test can be helpful in confirming the presence of scabies burrows. Ink is rubbed over a burrow (for example, with the surface of a pen nib) and is then wiped off with an alcohol swab. Ink will track into the burrow which outlines it. Skin scrapings may then confirm the presence of an adult mite or an egg. Permethrin cream is the intervention of choice, with two applications one week apart.

Patch testing
Latex allergy is more prevalent among nursing and medical staff because of chronic exposure, although the prevalence of latex allergy has reduced significantly with the use of nitrile gloves. In this case, the localisation of the itching to the web spaces and the papular rather than erythematous rash is more a pointer towards scabies rather than latex allergy as the underlying cause. Patch testing is useful for allergic contact type skin reactions.

Radioallergosorbent test (RAST) allergy screening
RAST testing is used for diagnosing skin allergy, but it is not as accurate as patch testing for pinpointing the specific cause. In this case, the papular nature of the rash coupled with localisation of the itching web Chat to withthe spaces is a greater pointer towards scabies as being responsible here, for which RAST testing is obviously not useful.

Trial of antihistamines
Antihistamines may have minor effects only in treating the itching associated with scabies, the likely diagnosis here. Identifying the cause of the rash using the ink test is much more important, as well as using an appropriate insecticide to clear the infestation.

Trial of steroids
A trial of steroids here is inappropriate without appropriate treatment to clear underlying scabies infestation first. Topical corticosteroids may be used to treat ongoing skin inflammation in patients with scabies, but only after they have been treated with permethrin first. ScabiesA 29-year-old woman, who is originally from Spain, comes to the Dermatology Clinic for review. She is concerned as she feels the skin over both her cheeks has begun to get darker, with what looks like extra skin tanning. On examination, you can see an area of blotchy darkened skin over both cheeks around 5–6 cm in diameter. General physical examination is unremarkable. Her body mass index is 23 kg/m 2. Investigations.

stem: A 55-year-old woman has developed slightly tender plum-coloured plaques, mostly on the upper limbs. She is feverish and somewhat unwell. She has a background of myelodysplastic syndrome. Her full blood count reveals neutrophilia. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Sweet's syndrome
Sweet’s syndrome is an uncommon condition of unknown aetiology. Various triggers are recognised, including drugs, infections and underlying cancers, but in many cases no precipitating factor is identified. Skin lesions are classically described as plum-coloured and may be papules, plaques or nodules; mucosal involvement and blistering may also occur. There is often fever and neutrophilia. Diagnosis can be confirmed on skin biopsy.

Erythema elevatum diutinum
Erythema elevatum diutinum is incorrect. Erythema elevatum diutinum is a rare vasculitic condition which typically causes a nodular eruption, especially on the back of the hands and over extensor surfaces. Patients usually remain otherwise well.

Erythema nodosum
Erythema nodosum is incorrect. Erythema nodosum is usually confined to the legs and tends to be tender very with no systemic symptoms (unless secondary to an underlying association).

Leukaemia cutis
Leukaemia cutis is incorrect. This can present with varying morphologies and would be compatible with the presentation described. However, the features are classical for Sweet’s syndrome, making this the best answer.

Pyoderma gangrenosum
Pyoderma gangrenosum is incorrect. Unless seen very early, presents as ulcers with a violaceous, undermined border.

stem: A 25-year-old healthcare assistant comes to the Dermatology Clinic for review. She has developed an extensive erythematous papular rash which she describes as intensely itchy. The itching is apparently worse at night, particularly in the web spaces between the fingers of both hands. Examination confirms the presence of scratch marks over the arms and upper body; the palms of the hands and soles of the feet appear to have been spared from the rash. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her skin rash?
explanation:
Scabies
This patient may well have acquired scabies infestation from a patient she was nursing. The clinical scenario of a widespread papular rash, with itching affecting the web spaces between the fingers most, fits with the diagnosis. Burrows can often be elucidated by using the ink test in the web spaces between fingers, where the ink tracks the burrow. Skin scrapings treated with 10% potassium hydroxide may also identify an adult mite, egg or egg shell on microscopy. Permethrin 5% cream is the intervention of choice for scabies. It should be applied head to toe, left on overnight, and repeated one week later.

Atopic eczema
Atopic eczema is associated with a generalised erythematous rash in severe cases, but it is usually worse on flexural skin surfaces, and the more severe symptoms of itching affecting the web spaces counts towards scabies as the underlying diagnosis. Investigations such as the ink burrow test are useful to confirm the presence of scabies burrows.

Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH)
DH is associated with an intensely itchy papular rash, although the rash in DH is more marked over the buttocks and the posterior thighs. In addition, some symptoms suggestive of coeliac disease, often found in patients with DH, would be expected. Where the rash is localised and there are gastrointestinal symptoms, an anti-tissue transglutaminase (TTG) antibody test is the first step to rule in or rule out DH and coeliac disease.

Lichen planus
Lichen planus is associated with a papular rash which often appears first over the flexural surface of both wrists. The papules are red or violet in colour and are topped with white streaks known as Chat Wickham’s striae. with Lace-like lesions are also found in the mouth. The generalised nature of the rash here would be very unusual for a diagnosis of lichen planus.

Pubic lice
In pubic lice infestation, the papular rash is usually much worse in the pubic and perianal region because this is where hair growth is most marked. The diagnosis is based on finding adult lice or eggs, and a fine-toothed comb may be useful in combing out the lice. Application of malathion or permethrin seven days apart is the intervention of choice.

stem: A 17-year-old girl with learning difficulties is admitted to hospital following an epileptic fit. The patient has a history of seizures since aged 12. The admitting doctor has documented hypopigmented macules on her abdomen and an acne-like eruption on her face. Examination of her fingers shows small periungual fibrous papules. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Tuberous sclerosis
Tuberous sclerosis is an autosomal dominantly inherited disorder with variable expression; most cases result from sporadic new mutations Epilepsy in infancy or childhood is often the presenting feature Learning difficulties are commonly seen, and a variety of developmental and psychiatric abnormalities can occur Ovoid hypopigmented macules (‘ash-leaf macules’) are commonly seen Facial angiofibromata are classically seen, particularly in the nasolabial folds and medial cheeks; these appear as pink or red papules and were previously erroneously referred to as ‘adenoma sebaceum’ Periungual fibromata arise as pink projections from the nail folds The ‘shagreen patch’ is a fibromatous, fleshy plaque usually on the lower back; it is a type of connective tissue naevus Fundoscopy may reveal signs of retinal hamartomata

Neurofibromatosis
Neurofibromatosis is incorrect. Neurofibromatosis is associated with epilepsy and learning difficulties, as well as skin signs including cutaneous neurofibromata, café-au-lait macules and axillary freckling. The skin signs alluded to in the scenario are much more suggestive of tuberous sclerosis.

Osler–Weber–Rendu disease
Osler–Weber–Rendu disease is incorrect. Osler–Weber–Rendu disease is hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia. This presents with dilated blood vessels on the skin and mucous membranes, in some cases with associated bleeding.

Refsum disease
Refsum disease is incorrect. Refsum disease is an autosomal recessively inherited condition characterised by retinitis pigmentosa and anosmia; other features can include muscle wasting, cerebellar ataxia, hearing loss, ichthyosis and cardiac arrhythmia.

Sturge–Weber syndrome.

stem: A 75-year-old man presents with an enlarging pigmented lesion. Histology confirms malignant melanoma. Which one of the following is the most helpful in estimating his prognosis?
explanation:
Depth of the tumour
This is a malignant tumour of melanocytes, which can affect all ages. It can arise in a pre-existing mole or de novo. It is a significant killer of young people but potentially curable if excised early. Various prognostic factors have been recognised in pre-metastatic melanoma. The most important of these is the Breslow thickness. This is the depth of the tumour measured by the histopathologist from the granular layer of the epidermis to the deepest area of involvement. The thicker the tumour is at excision, the higher the associated mortality. Ulceration is another poor prognostic sign.

Diameter of the tumour
Diameter of the tumour is incorrect. Diameter of the tumour is unhelpful prognostically. Melanoma usually goes through a radial growth phase, during which it enlarges horizontally. For reasons that are not understood, it then enters a vertical growth phase, associated with a relatively rapid increase in Breslow thickness and worsening of prognosis.

Melanoma subtype
Melanoma subtype is incorrect. Subtypes of melanoma include superficial spreading, nodular, acral lentiginous (including subungual) and lentigo maligna melanoma (LMM). In general, LMM tends to develop slowly with a prolonged in situ (lentigo maligna) phase, whereas nodular melanoma lacks a horizontal growth phase. Subungal melanoma does tend to carry a relatively worse prognosis, but this is due to more advanced disease at diagnosis. In each case, the prognosis is more related to the Breslow thickness than the subtype itself.

Number of other melanocytic lesions
Number of other melanocytic lesions is incorrect. The number of other melanocytic lesions has no bearing on the prognosis of a specific melanoma. However, those with very large numbers of moles, particularly atypical lesions, are more likely to develop melanoma in the first place and more at risk of acquiring a second primary.

Performance status.

stem: A 30-year-old female on returning from Brazil developed a non-healing ulcer on the left ankle. She had spent 2 weeks camping in the jungle where she remembers being bitten by flies. Which one of the following statements is the most likely?
options: Cutaneous leishmaniasis frequently precedes kala azar
Cutaneous leishmaniasis usually responds to oral penicillin
Leishmaniasis is transmitted by the bot fly
Lesions of leishmaniasis acquired in the Americas requires treatment due to the risk of mucosal
Mosquito nets are important in the prevention of leishmaniasis
explanation:
Lesions of leishmaniasis acquired in the Americas requires treatment due to the risk of mucosal
Lesions of leishmaniasis acquired in the Americas requires treatment due to the risk of mucosal disease. Leishmaniasis is caused the protozoan species Leishmania and is transmitted by female sandflies. Sandflies are only 1.5–3 mm in length and tend to feed at dawn and dusk. Their small size allows them to pass through standard mosquito nets: measures to prevent bites and thereby Leishmania infection include covering up with clothing, using insect repellents, and spraying of sleeping areas and clothing with permethrin. Manifestations of Leishmania infection depend on the species and the host response. Cutaneous leishmaniasis usually appears 2 weeks to 6 months after infection, but sometimes longer. Lesions are typically painless and most will resolve spontaneously to leave atrophic scarring. Treatment may be instituted to minimise complications such as scarring, superadded infection, and, in American leishmaniasis, the risk of later mucocutaneous disease. Antimonials are usually preferred: sodium stibogluconate may be administered intralesionally, or by intramuscular or intravenous injection. Cutaneous leishmaniasis does not progress to kala azar (visceral disease).

Cutaneous leishmaniasis frequently precedes kala azar
Cutaneous leishmaniasis frequently precedes kala azar is incorrect. Kala azar (visceral leishmaniasis) is a systemic infection which affects the liver, spleen and bone marrow. It ranges in severity and can be lifethreatening, particularly in immunosuppressed or malnourished individuals. It is characterised by fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia and hypogammablobulinaemia.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis usually responds to oral penicillin
Cutaneous leishmaniasis usually responds to oral penicillin is incorrect. Penicillin is not an effective treatment for leishmaniasis, which is caused by a protozoan rather than a bacterium.

Leishmaniasis is transmitted by the bot fly
Leishmaniasis is transmitted by the bot fly is incorrect. The bot fly (Dermatobia hominis) is a cause of cutaneous myiasis (infestation by the larvae of various types of fly). It does occur in Central and South America, but is not related to leishmaniasis.

Mosquito nets are important in the prevention of leishmaniasis.

stem: A General Practitioner is called to a nursing home to treat a 75-year-old man with severe pruritus. He has a background of advanced vascular dementia and is unable to give a history. The nurses report that he is often awake and itches his skin at night. On examination, he has excoriations over his trunk and limbs. There is some scaling over his palms, most prominently in the web spaces. Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the recommended management?
explanation:
Topical permethrin
Topical permethrin is used in the treatment of scabies, the likely cause of this patient’s itching. Scabies is caused by the infestation of the Sarcoptes scabiei mite. It is transmitted by close contact and is relatively common within nursing homes and other institutions. It presents with severe pruritus. If present, burrows (linear crusted lesions of a few millimetres in length) are pathognomonic and penile papules are also highly suggestive. It has a predilection for the web spaces and around the nipples. Scalp involvement only occurs in young babies and very debilitated adults. Excoriations tend to be prominent. Permethrin cream should be applied to the skin of the entire body and left for at least eight hours before washing, with retreatment one week later.

Oral mebendazole
Oral mebendazole with Oral mebendazole is used in the treatment of helminthic infections (eg threadworms), notChat of scabies infection.

Topical clotrimazole
Topical clotrimazole is used in the treatment of fungal infections (eg Candida). It would not be appropriate to give to this patient.

Topical fusidic acid
Topical fusidic acid treats bacterial skin infections such as non-severe cellulitis or folliculitis. It does not play a role in the treatment of scabies.

Topical hydrocortisone.

stem: A 54-year-old woman consults her GP because of persistent oral ulceration and the appearance of fragile blisters on the trunk. Examination reveals extensive erosion over the gingivae and a few eroded lesions on the skin. Histology demonstrates an intraepidermal split just above the basal layer, with evidence of acantholysis. Immunofluorescence confirms intercellular IgG deposition. Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Pemphigus vulgaris
Pemphigus vulgaris is characterised by mucosal involvement with ulceration (virtually universal and the presenting feature in up to 50%), usually with flaccid blisters, on the trunk in particular. As the split is superficial, the blister roof is fragile and easily disrupted to leave predominantly erosions. The blisters can be extended with gentle lateral pressure (Nikolsky’s sign). The typical changes on skin biopsy and direct immunofluorescence (on a perilesional skin sample) are as described in the clinical scenario. Pemphigus vulgaris is particularly associated with an Ashkenazi Jewish origin and is associated with antibodies against the desmosomal protein, desmoglein 3. Treatment usually begins with systemic corticosteroids and high doses may be required; steroid-sparing agents such as azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil are often used.

Bullous pemphigoid
Bullous pemphigoid is incorrect. In bullous pemphigoid, the split in the skin occurs at the dermoepidermal junction, leading to a relatively thick blister roof – prominent tense blisters are thus typical rather than erosions; extensive oral ulceration is unusual in pemphigoid; immunofluorescence shows linear IgG and C3 deposition.

Dermatitis herpetiformis
Dermatitis herpetiformis is incorrect. Dermatitis herpetiformis results in intensely itchy vesicles, especially on extensor surfaces; immunofluorescence shows linear IgA deposition.

Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita
Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita is incorrect. Most types of epidermolysis bullosa (EB) are congenital; there are acquired forms (EB acquisita), which mostly resemble bullous pemphigoid rather than pemphigus; immunofluorescence similarly reveals linear IgG deposition.

Linear IgA disease.

stem: A 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes presents for review. She presents with small, intensely itchy, excoriated papules with a few vesicles. These are particularly present on her elbows, extensor forearms and buttocks. She has been treated in the past for chronic diarrhoea, presumed to be due to diabetic neuropathy. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Dermatitis herpetiformis
The clinical description is classical for dermatitis herpetiformis, which most commonly begins in early adulthood; vesicles are usually quickly excoriated so may not be seen. HLA associations (B8, DR3, DQ2 in 80–90% of cases) are similar to those for coeliac disease, which virtually always co-exists. Skin biopsy reveals subepidermal blisters with neutrophil microabscesses in the dermal papillae. On immunofluorescence, there is positive granular staining for IgA in the dermal papillae. The patient should have appropriate investigations for coeliac disease; particularly in this case, where there is a history of diarrhoea, there is likely to be villous atrophy on jejunal biopsy. Treatment is with a gluten-free diet; control of the skin disease may also require dapsone or other sulfur drugs. Dapsone may cause haemolysis and methaemoglobinaemia, as well as liver pathology and polyneuropathy, so regular monitoring of both liver enzymes and blood count is necessary; it is also associated with drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS).

Eczema
Eczema is incorrect. Eczema is typically itchy, but the clinical signs described in the scenario do not suggest it – ill-defined, erythematous plaques with fine scale would be typical.

Epidermolysis bullosa
Epidermolysis bullosa is incorrect. There are various forms of epidermolysis bullosa, which may be congenital or occasionally acquired. It typically leads to blistering at sites of minor trauma such as the hands and feet, although types range in severity from trivial to devastating.

Folliculitis related to diabetes
Folliculitis related to diabetes is incorrect. Folliculitis, which is usually due to staphylococcal infection, presents with pustules rather than vesicles and is not usually pruritic.

Linear IgA disease.

stem: An 18-year-old man presents with a purpuric rash on his buttocks and legs. There is joint pain and one vomit containing coffee grounds. Blood testing reveals mild eosinophilia and a small rise in IgA levels. Urine testing reveals non-visible haematuria. He is usually well but finished a course of amoxicillin for a bad throat infection two weeks prior. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Henoch–Schönlein purpura
Henoch–Schönlein purpura (HSP) presents with purpura in dependent areas (e.g. buttocks and lower legs) Aside from the vasculitic rash, typical features include abdominal pain and vomiting, with or without upper or lower gastrointestinal haemorrhage; nephritis or less commonly nephrotic syndrome can occur and 1–5% of cases progress to kidney failure; arthralgia is common, particularly in the legs Although it mostly occurs in children between 4 and 15 years of age, it may be seen at any age Most studies suggest a male preponderance with a male to female ratio of about 2:1 The pathophysiology is not fully understood, but HSP is mediated by IgA, with deposition of complexes in affected organs Antigen triggers may include Drugs Foods Immunisation Various infections There may be no specific abnormalities on blood testing, although IgA is elevated in 50% of cases; eosinophilia and thrombocytosis may be present The illness is usually self-limiting, with most cases settling within 6 weeks Treatment is largely supportive; more severe cases are treated with systemic corticosteroids or occasionally steroid-sparing immunosuppressants

Drug-induced vasculitis
Drug-induced vasculitis is incorrect. The clinical features described are classical for HSP, although amoxillicininduced vasculitis is a valid differential diagnosis.

Idiopathic thrombocytopaenic purpura
Idiopathic thrombocytopaenic purpura is incorrect. Idiopathic thrombocytopaenic purpura might explain the rash and gastrointestinal bleeding, but not the other features described.

Polyarteritis nodosa
Polyarteritis nodosa is incorrect. Polyarteritis nodosa, as another systemic vasculitis, could explain all of the features described; however, elevated IgA and the constellation of findings fit best with HSP.

Thrombotic thrombocytopaenic purpura.

stem: A 42-year-old man with a history of diabetes mellitus presents with a large lesion on his left shin that over time has become scarred and yellowish in the middle. On examination, you can see a 6cm lesion on the left shin. The centre of the lesion is waxy, yellow and atrophic, with prominent blood vessels and evidence of ulceration. The edges are red–brown in colour. He has bilateral peripheral neuropathy and doesn’t report the area as being particularly painful. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Necrobiosis lipoidica
The position and nature of the lesion seen here are typical for necrobiosis lipoidica. It is a rare condition that mainly affects diabetics. The lesion is usually painless, and can ulcerate following injury. Treatment is not always satisfactory and may include topical or intra-lesional steroids, and systemic agents such as cyclosporine.

Arterial ulcer
Arterial ulcer is incorrect. Arterial ulcers are common in the latter aspect of the lower leg and occur due to poor arterial circulation. They are painful, often deep, with a punched-out appearance and may be surrounded by pale, shiny and hairless atrophic skin.

Venous ulcer
Venous ulcer is incorrect. These frequently occur on the medial aspect of the lower shin (gaiter area) due to venous insufficiency and stasis of blood in the legs. Commonly they are associated with varicose veins, and venous eczema. Clinically the ulcer is weepy, often shallow, with sloping edges. Treatment aims to minimise venous pooling by using compression dressings.

Pyoderma gangrenosum
Pyoderma gangrenosum is incorrect. This is a very painful, rapidly enlarging ulcer with violaceous, undermined borders. It often occurs at sites of injury in patients with inflammatory bowel disease or rheumatoid arthritis. Treatment options include topical corticosteroids and calcineurin inhibitors, oral steroids and systemic agents such as cyclosporine.

Dermatitis artefacta.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with a lesion on the left side of the lower abdomen. She says this began as a raised lesion but rapidly enlarged to become an ulcer. There is a history of Crohn’s Disease, although this is currently well controlled with systemic agents. On examination, you can see a 4 cm, ulcerated area on the abdomen that is abutting an ileostomy and has a bluish discolouration around the edge and a necrotic, pus-filled core. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Patch testing series that include the stoma bag material
explanation:
Topical tacrolimus
Tacrolimus (a calcineurin inhibitor) as an ointment can be used topically in a similar way to steroids, in order to suppress inflammation. Tacrolimus is particularly effective against peristomal pyoderma gangrenosum, with an efficacy superior to that of clobetasol.

Cyclosporine
Cyclosporine is incorrect. The diagnosis here is of pyoderma gangrenosum, a painful, rapidly expanding ulcer with violaceous, undermined edges and a necrotic pus-filled centre. Diagnosis is mainly clinical as histological findings are non-specific. Cyclosporine is often used in the treatment but is usually reserved for severe cases that are refractory to topical interventions.

Wound debridement
Wound debridement is incorrect. One feature of pyoderma gangrenosum is that of pathergy, where new lesions appearance at sites of trauma. Therefore, debridement should be avoided during the active stage of the disease as it may result in worsening of the ulcer.

Patch testing series that include the stoma bag material
Patch testing series that include the stoma bag material is incorrect. Peristomal pyoderma gangrenosum is a well-recognised entity, especially in those with inflammatory bowel disease. These, coupled with the classical clinical findings described above, make for a straightforward diagnosis of pyoderma gangrenosum with no evidence of a contact allergic reaction.

Topical betamethasone.

stem: Which one of the following is a feature of the Sézary syndrome?
explanation:
T-cell malignancy
Sezary syndrome(SS) and mycosis fungoides (MF) are the most common subtypes of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma. These conditions are relevant to MRCP because of their characteristic cutaneous presentation with erythroderma, classically affecting a middle-aged male. MF and SS probably represent spectra of the same condition, with SS representing the more severe end of the spectrum. MF may present with solely with patches of erythematous skin change, whilst SS typically presents with widespread erythroderma (sometimes with keratoderma as well) accompanied by leukaemic infiltration of the bone marrow. Histology of the skin and bone marrow would be expected to demonstrate a common clonal proliferation of T cells (specifically CD4 +ve T helper type).

B-cell lymphoma
B-cell lymphoma is not a feature of the Sézary syndrome. The differential for cutaneous B-cell lymphoma includes follicular lymphoma, marginal zone lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

Macrophage disorder
Macrophage disorder is not a feature of the Sézary syndrome. Macrophages play major roles in many chronic diseases. Macrophage activation syndrome is a severe complication of childhood rheumatic disease, particularly systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis.

Natural killer cell deficiency
Natural killer cell deficiency is not a feature of the Sézary syndrome. Natural killer cells have cytolytic functions against tumour cells and virus-infected cells.

Neutrophil disease.

stem: A 55-year-old man has non-infective, necrotising ulcers on his lower limbs. A diagnosis of pyoderma gangrenosum is made. He is currently being investigated by his GP for lower back pain. Which one of the following underlying conditions is he most likely to have?
explanation:
Multiple myeloma
The diagnosis here is pyoderma gangrenosum. Pyoderma gangrenosum (PG) typically starts as inflammatory pustules or papules most commonly on the legs. These enlarge rapidly and the overlying skin breaks down to produce large necrotic ulcers with a sloughy base, and a raised, purplish, undermined border. It is often multifocal. Pain tends to be prominent. Many associations have been described, the strongest of which seem to be: Inflammatory bowel disease, either ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s disease Rheumatoid arthritis Haematological disorders including myeloid leukaemias, myelofibrosis, myeloma and monoclonal gammopathies Arthritides, especially rheumatoid disease Diabetes. Treatment is usually with topical and oral corticosteroids; various steroid-sparing agents are also used.

Autoimmune thrombocytopenia
Autoimmune thrombocytopenia is incorrect. There is no clear association between PG and autoimmune thrombocytopenia; there is a reported case of PG with idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura, but the patient also had an IgA monoclonal gammopathy, which is more likely to be relevant.

Gout
Gout is incorrect. Gout is not associated with PG, although various forms of inflammatory arthritis are.

Haemochromatosis
Haemochromatosis is incorrect. Haemochromatosis is not associated with PG, although cases in patients with hepatitis C and autoimmune hepatitis have been reported.

Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma.

stem: A 44-year-old woman has been admitted to hospital with pneumonia. She has now developed a rash on the palms and soles made up of lesions with concentric erythematous rings. She also complains of painful mouth ulcers. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Erythema multiforme
Erythema multiforme is a reactive eruption, which is charactised by target lesions (concentric rings with a least three hues per individual lesion); these tend to predominate at acral sites and mucosal involvement can take place. It is typically associated with infection, most commonly herpes simplex virus; it can also follow mycoplasma infection, as is likely in this scenario; it has been associated with a variety of other viral infections, including HIV and hepatitis viruses. Occasionally, erythema multiforme occurs as a drug eruption: culprit drugs include anticonvulsants, sulfonamides, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and penicillins.

Erythema nodosum
Erythema nodosum is incorrect. Erythema nodosum is a reactive panniculitis that gives rise to tender lumps usually on the shins.

Fixed drug eruption
Fixed drug eruption is incorrect. Fixed drug eruption leads to one or more discrete macules or plaques, sometimes with central blistering, following exposure to the causative drug; on rechallenge, the lesions reappear at exactly the same site.

Pemphigus vulgaris
Pemphigus vulgaris is incorrect. Pemphigus vulgaris is an immunobullous disease, which presents with superficial blistering and erosions, affecting skin and mucosal surfaces.

Toxic epidermal necrolysis.

stem: A 78-year-old man with a history of chronic venous insufficiency presents with a very well-demarcated area of intense erythema on the left leg. There is induration and a raised border. What organism is most likely to be responsible for this clinical picture?
explanation:
Group-A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus
This is the typical picture of erysipelas (also known as St Anthony’s fire), a superficial form of cellulitis caused by group-A Streptococcus (S. pyogenes). It is characterised by the distinctive warm, red, tender skin lesion with induration and a sharply defined, raised, rapidly advancing border. Vesicles or bullae may develop, and desquamation of the area may occur after 7–10 days. The face is also commonly affected. There is often an associated raised white blood cell count; blood cultures are only positive in 5% of affected patients. Culture of aspirated fluid has a low organism yield. Treatment of choice is intravenous or oral penicillin, depending on the severity of the lesion.

Haemophilus influenzae
Haemophilus influenzae is incorrect. H. influenzae sometimes causes cellulitis in babies, particularly affecting the head and neck.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is incorrect. P. aeruginosa is a common coloniser of ulcers, but rarely causes cellulitis.

Staphylococcus aureus
Staphylococcus aureus is incorrect. S. aureus commonly causes skin and soft tissue infection including cellulitis, but the clinical picture described is classical for erysipelas.

Viridans streptococci.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents to his GP with a rash on his legs. On examination, there are a number of discrete, tender, red nodules. He denies systemic symptoms and has no significant past medical history. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Erythema nodosum
Erythema nodosum is an acute panniculitis (inflammation in the fat) that produces tender nodules or plaques on the shins and occasionally elsewhere. Lesions are usually well circumscribed. The overlying skin is erythematous but otherwise normal, with no scaling. Firm induration is typical and the lesions may be exquisitely tender. It may be idiopathic, but is associated with: Sarcoidosis Inflammatory bowel disease Streptococcal infections Tuberculosis Treatment with sulfonamides or the oral contraceptive pill Pregnancy. Treatment is usually with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.

Erysipelas
Erysipelas is incorrect. Erysipelas is a form of cellulitis caused by group-A Streptococcus. It usually causes confluent erythema rather than discrete lesions and is not typically particularly tender. It is usually accompanied by fever and malaise.

Insect bites
Insect bites is incorrect. Most insect bite reactions are papular rather than nodular, and are itchy rather than tender. Occasionally, they may blister.

Leukocytoclastic vasculitis
Leukocytoclastic vasculitis is incorrect. Leukocytoclastic vasculitis leads to purpuric papules, rather than nodules. As this may be idiopathic, there may be no associated symptoms.

Post-traumatic ecchymoses.

stem: A 23-year-old man visits a local GP while on holiday in the UK from Australia. He has noted a lesion on his penis that was initially nodular and painless, but has progressed over time to form a heaped-up ulcer. Sampling from the lesion reveals large, infected, mononuclear cells containing many Donovan bodies. What diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Granuloma inguinale
Granuloma inguinale is an infection caused by Klebsiella granulomatis (previously known as Calymmatobacterium granulomatis). This is a Gram-negative bacillus that reproduces within neutrophils, plasma cells and histiocytes, causing the infected white cells to rupture with the release of 20–30 organisms. The key features are a primary, painless, indurated nodule that progresses to a heaped-up ulcer, and the presence of infected mononuclear cells containing many Donovan bodies (the infection is also known as donovanosis). The infection is endemic in Australia, India, the Caribbean and parts of Africa, and transmission is associated with unprotected sexual intercourse. Treatment is usually with doxycycline or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and patients are advised to refrain from sexual intercourse until the lesion has healed. Follow-up is advised to ensure complete resolution. Other options The finding of Donovan bodies invalidates all of the other options.

Chancroid
Chancroid is incorrect. Chancroid is caused by infection with Haemophilus ducreyi and leads to genital ulcers and lymphadenopathy, both of which are painful. It mainly occurs in Africa, the Caribbean and Southwest Asia.

Genital herpes
Genital herpes is incorrect. Genital herpes causes multiple painful vesicles which may result in erosions.

Lymphogranuloma venereum
Lymphogranuloma venereum is incorrect. Lymphogranuloma venereum results from specific Chlamydia strains. It begins with painless papules or ulcers, which quickly heal. These are followed several weeks later by painful enlargement of the inguinal lymph nodes (known as buboes).

Penile carcinoma.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is seen in the dermatology clinic with an acute episode of erythroderma. She has a history of chronic skin problems for which she has required ongoing treatment. What is the most likely underlying cause of her current presentation?
explanation:
Eczema
Erythroderma is the term applied to any inflammatory skin disorder covering in excess of 90% of the body surface. In adults, it is most commonly due to eczema and psoriasis. Other causes include - drug eruption, cutaneous lymphoma and pityriasis rubra pilaris. Complications of erythroderma are those resulting from skin failure, which include hypothermia, hypovolaemia, protein loss, electrolyte disturbances and increased susceptibility to infection. General management involves work-up to assess for the underlying diagnosis (if not already apparent) and any complications, resuscitation if indicated and application of greasy emollients to reduce transepidermal water loss. Specific treatment depends on the underlying diagnosis.

Drug eruption
A cutaneous adverse drug reaction may lead to erythroderma, but this is less likely in view of the history of preexisting skin disease.

Mycosis fungoides
Mycosis fungoides can lead to erythroderma, but this is much less common than eczema or psoriasis.

Pityriasis rubra pilaris
Pityriasis rubra pilaris is a rare skin condition of unknown aetiology. Features include extensive psoriasiform plaques with a rather orangey colour, palmoplantar hyperkeratosis and follicular plugging. Erythroderma can occur, classically with ‘islands of sparing’.

Underlying malignancy.

stem: A 47-year old man presents with multiple lustreless toenails. He has no past medical history, and there is no other skin or scalp lesion. What is the most appropriate investigation?
explanation:
Nail clippings for mycology
Nail clippings for mycology are most helpful here as the most common reason for lustreless or dystrophic nails is fungal infection. The nails are stained with potassium hydroxide (KOH) so that the dermatophytes can then be identified by microscopy.

Blood cultures
Blood cultures is incorrect. Given limited infection involving nails only, means that blood cultures are not indicated.

C-reactive protein (CRP)
CRP is incorrect. CRP is an acute phase protein, given therefore that there is local nail infection only, CRP is unlikely to be elevated.

Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
ESR is incorrect. Similar to CRP, ESR has no value given the very limited nature of the nail infection.

Wood’s lamp examination.

stem: A 27-year-old woman attends the clinic for review. She is skin type 1 and lived in Australia prior to moving to the UK. She is extremely concerned about a mole on her back. Which of the following features would make you most concerned about a possible melanoma?
explanation:
Diameter 7 mm
The ABCDE criteria were developed as an educational tool about melanomas and summarise the features which raise the possibility of a malignant melanoma: Asymmetry – if the two halves of the area of concern differ in shape Border – if the edges of the area are irregular or blurred Colour – the presence of several colours is more worrying, for example if there are different shades of black, brown and pink Diameter – most melanomas are at least 6 mm in diameter Expert – Evolving or Expanding- if a mole changes in size, shape or colour. Or indeed starts bleeding/ scabbing . ‘if in doubt, check it out!’ Therefore, blue-black in colour, regular border, smoothly raised region and uniform pigmentation are all nonconcerning features and can very easily be seen in a benign mole. However, a diameter of 7 mm is really quite large and should prompt specialist review, especially in someone of skin type 1 with a history of lots of sun exposure, as would be expected living in Australia. Other risk factors for melanoma include a positive family history for melanoma, use of sunbeds, previous sunburn and having many moles.

Blue or black in colour
Blue-black in colour is incorrect. As long as the colour is uniform, darker pigmentation doesn’t signify increased risk of malignancy.

Regular border
Regular border is incorrect. It’s an irregular border that signifies increased risk of malignancy.

Smoothly raised lesion
Smoothly raised lesion, is incorrect. It’s irregular character to the shape of the mole which signifies risk.

Uniform pigmentation.

stem: A 54-year-old woman who works outdoors as a building surveyor presents with a red, scaly rash affecting her face, scalp, neck and hands. She is concerned that the areas affecting her scalp are causing bald patches. Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) are negative. Some earlier lesions are now scarring and showing change in pigmentation. What is the diagnosis that fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Discoid lupus erythematosus
All of the features described fit with this condition. DLE is also known as chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus It is characterised by well-demarcated, scaly, erythematous plaques in sun-exposed areas These result in scarring, which can result in patchy alopecia in hair-bearing areas such as the scalp; postinflammatory hyper- and hypopigmentation may be striking It is more common in women; only a minority of patients presenting with DLE will progress to systemic lupus erythematosus, and ANA is typically negative The diagnosis is usually confirmed histologically Meticulous sun protection is important and initial treatment otherwise is with very potent topical steroids (this is one of the few indications for high-potency steroid use on the face) Second-line therapy includes antimalarials, usually hydroxychloroquine, immunosuppressants and acitretin

Eczema
Eczema, is incorrect as this is not usually photodistributed and does not result in alopecia.

Lichen planus
Lichen planus, is incorrect as this is not photodistributed. One of its forms, known as lichen planopilaris, does cause scarring alopecia on the scalp, but it is very unusual for this to occur elsewhere.

Psoriasis
Psoriasis, is incorrect, as this does not lead to scarring or alopecia.

Tinea capitis et corporis.

stem: Which one of the following would be the most appropriate long-term management in this case?
explanation:
Switch to nitrile gloves
This nurse unfortunately has developed a contact allergy to latex; withdrawal of the latex challenge is the intervention of choice. In the long term, latex rechallenge may lead to increasingly severe allergic reactions, and several prosecutions have occurred within the context of the NHS over latex allergy.

Oral corticosteroids
Oral corticosteroids is incorrect. Oral corticosteroids may be used in severe allergy for short-term relief, but not for long-term management.

Topical antihistamine cream
Topical antihistamine cream is incorrect. Topical antihistamines may themselves lead to skin hypersensitivity, ergo they should be avoided.

Topical corticosteroid cream
Topical corticosteroid cream is incorrect. A topical corticosteroid cream may be used for short-term relief from severe allergies, but not for long-term management.

Topical tacrolimus.

stem: A 19-year-old student has just returned to university for the start of the spring term. He gives a history of a dry, red patch of skin on his chest, which was followed about 3 days later by the development of asymptomatic oval macules of about 1cm in diameter over the rest of his trunk; these are pink and slightly scaly. He is otherwise well. Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Pityriasis rosea
The first clinical lesion to appear in pityriasis rosea is known as the ‘herald patch’, an isolated erythematous, scaly plaque appearing on the trunk. Multiple oval macules appear, typically around 2–4 days later, predominantly on the trunk in a “Christmas tree” configuration; the proximal limbs may also be affected. Involvement of the hands, feet or scalp is rare. Severe itching is uncommon and the eruption is usually asymptomatic. Pityriasis rosea usually remits without treatment within 4–8 weeks. Cases occur with increasing frequency in spring and autumn, suggesting a possible viral aetiology.

Darier’s disease
Darier’s disease is incorrect. This is a genodermatosis, which would not typically present acutely. It is characterised by warty papules in seborrhoeic areas (e.g. scalp, central chest and back), and there may be palmar pits and nail dystrophy.

Guttate psoriasis
Guttate psoriasis is incorrect. This can present similarly to pityriasis rosea with acute-onset, asymptomatic, superficial, scaly plaques. However, the lesions are often smaller (around 0.5cm) and classically follow a streptococcal infection. The history of a herald patch makes pityriasis rosea clearly the best answer here.

Pityriasis versicolor
Pityriasis versicolor is incorrect. This is caused by overgrowth of the (usually) commensal yeast, Malassezia furfur. It typically presents in young adults in warm weather or after a sunny holiday, with asymptomatic hypoor sometimes hyperpigmented macules with very fine peripheral scaling; it is usually confined to the trunk. The history of a herald patch makes pityriasis rosea clearly the best answer here.

Secondary syphilis.

stem: A 34-year-old pet-shop owner presents with a bald patch on his scalp. He has noticed it increasing in size over the past couple of weeks and the area is beginning to itch. On examination there is inflammatory change and some skin scaling. Examination under Wood’s lamp reveals bright-green immunofluorescence. Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Microsporum canis infection
Tinea capitis is the term given to fungal (dermatophyte) infection of the scalp. Most cases are due to either Trichophyton tonsurans or M. canis. Tinea capitis is much more common in young children than other age groups. M. canis is a zoophilic dermatophyte, which despite its name is usually acquired from infected cats. M. canis displays characteristic green fluorescence when illuminated under Wood’s lamp (ultraviolet [UV] light with a wavelength > 365 nm). Diagnosis is confirmed via direct microscopy of scrapings, brushings or plucked hairs suspended in potassium hydroxide, preferably followed by successful culture. Tinea capitis always requires treatment with systemic antifungals, usually terbinafine; alternatives are itraconazole, or griseofulvin, which is licensed for young children.

Alopecia areata
Alopecia areata is incorrect. Although this typically leads to bald patches, there are no associated skin changes and no fluorescence under Wood’s lamp.

Psoriasis
Psoriasis is incorrect. This almost never leads to significant alopecia, and there is no fluorescence under Wood’s lamp.

Seborrhoeic dermatitis
Seborrhoeic dermatitis is incorrect. This is a diffuse rather than localised condition; it does not lead to alopecia and there is no fluorescence under Wood’s lamp.

Trichophyton rubrum infection.

stem: A 24-year-old woman is referred by her GP with a number of large boil-like lesions that have appeared on her back over the course of a few days. She is awaiting investigations by a gastroenterologist for diarrhoea and has been found to be anaemic. On examination in the dermatology clinic, three out of the four lesions have broken down, leaving large ulcerated painful areas. Which diagnosis fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Pyoderma gangrenosum
Many associations have been described, the strongest of which seem to be: inflammatory bowel disease (as suggested by the scenario), either ulcerative colitis or Crohn’s disease haematological disorders, including myeloid leukaemias, myelofibrosis, myeloma and monoclonal gammopathies arthritides especially rheumatoid disease diabetes. Each lesion typically begins with a papule or pustule, most commonly on the leg; it is often multifocal. Lesions rapidly enlarge and break down to form painful, necrotic ulcers; these may be deep and purulent, and the border is undermined and violaceous. Patients with inflammatory bowel disease may develop PG adjacent to a stoma. Treatment options include: very potent topical steroids prednisolone cyclosporine or other immunosuppressive agents dapsone tetracycline antibiotics (for their anti-inflammatory effects).

Erythema induratum
Erythema induratum is a type of panniculitis (inflammation of the fat) associated with tuberculosis. It presents with tender red lumps; ulceration is possible but not typical. While one might postulate intestinal tuberculosis and associated erythema induratum, the limited information in the scenario makes inflammatory bowel disease with pyoderma gangrenosum the better choice.

Erythema multiforme
Erythema multiforme is incorrect. This typically presents with target lesions, which sometimes blister centrally but do not ulcerate.

Necrobiosis lipoidica
Necrobiosis lipoidica is incorrect. This usually presents on the legs with atrophic, yellowish plaques. Ulceration can occur due to the atrophy, but is secondary to trauma.

Pyogenic granuloma.

stem: An 18-year-old man who has used topical corticosteroids for many years for eczema comes to the clinic with a new rash. He has an extensive rash consisting of 2–5mm violet/red papules affecting his wrists, forearms, legs and genitals. He tells you that he finds the rash itchy, particularly at night. There is no other past medical history of note, although he has recently completed a course of amoxicillin for a respiratory tract infection. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lichen planus
The distribution and character of the rash seen here fits best with a diagnosis of lichen planus. The cause of lichen planus is unknown, although in all likelihood it is an immune-mediated disorder, occurring most commonly in patients above the age of 45 years, although in reality it can present at any age. Topical steroids are considered first-line therapy for lichen planus, although evidence supporting their use is weak. Evidence exists for a number of topical and systemic steroid-sparing agents.

Drug reaction
Drug reaction is incorrect. Drug reactions commonly lead to a generalised rash.

Eczema herpeticum
Eczema herpeticum is incorrect. Eczema herpeticum occurs in areas of pre-existing eczema.

Scabies
Scabies is incorrect. In scabies the itching/rash is most severe in the webspaces of the hands feet and genital region.

Worsening eczema.

stem: A 27-year-old patient with ileocaecal Crohn’s disease presents to his GP with a non-pruritic rash on his right leg which has been progressing in the last 2 weeks. The rash looks like a collection of discrete pustules, some of which had coalesced to form what looks like an ulcer. There are no other rashes and his nails look normal. He has no other past medical history and is on azathioprine and infliximab for the Crohn’s disease. What is the most likely diagnosis for the rash?
explanation:
Pyoderma gangrenosum
Pyoderma gangrenosum is an extra intestinal manifestation of IBD and occurs in up to 2% of patients. It can occur anywhere on the body but is common on the legs. It starts off as discrete pustules which then coalesce and form ulcerations with erythematous or violacious edges. Treatment involves topical wound management and high dose steroids with or without minocycline. Recurrence is common.

Erythema nodosum
Erythema nodosum is incorrect. Erythema nodosum is the most common cutaneous manifestation of IBD affecting women more than men. They are characterised by tender warm nodules, typically on the shins. Histology reveals septal panniculitis.

Vasculitis
Vasculitis is incorrect. Vasculitis is a known adverse reaction related to anti-TNF therapy such as infliximab. The most common presentation is of purpura on the upper or lower extremities, and they may be accompanied by fevers, fatigue, arthralgia, peripheral neuropathy or abdominal pain.

Pustular psoriasis secondary to infliximab
Pustular psoriasis secondary to infliximab is incorrect. Pustular psoriasis can occur due to infliximab therapy and presents with scattered pustules or vesicles, typically on the trunk.

Sweets syndrome.
